results.summary: Exploratory, post-hoc analysis (about 49 tests, no multiplicity correction) of why plain int4 collapses on 4 of 55 models (retention below 0.5) and degrades on 8 (below 0.95). Plain int4 uses one scale per token vector (float16 of the max absolute component, levels -7..7), so one large component sets the step for all other components of that token. The data point to two failure signatures, one where only int4 fails and one where int4 and binary fail together. Both are repaired by mean-centring. Dimension, dtype, vectors per page, baseline score and family do not explain the collapse. The geometry reports cover too few datasets to test the shared-mean hypothesis. Raw vectors were not kept, so every mechanism is inferred from retention tables. Modality is fully confounded with dataset. I could not write REPORT.md because the harness refused report files from subagents, so the full report is this structured output and the scripts and tables are in the research folder.
data_issues: In measured.json the 14 text-model entries labelled metric ndcg@5 actually hold ndcg@10. The baseline equals the wide-file ndcg@10 baseline exactly and the retention differs from the true ndcg@5 retention by up to 0.0325 (mean 0.0058). Image entries match ndcg@5 exactly (checked in s02_consistency.py). This analysis used the wide-file ndcg@5 wherever available.

The raw vectors were not kept, so mean-vector norm, outlier coordinates and anisotropy cannot be computed for any collapsed model. The geometry reports cover only 7 datasets (ColPali v1.3 on two splits, colqwen2-v1.0-merged on two, colqwen2.5-v0.2 on two, answerai-colbert-small on SciFact).

Four models (answerai-colbert-small-v1, colpali-v1.3-merged, colqwen2-v1.0-merged, colqwen2.5-v0.2) have only the older measured.json labels ('none > int4' etc.). Their int4(mean) is missing, and the campaign wide files cover only 47 of 55 models.

Four wide files (nemotron 4B/8B, tomoro-4b, colqwen3.5-4.5B-v3) have no model id in the encoder field, so I mapped them by file name. The encoder dtype field is mostly None for text models, so inference dtype is unknown for 16 text-model entries.

Retention is relative to float16-inference baselines for 13 image models, including Nemotron 8B and EVIE (no float32 encode exists). The EVIE-8B run used a 1024-token page budget, which differs from the other models.

The most informative missing data points were never measured: nvidia llama-nemotron-colembed-vl-3b-v2 (3072 dimensions) failed at encoding, and the two llama-nemoretriever models and ColVec1.1-4b are unmeasured.

CIs in the source files are bootstrap over queries and ignore corpus sampling. DocVQA and InfoVQA rows for the same model are not independent, so model-level means treat them as replicates. Hub download counts are missing for EvoQwen2.5 and are 0 for some merged repos.
I did not write REPORT.md because the harness refused report files from subagents, so the report text is this output. Scripts, tables and toy.json are in the research folder.

findings.title: Collapse is a stable model property, repaired by centring, and not caused by dtype or token count
findings.claim: Nemotron 4B and 8B lose nearly everything under plain int4 on both datasets, while centred int4, int8, binary and lloyd2 hold. So the damage comes from how plain int4 allocates its range, not from lost information. Centred int4 is at least 0.98 in 86 of 88 rows. The two exceptions are LateOn (0.948) and colpali-v1.3-hf DocVQA (0.975).
findings.evidence: Plain int4 retention on Nemotron is 0.004 to 0.011 on both datasets, and every 95% CI upper bound is at most 0.021. In the same rows centred int4 is 0.996 to 1.002, int8 is 0.989 to 1.002 and binary is 0.989 to 0.998. The 4B was run in float32 and the 8B in float16, and both collapse. Plain int4 applied after hierarchical_merge keeps the collapse (0.005 to 0.014 relative to the merged-only score). EVIE-4.5B and EVIE-8B, float16 at 2048 and 4096 dimensions, retain 1.001 and 1.001 (CI width under 0.01).
findings.method: Descriptive table of per-model retentions from the wide files plus the measured.json fill-ins, and CI inspection. Source CIs are query bootstraps, which ignore corpus sampling.
findings.confounds: Only 2 Nemotron checkpoints, which are siblings. The 8B baseline is float16 inference. Retention above 1 is noise. The 4B/8B pair shares a backbone and training recipe, so the replication is weaker than 4 rows suggest.
findings.practical_implication: Plain int4 should stay out of default search spaces (it already is), and centred int4 or int8 should be the documented 4-bit and 8-bit paths. Nemotron needs centring.
findings.question: int4-collapse

verdict.recomputed: Recomputed from measured.json and the wide/campaign files (scripts a.py, b.py, c.py in the folder). Nemotron plain int4 retention: 4B 0.009 (DocVQA) and 0.004 (InfoVQA); 8B 0.011 and 0.007. CI upper bounds: 0.018, 0.008, 0.021, 0.014, so all are at most 0.021. Centred int4 on the same rows: 0.997/0.998, 1.002, 0.996, 0.999-1.002. Int8 is 0.989-1.002, binary 0.989-0.998 and lloyd2 0.987-1.000. Plain int4 after hierarchical_merge(0.33 or 0.25) is 0.004-0.014, which stays collapsed. Registry evidence confirms the 4B baseline is float32 and the 8B baseline is float16. EVIE-4.5B and EVIE-8B plain int4 are 0.999-1.003 (CI half-width under 0.007) and centred int4 is 0.999-1.001. The 86/88 count reproduces: of 88 model-dataset rows with both codecs, centred int4 retention is below 0.98 only for LateOn SciFact and colpali-v1.3-hf DocVQA (0.975). LateOn is 0.951 in measured.json and 0.948 in the wide file, so the stated 0.948 matches the wide file only. Across all 88 rows, plain int4 is below 0.9 in 8, namely 4 Nemotron rows plus mxbai-edge-17m (0.27), LateOn (0.30-0.28), mLateOn (0.77-0.75) and mxbai-edge-32m (0.79). Plain int4 is at least 0.93 for every other row. Six model-dataset pairs (answerai, colpali-v1.3-merged, colqwen2-v1.0-merged, colqwen2.5-v0.2) have no int4 rows, so 88 is not the full count.
verdict.issues:
1. "Stable model property" rests on 2 sibling checkpoints, which is effectively one backbone and recipe replicated across 2 datasets. Dtype is not isolated: 4B float32 vs 8B float16 also differ in size and dimension (2560 vs 4096). The argument that dtype is not the cause is only that EVIE float16 does not collapse. That is consistent but indirect, since model differs along with dtype.
2. "Centred int4 repairs it" holds for Nemotron. It is not general: for LateOn centred int4 only recovers to 0.948 from 0.28 (below the 0.98 bar, CI [0.917,0.977]), and for mLateOn plain int4 is 0.75 while centred is 1.001. The 2 exceptions are named, but the claim implies a clean repair story. Partial collapses elsewhere (4 of 8 rows below 0.9 are text models) show the pattern is a continuum, not unique to Nemotron.
3. "Binary and lloyd2 hold" is true for Nemotron but not in general: mLateOn binary 0.71, LateOn lloyd2 0.82 and mLateOn lloyd2 0.935. So the "not lost information" inference is true for Nemotron but those codecs are not safe elsewhere.
4. The mechanism (range allocation, probably a dominant mean or outlier direction) is inferred from the centred fix and was not directly measured. No per-dimension range or vector statistic was checked here. It is plausible and the stage code (a per-vector max-abs scale on the uncentred vector) matches it, but the mechanism is not demonstrated.
5. The merged-then-int4 numbers are relative to the original baseline. Relative to the merged-only score they are similar (0.014/0.992), so the claim holds.
6. CIs are query bootstraps over 450-500 queries on 500 pages. Corpus sampling is ignored, but the collapse is 2 orders of magnitude beyond any such uncertainty, so this does not affect the main point. It matters more for the 0.975 and 0.948 exceptions. Retention above 1 is noise. Exploratory post-hoc, with 2 codec comparisons across 88 rows and no formal tests; the descriptive comparison needs none.
7. Nemotron-3B-v2 was never measured (killed for memory), so the 2-checkpoint count is an upper bound.
verdict.corrected_claim: Plain int4 collapses to about 0.004-0.011 retention on both Nemotron checkpoints (4B float32 baseline, 8B float16 baseline) on DocVQA and InfoVQA (all 95% CI upper bounds at most 0.021, query-bootstrap), while centred int4, int8, binary and lloyd2 stay at 0.987-1.002. The collapse also survives hierarchical merging. EVIE float16 (2048 and 4096 dimensions) does not collapse (0.999-1.003). This is consistent with the damage coming from how plain int4 sets its per-vector range rather than from information loss, but that mechanism is inferred, not measured. Since the two Nemotron models are siblings, it counts as one model family replicated across 2 datasets, so dtype and token count are made unlikely as causes but not isolated. Plain int4 is a model-dependent, graded risk: 8 of 88 rows are below 0.9, including 4 text-model rows (mxbai-edge-17m 0.27, LateOn 0.28-0.30, mLateOn 0.75-0.77, mxbai-edge-32m 0.79). Centred int4 is at least 0.98 in 86 of 88 rows, the exceptions being LateOn SciFact (0.948 wide file, 0.951 measured.json) and colpali-v1.3-hf DocVQA (0.975). Centring does not rescue every collapsing model (LateOn stays below 0.98), and binary and lloyd2 are not safe in general (mLateOn binary 0.71, LateOn lloyd2 0.82).

findings.title: Two failure signatures: int4-only collapse versus int4 and binary failing together
findings.claim: The 8 degraded models split by their binary score. Nemotron 4B/8B and LateOn keep binary at 0.98 or above while int4 fails, which is what a few coordinates setting the per-vector scale would produce. Four text models (mxbai-edge-17m, mxbai-edge-32m, mLateOn, GTE-ModernColBERT) lose int4 and binary by almost the same amount, which fits a shared offset across many coordinates making the signs uninformative. Centring repairs the second group to 0.987 to 1.001. LateOn is the exception: centred int4 reaches only 0.948 against binary 0.981.
findings.evidence: Signature A (int4 deficit, binary deficit): Nemotron 4B (0.994, 0.007), Nemotron 8B (0.991, 0.006), LateOn (0.718, 0.019). Signature B: mxbai-17m (0.765, 0.715), mxbai-32m (0.220, 0.252), mLateOn (0.248, 0.289), GTE (0.073, 0.118), answerai (0.103, 0.059). In the 5 models with binary retention of 0.95 or below, int4 and binary deficits correlate with Pearson 0.988 (p=0.002) and Spearman 0.90 (p=0.037). Across all 15 text models Spearman(int4, binary) is 0.60 (p=0.019, bootstrap CI -0.00 to 0.95), and for 40 image models it is 0.12 (p=0.46). A synthetic toy (not real data) shows a single-coordinate offset collapsing int4 with binary and int8 intact, a dense offset collapsing int4 and binary together, and centring fixing both. int8 stays at 0.989 to 1.002 in all collapsed rows.
findings.method: Model-level deficit comparison, Pearson and Spearman with bootstrap CIs over models, and a numpy toy that mirrors the package's int4, int8 and binary rules. The toy is mechanism illustration only.
findings.confounds: Only 8 degraded models, and a post-hoc split on binary retention at 0.95. Signature B is 5 text models on one dataset, with two mxbai siblings. The toy uses synthetic offsets and a topic-retrieval task, so it cannot show that real vectors have these offsets. The vectors were not kept, so neither the outlier nor the shared-offset account can be checked directly.
findings.practical_implication: A 1-bit versus 4-bit comparison on a vector sample can tell the two cases apart cheaply. A pre-flight check on max abs component times sqrt(d) over the vector norm, and on cosine to the corpus mean, is a candidate screen, but it is untested and needs vectors saved from the next batch.
findings.question: int4-collapse

verdict.recomputed:
The per-model numbers reproduce. I recomputed them from the campaign wide JSONs ("retention:ndcg@5") and from measured.json.

Wide-file deficits (1 minus retention):
- mxbai-17m: int4 0.765, binary 0.715.
- mxbai-32m: int4 0.220, binary 0.252.
- mLateOn: int4 0.248, binary 0.289.
- GTE-ModernColBERT: int4 0.073, binary 0.118.
- LateOn: int4 0.718, binary 0.019. Centred int4 is 0.948 against binary 0.981.
- Centred int4 for the four Signature B text models is 0.987 to 1.001.
- int8 is 0.990 to 1.002 in those collapsed rows.
- Nemotron 4B and 8B have int4 retention of 0.004 to 0.011 and binary of 0.989 to 0.998, on both DocVQA and InfoVQA.

measured.json gives somewhat different values for the same models (for example mLateOn int4 retention 0.765 against 0.752 in the wide files). The claim uses the wide-file values.

Correlations:
- Text models, Spearman(int4, binary): I get 0.635 (p=0.015) on the 14 wide-file text models that have all four labels. The claim has 0.60 on 15. The measured.json version gives 0.65 on 14. The bootstrap CI I got on measured.json is 0.08 to 0.97, so it is wide.
- Image models, per-model mean over datasets: Spearman 0.07 for 37 models, which does not conflict with the claim's 0.12 for 40.
- Five-model subset (binary retention 0.95 or below, using the claim's numbers): Pearson 0.988 and Spearman 0.90, as claimed. An exact permutation p for Spearman 0.90 at n=5 is 0.042 one-sided, so about 0.08 two-sided. The claim's 0.037 comes from scipy's t approximation, and I do not reproduce it.

Robustness of the five-model subset (Pearson, Spearman):
- Drop mxbai-17m: 0.934, 0.80.
- Drop mxbai-32m: 0.989, 0.80.
- Drop mLateOn: 0.991, 0.80.
- Drop GTE: 0.987, 1.00.
- Drop answerai: 0.999, 1.00.
- Drop both mxbai siblings, leaving 3 models: 0.917, 0.50. At n=3 this is uninformative.

Ratio of int4 deficit to binary deficit in Signature B:
- 17m: 1.07
- 32m: 0.87
- mLateOn: 0.86
- GTE: 0.62
- answerai: 1.75

The deficits are close but not equal. The scripts are b.py, c.py and d.py.
verdict.issues:
1. The empirical split is real. Nemotron and LateOn lose int4 only. The four text models lose int4 and binary by similar amounts. Centring repairs int4 for those four, and int8 is intact throughout.
2. The 5-model correlation (r=0.988) is weak evidence. The set is selected on binary retention of 0.95 or below, which is post-hoc and based on the outcome. It has n=5, including two mxbai siblings, and all five are text models on one dataset. The Spearman p of 0.037 is optimistic. The exact permutation p is about 0.04 one-sided, and not significant at conventional levels once the post-hoc selection is counted. Spearman falls to 0.5 on the three non-mxbai models.
3. The 15-model Spearman CI includes about 0. In my measured.json bootstrap it excludes 0 only barely, from 0.08. The claim's own CI of -0.00 to 0.95 is borderline. The overall text correlation is likely driven by the same degraded models plus several mild binary-only losers, such as LFM2.5 with binary deficit 0.23 and int4 deficit 0.016. Those models show binary loss without int4 loss, which is a third pattern the two-signature story does not address.
4. The two signatures are a dichotomy chosen after seeing the data, with 8 models. Nothing was run on the mechanism itself, so the account is a hypothesis. A few coordinates setting the per-vector scale and a shared offset across many coordinates are the proposed causes. The vectors were not kept, and the toy only illustrates the idea. A direct check would be per-model kurtosis, max-to-median coordinate ratio and mean-offset norm, which needs the vectors.
5. "Almost the same amount" overstates GTE, whose int4 deficit is 0.62 of its binary deficit, and answerai, which the claim lists among Signature B, whose int4 deficit is 1.75 times its binary one. answerai is not in the campaign wide set I could recompute, so its figures were taken from the claim.
6. The image result (no int4-binary link) is confounded with dataset and modality. Nemotron is image, and the Signature B models are all text on SciFact.
7. LateOn's centred int4 of 0.948 does fall short of the other four, so a single account does not cover it. The claim says as much.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among 8 degraded models, two descriptive patterns appear, identified post hoc. (A) Nemotron 4B and 8B (image) and LateOn (text) lose int4 almost entirely while binary stays at 0.98 or above. (B) mxbai-edge 17m and 32m, mLateOn, GTE-ModernColBERT and possibly answerai (all text, SciFact) lose int4 and binary by similar but not equal amounts, with int4 deficit between 0.6 and 1.75 times the binary deficit. Centring repairs int4 for the four Signature B models I could recompute to 0.987 to 1.001, and for LateOn only to 0.948. int8 is intact. The correlation across Signature B models (r=0.99, n=5, two of them siblings, grouped by a post-hoc binary cutoff) is suggestive only. The exact permutation p is about 0.04 one-sided, and Spearman falls to 0.5 without the mxbai pair. The explanations (outlier coordinates setting the scale versus a shared offset) are untested hypotheses supported only by a synthetic toy. The text-model Spearman of 0.6 across all text models (n=14 or 15) has a CI that reaches zero. The image/text contrast is confounded with dataset.

findings.title: Token merging amplifies plain-int4 loss on text models but not image models
findings.claim: Applying plain int4 after hierarchical_merge hurts text models more than plain int4 alone, and more so at the heavier merge. This is consistent with merging averaging away token-specific residual while a shared offset survives. It is not seen on image models, apart from the already-collapsed Nemotron.
findings.evidence: Text, 28 rows: median merged-int4 relative to merge-only is 0.976, against 0.982 for plain int4 alone. The paired Wilcoxon gives p=0.0007, and 54% of rows lose more than 1 extra point. Image, 148 rows: medians are 0.999 for both, p=0.78. LFM2-ColBERT-350M falls from 0.980 to 0.585 relative (merge 0.33) and 0.648 (merge 0.25), while its centred version holds at 0.97 to 1.00. The merge-0.25 value is lower than merge-0.33 in 11 of 14 text models (higher in 2); on image models the split is 12 lower and 9 higher. Text rank agreement between plain int4 alone and merge-0.25 plus int4 is rho 0.95. After merge, centred int4 stays at least 0.97 of merge-only in all but 3 of 176 rows; the 3 are LateOn at 0.92 and LFM2 at 0.968.
findings.method: Ratio of the plain-int4-after-merge retention to the merge-only retention from the wide files (ndcg@5), then paired Wilcoxon, sign counts and Spearman, split by modality.
findings.confounds: Modality equals dataset, so this cannot be separated from SciFact geometry. The ratio uses merge-only retention, which is itself noisy and low for some models. Two merge levels per model are not independent. LateOn after centring still loses 7 to 8 points relative, so a shared mean is not the whole story for it.
findings.practical_implication: A model that looks safe for plain int4 alone (LFM2-ColBERT at 0.98) can become unsafe once pooled. A codec choice made before merging should be re-checked after the full pipeline, and centred int4 should be preferred in stacked pipelines.
findings.question: int4-collapse

verdict.recomputed:
From the wide files (92 files, 176 model-dataset-merge rows) I recomputed these:
- Text, 28 rows, 14 models: median merged-int4 / merge-only is 0.976, against 0.9816 for plain int4 alone. Row-level paired Wilcoxon p=0.0007. 53.6% of rows lose more than 1 extra point.
- Image, 148 rows, 41 models: medians are 0.9990 against 0.9992, p=0.78. Per-model p=1.0.
- LFM2-ColBERT-350M: merge-only 0.858 (merge 0.33) and 0.755 (merge 0.25). Merged-int4 is 0.502 and 0.489 in absolute terms, so 0.585 and 0.648 relative to merge-only.
- Centred int4 after merge stays at or above 0.97 of merge-only in all but 3 of 176 rows: LateOn 0.927 and 0.922, LFM2 0.968. All three are text rows.
- The per-model analysis (14 text models, merge levels averaged) is below. The row-level numbers above are as claimed; the model-level ones are the ones to trust.
  - Merged-int4 relative to merge-only is worse than int4 alone in 12 models and better in 2.
  - The median model-level difference is -1.25 points.
  - A bootstrap over models gives a 95% interval of [-9.7, -0.1] points for the median difference.
  - The Wilcoxon p is 0.011, not 0.0007.
  - Without LFM2 the p is 0.027, with the same median difference.
- The model-level medians are almost identical: 0.9808 for merged-int4 against 0.9816 for int4 alone.
- The difference is driven by a few models. The largest per-model differences are LFM2 -36 points, mLateOn -13, LateOn -11 and mxbai-edge -10. The next is GTE-ModernColBERT at -3.6.
- Merge 0.25 is lower than merge 0.33 in 11 text models and higher in 3. The claim says 11 and 2.
- For images the count is 45 lower and 29 higher across the 74 model-datasets, not 12 and 9. The claim's unit probably differs.
- Image rows lose almost nothing under plain int4 alone (median 0.9992), so there is little to amplify. Part of the contrast is a ceiling effect.
- I did not recompute the rho of 0.95 or the Nemotron exception.
verdict.issues:
1. Pseudo-replication. The p=0.0007 treats the 28 rows as independent, but they are two merge levels of 14 models. At model level p=0.011. The interval for the median difference nearly touches zero.
2. A tail drives it. Four models (LFM2, mLateOn, LateOn, mxbai-edge) carry most of the effect, and the median model barely moves, with medians of 0.981 against 0.982. "Hurts text models more" overstates a typical effect of about 1 point.
3. Dataset and modality are confounded. SciFact versus the two ViDoRe sets cannot be separated from text versus image. Image int4 is near the ceiling, so there is little room for amplification.
4. The mechanism is only a hypothesis. LateOn still loses 7 to 8 points after centring, so a shared mean is not the full explanation.
5. Merge-only retention is itself low for text, with a minimum of 0.755. A ratio against a noisy denominator inflates the apparent effect.
6. Counts differ slightly from the claim. The merge-0.25-below-0.33 split in text is 11 against 3, not 11 against 2. The image split depends on the unit used.
7. This is post-hoc exploratory analysis. I ran roughly 10 tests.
8. The float16-inference baselines were not examined.
verdict.corrected_claim: On SciFact text models, plain int4 after hierarchical_merge loses more than int4 alone. The median per-model gap is about 1.25 points relative to merge-only (bootstrap 95% interval roughly -10 to 0 points; model-level Wilcoxon p about 0.01). It is concentrated in a few models: LFM2-ColBERT (-36 points), mLateOn, LateOn and mxbai-edge. Centred int4 is nearly unaffected, with 3 exceptions among 28 text rows. On ViDoRe image models no effect is detectable (medians 0.999 for both, p=0.78), but plain int4 alone costs almost nothing there, so there is little room to amplify. The text-versus-image difference cannot be separated from the dataset, and the shared-offset explanation is untested.

findings.title: Dimension, dtype, vectors per page, baseline and family do not predict collapse
findings.claim: No simple registry attribute explains the pattern. Width is not sufficient (EVIE at 2048 and 4096 dimensions is fine while Nemotron collapses), float32 and float16 inference behave alike, and family explains little (lightonai text models span 0.282 to 1.002). The text-versus-image gap is large but cannot be attributed to modality.
findings.evidence: Model-level Spearman with plain-int4 retention: log2 dimension 0.12 (n=55, bootstrap CI -0.20 to 0.42); vectors per page 0.27 (CI -0.01 to 0.50); baseline nDCG -0.01 (image), -0.42 (text, p=0.11) and 0.09 (all). Float32 versus float16-inference image models: Mann-Whitney p=0.62 (n=26 and 13, one collapse in each) and p=0.98 within 128-d. Image models at 128 to 640 dimensions: 0 of 36 degraded (exact 95% upper bound 0.097). Degraded: 6 of 15 text and 2 of 40 image (Fisher OR 12.7, p=0.0034); for collapse below 0.5 it is 2 of 15 versus 2 of 40 (p=0.30). Within image models, DocVQA and InfoVQA plain-int4 ranks correlate at rho 0.24 (n=40), or 0.12 without Nemotron, so outside the collapsed models the variation is noise around 1.0. Collapse prevalence is 4 of 55 models, and the 8 degraded models hold 22% of the measured set's Hub downloads (the 4 collapsed ones 1%).
findings.method: Spearman with bootstrap CI over models, Mann-Whitney, Fisher exact, Clopper-Pearson bounds, all at model level (mean over datasets).
findings.confounds: Modality, dataset, tokenizer family and lab are all confounded. Only 4 models are 2048 dimensions or wider (2 families). The 16 text models have unknown dtype. Two datasets treated as replicates. Few models per family, with correlated siblings. Because the collapsed set is only 4 models, null results here have low power.
findings.practical_implication: Do not gate int4 on dimension or dtype alone. The relevant property is probably the output head or basis, which the registry does not record, so the guard has to be an empirical check on a sample of vectors.
findings.question: int4-collapse

verdict.recomputed:
I recomputed everything from measured.json (plain "int4" row, mean over datasets) and the registry.

Denominator: only 51 of 55 models have a plain-int4 row. The 4 without one are answerai-colbert-small-v1 (text) and colpali-v1.3-merged, colqwen2-v1.0-merged and colqwen2.5-v0.2 (image). The split is 14 text and 37 image, not 15 and 40, and the "n=55" in the evidence is wrong.

Spearman with bootstrap CI over models, against plain-int4 retention:
- log2 dimension: 0.09 (CI -0.23 to 0.41). Without Nemotron it is 0.27 (p=0.06).
- vectors per page: 0.31 (CI 0.02 to 0.56). The claim gave 0.27 (-0.01 to 0.50). The lower bound now just excludes 0, so this is a weak positive association, not a null.
- baseline nDCG, all models: -0.02 (CI -0.30 to 0.28).
- baseline nDCG, image: -0.04 (p=0.81).
- baseline nDCG, text: -0.54 (n=14, p=0.047, CI -0.92 to 0.02). The claim gave -0.42, p=0.11. This is borderline and driven by a few points.

Collapse and degradation:
- Collapse below 0.5 gives 4 models: Nemotron 4B (0.006), Nemotron 8B (0.009), mxbai-edge-17m (0.268) and LateOn (0.297). That is 2 of 14 text and 2 of 37 image.
- Retention below 0.95 gives 7 models, not 8: 5 of 14 text and 2 of 37 image. Fisher OR 9.7, p=0.0125. At a 0.90 cutoff it is 4 of 14 versus 2 of 37, p=0.041.
- The claimed "6 of 15 versus 2 of 40, p=0.0034" could not be reproduced at any cutoff I tried (0.90, 0.95, 0.98). This is a post-hoc cutoff scan, so treat the p-values as exploratory.

Other checks:
- Float16 versus float32 inference, image models: 13 versus 24 (the claim said 13 versus 26). Mann-Whitney p=0.45 (the claim said 0.62). One degraded model in each group, so the claim holds.
- Image models at 128 to 640 dimensions: 0 of 33 below 0.95 (the claim said 36). The minimum is 0.992.
- EVIE at 2048 and 4096 dimensions retains 1.001 and 1.0007, while Nemotron at 2560 and 4096 collapses. This holds.
- lightonai text models range from 0.297 (LateOn) to 1.003 (colbertv2.0), so within-family spread is large. The claim said 0.282 to 1.002. The exact values differ slightly, but the pattern holds.
- Image-only DocVQA versus InfoVQA rank correlation: rho 0.21 (n=37), or 0.07 (n=35) without Nemotron. The claim said 0.24 and 0.12. The conclusion is the same: outside the collapsed models the variation is noise.
- Hub downloads: the 7 models below 0.95 hold 3.6% of the measured set's downloads, and the 4 collapsed ones hold 1.1%. The claimed 22% for 8 degraded models is not reproducible. At a 0.99 cutoff, 10 models hold 8.9%. One model, EvoQwen, has no download figure. 1. The n=55 and the 15 text / 40 image counts are wrong. Four models lack a plain-int4 row, so the true count is 51 (14 text, 37 image). Several statistics shift slightly as a result.

At the stricter cutoff for collapse below 0.5 the gap is absent (2 of 14 versus 2 of 37), which supports the claim that it cannot be attributed to modality.
8. The test count is not reported. I ran about 15 tests, none corrected.
9. The 16 text models have unknown inference dtype, so the float16 comparison covers image models only.
verdict.corrected_claim: Across the 51 models with a plain-int4 measurement (14 text, 37 image; 4 of the 55 lack this row), no single registry attribute clearly predicts int4 collapse, but power is low. Four models collapse below 0.5: two Nemotron siblings and two small text ColBERTs. Seven fall below 0.95. Dimension is not a sufficient explanation: Spearman 0.09 (CI -0.23 to 0.41), and EVIE at 2048 and 4096 dimensions is intact while Nemotron collapses. Float16 versus float32 inference shows no detectable difference among image models (1 of 13 versus 1 of 24 degraded, Mann-Whitney p=0.45). Vectors per page shows a weak positive association (rho 0.31, CI 0.02 to 0.56) that is confounded with modality. The text baseline-nDCG correlation is borderline (rho -0.54, p=0.047, n=14). Text models are degraded more often than image models (5 of 14 versus 2 of 37 below 0.95, Fisher p=0.0125, exploratory and cutoff-dependent). The gap disappears for collapse below 0.5 (2 of 14 versus 2 of 37) and is confounded with dataset, lab and tokenizer. Image models at 128 to 640 dimensions show no degradation (0 of 33). The degraded models hold about 4% of the measured set's Hub downloads, not 22%.

findings.title: Small output dimension may add risk for text models (weak)
findings.claim: The text models with output dimension below 128 are all degraded, and the toy suggests a possible mechanism: dense offsets hurt more at small d, while a single-coordinate offset collapses int4 at a smaller offset as d grows, which would make risk non-monotone in dimension.
findings.evidence: Text models with dimension below 128 (mxbai-17m at 48, mxbai-32m at 64, answerai at 96): 3 of 3 degraded versus 3 of 12 at 128-d (Fisher exact p=0.044, two-sided). Within text, Spearman(int4, log dim) is 0.56 (p=0.031, bootstrap CI 0.19 to 0.84, n=15). Toy collapse onset (unit-norm tokens, 150 documents): dense offset coefficient about 4 at d=48 (int4 0.71, binary 0.64) but no collapse by 8 at d=640 or 2560; single-coordinate offset about 4 at d=128, about 2 at d=640, about 1 at d=2560 (int4 0.03).
findings.method: Fisher exact on text models split at 128 dimensions, Spearman, and the numpy toy over d in 48, 128, 640, 2560.
findings.confounds: Three low-dimension models, two of them mxbai siblings. Dimension is entangled with model size, since the small mxbai models are the 17M and 32M ones. The toy is synthetic with a perfectly separable task, so its thresholds are sharper than real ones.
findings.practical_implication: Treat very small embedding widths in text models as a risk factor for plain int4 and binary and verify with int4(mean), but do not rely on dimension as a rule.
findings.question: int4-collapse

verdict.recomputed:
The numbers reproduce from the raw files. The 3 sub-128-d models' int4 ndcg@5 retention is 0.268 (mxbai-17m, 48-d), 0.792 (mxbai-32m, 64-d) and 0.899 (answerai, 96-d). The answerai value is not in measured.json, so I took it from reports/universal/text/text-answerai-colbert-small-v1-scifact.json (label 'int4 per-vector').
The 12 text models at 128-d have int4 retention 0.9918, 0.9828, 1.0053, 0.9973, 0.9881, 0.9941, 0.9361 (GTE-ModernColBERT), 0.2967 (LateOn), 0.9963, 1.0026, 0.7653 (mLateOn) and 0.9855.
- Fisher exact with 'degraded' = int4 retention below 0.95 (or 0.97): 3/3 versus 3/12, p=0.044 two-sided.
- Moving the degraded cutoff changes the result. At 0.90 it is 3/3 versus 2/12, p=0.022. At 0.99 it is 3/3 versus 6/12, p=0.23.
- Mann-Whitney, low-d below 128-d, one-sided: p=0.024.
- Spearman(int4, log dim) over the 15 text models: 0.556, p=0.031. The bootstrap 95% CI is 0.19 to 0.84, with 4839 usable resamples out of 5000.
- Spearman after dropping mxbai-17m: 0.41 (p=0.15). After dropping mxbai-32m or answerai: 0.52 (p=0.059). After dropping both mxbai models: 0.31 (p=0.30).
- Spearman after dropping the three collapsed 128-d ModernBERT-family models (LateOn, mLateOn, GTE): 0.76 (p=0.004). This does not rescue the claim, because it removes the counter-evidence to a dimension effect.
- I did not rerun the toy simulation. Everything about the toy mechanism below is unverified by me.
Tests run: 4 Fisher cutoffs, 1 Mann-Whitney, 1 Spearman with bootstrap, 5 leave-out variants. I did not correct for multiple testing.
verdict.issues:
1. Fragile to the cutoff. The Fisher p of 0.044 holds only for cutoffs of about 0.90 to 0.97. At a 0.99 cutoff, half the 128-d models also count as degraded and p=0.23.
2. Fragile to single models. The Spearman p-value rises above 0.05 once either mxbai sibling is dropped, and the correlation is 0.31 with both dropped. The same family appears twice among the three low-d models.
3. Dimension is not the only thing that varies. Two 128-d models collapse as badly (LateOn 0.30, mLateOn 0.77) and a third drops to 0.94 (GTE), so collapse occurs without small d. All three belong to the lightonai ModernBERT-family, which are also correlated siblings. Meanwhile many 128-d models are fine, including colbert-bert-tiny, a very small model. That argues against model size as the driver.
4. A large part of the effect is probably a per-model offset or centring issue rather than dimension. int4(mean), which centres first, restores retention for every collapsed model: mxbai-17m 0.993, mxbai-32m 0.986, LateOn 0.951, mLateOn 1.000, GTE 0.998. This supports an offset mechanism but says nothing about d itself.
5. n=3 low-d models, so the Fisher p is borderline and exploratory. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling. The set is single-dataset text only (SciFact), so dimension is confounded with the model family and with the particular checkpoints.
6. The claim of a non-monotone risk comes only from the synthetic toy. The data cannot test it, because there is no text model above 128-d and no dimension coverage between 128 and larger values. The claim is rightly labelled weak.
verdict.corrected_claim: All 3 text models below 128-d (48, 64 and 96) lost substantial int4 accuracy on SciFact (retention 0.27, 0.79 and 0.90). At 128-d, 3 of 12 did the same. This difference is nominally significant (Fisher p=0.044) only at a degraded cutoff of about 0.90 to 0.97; it disappears at 0.99 (p=0.23). The Spearman association with log dimension (0.56) does not survive dropping one or both mxbai siblings (0.52 and 0.31). With only 3 low-d models, two of them siblings, this is at best a weak hint. The same collapses occur at 128-d in the lightonai ModernBERT-family models, and centring before int4 recovers all of them, so a model-specific offset is the better-supported explanation than dimension. The non-monotone-in-dimension mechanism rests only on a synthetic toy that I did not rerun and that has no empirical test in these data.

Query cosine to the corpus mean tracks plain-int4 loss across them, but the signal is carried by the one text point (answerai, 0.944), and corpus mean-vector norm does not predict int4 loss. So the shared-mean-offset hypothesis is not confirmed or refuted for the collapsed models.

Image-only, n=6: query cosine rho -0.71 (p=0.11), mean norm rho -0.09 (p=0.87). Text answerai has mean norm 0.905 against 0.22 to 0.31 for the image sets, and centred binary collapses to 0.011 there (0.952 to 0.993 on image sets). The only image set with visible int4 loss is ColPali DocVQA (query cosine 0.131, int4 0.975).
findings.method: Spearman correlations over the 7 geometry datasets joined to int4, binary and centred-binary retention.
findings.confounds: 7 datasets, 3 models plus the same model across two datasets (not independent). Six of the seven are image models at 128 dimensions with int4 within noise of 1.0. One text point drives all correlations. No collapsed model has geometry.
findings.practical_implication: To test the shared-mean and outlier-coordinate accounts, run the existing geometry script on a few thousand vectors each from Nemotron, LateOn and mxbai-edge-17m and add max-component-over-RMS and per-coordinate mean to the report.

findings.title: The codec order is three tiers, not a strict ladder
findings.claim: Concordance across the six codecs is moderate (Kendall W about 0.5) and driven by three tiers. Float16, int8 and int4(mean) are ties for most units, lloyd2 sits in the middle, and binary is last. Only 24% of units follow the strict weak order, rising to 57% at a 0.002 tolerance, 78% at 0.005 and 90% at 0.01.
findings.evidence: Kendall W is 0.463 with exact ties and 0.509 with a 0.002 tie tolerance (model-cluster bootstrap 95% CI 0.42 to 0.60; chi2 224, p about 2e-46, n=88 units). Mean ranks (6 is best): float16 4.52, int8 4.44, int4(mean) 4.24, int4 3.78, lloyd2 2.51, binary 1.51. Pairwise at 0.002: float16 vs int8 is 9 greater, 74 tied, 5 less. Int8 vs int4(mean) is 26, 42 and 20. Lloyd2 beats binary in 67 units and loses in 9 (mean diff +0.0086, bootstrap 0.0009 to 0.0168). W by subgroup: fp32-inference 0.62, fp16-inference 0.38, SciFact 0.52, DocVQA 0.54, InfoVQA 0.51. Strict order float16 >= int8 >= int4(mean) >= lloyd2 >= binary holds in 21/88 at eps 0, 50 at 0.002, 69 at 0.005, 79 at 0.01.
findings.method: Kendall W with tie correction, cluster bootstrap over models (1000 draws), exact binomial sign tests on 15 codec pairs with ties dropped, bootstrap CIs of the mean difference over units, and counts of weak-order conformance at several tolerances.
findings.script_path: C:/Users/Lenovo/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Lenovo/07215cc9-ee09-45ef-91e1-819ae4093530/scratchpad/research/codec-ladder/a1_concordance.py (loader load.py, prep.py; conformance counts in a8_final.py)
findings.confounds: Units are not independent: 37 models appear twice and there are sibling checkpoints (cluster bootstrap used for W only). Tie tolerance is arbitrary. Median query-bootstrap half-widths are int8 0.0009, int4(mean) 0.0081, lloyd2 0.015 and binary 0.0168, so ranks within tier A are mostly noise. 26 units are fp16-inference, where the float16 codec is the identity. Modality and dataset are confounded for SciFact.
findings.practical_implication: Present the codecs as tiers (float16, int8 and int4(mean) near lossless; lloyd2; binary), not as a ranked ladder, and do not expect the order to be stable between models.

verdict.recomputed: Own script rebuilt 88 units from campaign/*/wide and reports/universal/wide JSONs (ndcg@5 retention, six codecs float16, int8(per_vector), int4(mean), int4, lloyd2(7), binary). The 88 units reproduce, and 26 units are fp16-inference. Kendall W with tie correction is 0.463 at exact ties, matching the claim. With a pairwise 0.002 tie tolerance I get 0.480, not 0.509; the tie rule is unspecified and mine is only one choice. Model-cluster bootstrap CI (1000 draws) is 0.375 to 0.556 at eps 0 and 0.404 to 0.568 at eps 0.002, a little lower than the claimed 0.42 to 0.60. Mean ranks at eps 0 are 4.55, 4.45, 4.32, 3.80, 2.40, 1.49, close to the claim's. Weak-order counts for float16>=int8>=int4(mean)>=lloyd2>=binary match exactly: 21, 50, 69, 79 of 88 at eps 0, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01. Pairwise counts at 0.002 match: float16 vs int8 is 9/74/5 (sign test p 0.42), int8 vs int4(mean) is 26/42/20 (p 0.46), lloyd2 vs binary is 67 greater and 9 less. The mean lloyd2 minus binary difference is +0.0086, with a unit bootstrap CI of 0.0003 to 0.0170 and a model-cluster CI of 0.0005 to 0.0164. Median query-bootstrap half-widths match (0.0009, 0.0081, 0.015, 0.0168). By subgroup, W at eps 0 / 0.002 is: fp32 0.55/0.57, fp16 0.34/0.32, SciFact 0.45/0.53, DocVQA 0.53/0.53, InfoVQA 0.43/0.45. Robustness checks: leave-one-model-out W (eps 0.002) is 0.476 to 0.493, and the lloyd2 minus binary mean is 0.0061 to 0.0105. After collapsing to per-model means, lloyd2 beats binary in 66 models and loses in 9 (p 8e-12). The direction holds in every dataset: DocVQA +0.013, InfoVQA +0.005, SciFact +0.005 mean (median +0.013). W within the top three codecs alone (float16, int8, int4(mean)) is 0.016, which supports the claim that they are ties. W on a lloyd2/binary/int4(mean) triple is 0.63.
verdict.issues:
1. Tie-tolerance dependence: the W at eps 0.002 and its CI depend on the tie rule, and I could not reproduce 0.509. The qualitative result is unchanged.
2. Tier A (float16, int8, int4(mean)) is not an exact tie. int4(mean) is less than float16 in 17 units and greater in 27 at 0.002. Mean retention is 1.0000, 0.9996 and 0.9984, so int4(mean) is slightly lower on average, and the tie is mostly within noise.
3. int4 (non-mean) is a fourth, messy codec. It sits between tier A and lloyd2 by mean rank, but its mean retention is 0.930, lower than lloyd2's 0.970 and binary's 0.962. It is a high-variance outlier codec with large losses on some models. The mean int4 minus int4(mean) difference is -0.068 (SciFact -0.14, DocVQA/InfoVQA -0.054), but the medians are near 0. The headline mean-rank ordering therefore hides that int4 usually ties tier A and sometimes collapses. The strict-order test also silently omits int4.
4. The lloyd2 over binary gap is small, with lloyd2 +0.0086 and a lower CI bound near 0. In mean retention terms lloyd2 and binary are close (0.970 vs 0.962). Only 13 of 88 unit differences exceed the combined query-bootstrap half-widths (a conservative check that ignores pairing). The 9 units where lloyd2 loses by more than 0.002 include 5 SciFact models with large deficits of -0.10 to -0.16 (GTE-ModernColBERT, LateOn, mxbai-edge-32m). So "binary is last" is not true for those text models, and the SciFact result is a matter of degree, not a clean order.
5. Non-independence: colbertv2.0_scifact appears twice (colbert-ir and lightonai folders), so there are 87 distinct models, and sibling checkpoints are numerous. Sign-test p-values on units are therefore overstated, and the chi2 p~2e-46 is not credible as stated. The per-model collapse is still significant for lloyd2 vs binary.
6. fp16-inference units: W is much lower (0.34 vs 0.55 at eps 0). The float16 codec is nominally an identity there, but retention deviates from 1 by up to 0.0012, so those units carry only noise in the top tier. Several fp16 baselines also reduce the rank contrast.
7. Dataset and modality are confounded for SciFact (14 units, 13 models), and the subgroup W values have wide, unreported uncertainty.
8. Post-hoc analysis, with about 15 pair tests plus several W variants and no multiplicity correction.
verdict.corrected_claim: Across 88 model-by-dataset units (87 distinct models; post-hoc, exploratory), codec rank agreement is moderate, with Kendall W of about 0.46 (exact ties) to 0.48 (0.002 tolerance; model-cluster CI roughly 0.38 to 0.57). Float16, int8 and int4(mean) are statistically indistinguishable in sign tests (W within that triple is about 0.02). int4(mean) loses a little on average (mean retention 0.998 vs 1.000). Lloyd2 sits below that tier, and binary is usually, but not always, below lloyd2. Lloyd2 beats binary by a small mean of about 0.009 (CI roughly 0.0005 to 0.017), and the direction holds in all three datasets and in 66 of 75 non-tied models. However, five SciFact models show large lloyd2 deficits of 0.10 to 0.16, and plain int4 (without mean-centring) is a high-variance fourth codec, so "three tiers" is a simplification. Weak-order conformance of 24%, 57%, 78% and 90% at tolerances 0, 0.002, 0.005 and 0.01 reproduces. Unit-level p-values and the chi2 figure overstate certainty because sibling checkpoints and the duplicated colbertv2.0 are not independent.

findings.title: Uncentred int4 collapses on specific models; int4(mean) repairs it
findings.claim: The main order-breaker is uncentred int4: it drops to 0.004 to 0.28 on nemotron-colembed (4b and 8b, both datasets) and on several ModernBERT and mxbai text models, while int4(mean) on the same units stays at 0.948 or above. This is a family or training property, not a dimension effect, because other wide models (EVIE 2048/4096) do not fail.
findings.evidence: Int4 below 0.97 in 9/88 units (below 0.90 in 8; Wilson 5 to 17%). Nemotron 4b/8b: DocVQA 0.0086 and 0.0109, InfoVQA 0.0039 and 0.0066. Text: mxbai-edge-17m 0.235, LateOn 0.282, mLateOn 0.752, mxbai-edge-32m 0.780, GTE-ModernColBERT 0.927. Int4(mean) on those units is 0.948 to 1.0, with an overall minimum of 0.948 and 1/88 below 0.97 (Wilson 0 to 6%). Tail counts below 0.99: int8 1, int4(mean) 6, int4 17, lloyd2 29, binary 57. Int4(mean) costs a median of +1.0 KB per doc over int4 (range 0.04 to 32.8 KB). Median int4 is 0.9989, so the typical case is fine.
findings.method: Tail-risk counts with Wilson intervals and listing of units below thresholds. The mechanism (a shared mean offset or outlier components inflating the per-vector scale) is inferred only from the fact that centring repairs it. Raw vectors were not inspected.
findings.confounds: Only 7 models fail, and 5 of them are SciFact, so text and image tail incidence is confounded with dataset. Two nemotron checkpoints are siblings. Mechanism untested.
findings.practical_implication: Never ship uncentred int4 unmeasured. Int4(mean) is the only sub-8-bit codec with a worst case of 0.948 across all 88 units, at near-zero byte cost.

Nemotron 4b/8b in measured.json: int4 0.0039 to 0.0109 on both datasets; int4(mean) 0.996 to 1.002. The EVIE 4.5B and 8B models have int4 around 1.00 and int4(mean) around 1.00.

Tail counts below 0.99 depend on the source. Wide files only (80 units): int4 13, int4(mean) 6, int8 0, lloyd2 27, binary 54. measured.json (88 units): int4 15, int4(mean) 4, int8 2, lloyd2 28, binary 57. The claim's 17/6/1/29/57 is not exactly either one, probably a mix. The rounded 3-decimal values in measured.json give small differences, e.g. mxbai-edge-17m 0.268 against 0.235 unrounded, and the wide files give 0.235.

Cost: the median int4(mean) minus int4 difference is about 1.0 BYTES per doc (range 0.04 to 32.8 bytes), not KB. Examples: colpali about 1 byte; nemotron about 20 bytes per doc. The code in stages/quantize.py shows int4(mean) stores one mean vector for the whole corpus (overhead_bytes = dim*4), amortised over 500 to 5183 docs.
verdict.issues:
1. UNIT ERROR (refuted part): the claimed cost of "+1.0 KB per doc, range 0.04 to 32.8 KB" is really bytes. The real cost is one dim-length float32 mean vector per corpus, e.g. 10 KB for 2560-dim and 16 KB for 4096-dim, so it is negligible per doc. This understates how cheap the repair is by about 1000x.
2. Tail counts do not match exactly. Counts below 0.99 vary by source (see recomputed), and int8 is 0 to 2 depending on source. The conclusion that int4(mean) is far tighter than int4 holds either way, but the exact counts, and int8 "1", are not reproducible as stated. The 0.97 and 0.90 counts do reproduce.
3. "int4(mean) stays at 0.948 or above" is true but hides that the LateOn int4(mean) is 0.948 with a query-bootstrap CI of about [0.917, 0.977]. That is a residual loss, not a full repair, for this one unit. Other repaired units have CIs spanning 1.0.
4. The effective number of independent failure families is small. Nemotron 4b and 8b are siblings, so the 4 image units come from one training recipe. The text failures are 4 models (LateOn, mLateOn, mxbai-edge-17m/32m), and LateOn/mLateOn are siblings. That is about 3 independent families, the number the claim should be read against.
5. "Several ModernBERT" is overstated. Reason-ModernColBERT (0.996) and ColBERT-Zero (0.994), also ModernBERT-based, do not fail; GTE (0.927) is mild; colmodernvbert (image) is fine. mxbai-colbert-large (0.986) is fine while the edge siblings fail. So the failures follow specific checkpoints or training, not an architecture.
6. "Not a dimension effect" is only weakly supported. EVIE (2048/4096) passes, but nemotron fails at 2560/4096 and the mxbai-edge models fail at 48/64, while 128-dim models mostly pass. Dimension is not the discriminator, and the claim stands as "unexplained checkpoint property". The stage code (per-vector amax scale, 15 levels) is consistent with the mean/outlier mechanism, but no raw vectors were inspected, so the mechanism stays untested.
7. Dataset/modality confound: 4 of the 9 failing units are image (nemotron), 5 are SciFact text. Text units are 5 of the 9 and nemotron is the only image family failing. Wilson intervals treat units as independent, but units come from 55 models with two datasets each, so they are clustered. Retention uses query-bootstrap CIs that ignore corpus sampling.
verdict.corrected_claim: Uncentred int4 (per-vector max scaling) is catastrophic on the nemotron-colembed-vl 4b/8b siblings (retention 0.004 to 0.011 on DocVQA and InfoVQA) and severely degraded on LateOn (0.28), mxbai-edge-17m (0.24), mLateOn (0.75) and mxbai-edge-32m (0.78); GTE-ModernColBERT is mildly affected (0.93). Other checkpoints in the same families (Reason-ModernColBERT, ColBERT-Zero, mxbai-colbert-large, EVIE, Tomoro) are unaffected, so this is a checkpoint-specific property that is not explained by dimension or architecture. Subtracting a corpus-mean vector (int4(mean)) brings these units back to 0.948 to 1.00 (LateOn is the weak case, 0.948 with CI about 0.92 to 0.98). The 9/88 and 1/88 unit counts reproduce; exact below-0.99 tail counts depend on data source (int4 13 to 15, int4(mean) 4 to 6). The repair costs one mean vector per corpus, about 1 byte per doc on average (range 0.04 to 33 bytes), not 1 KB. About 3 independent families are involved; the mechanism is inferred and untested, and exploratory.

findings.title: Binary and lloyd2 fail together on the same text models
findings.claim: Where lloyd2 collapses, binary usually does too, mostly on SciFact models. In a few units the usual lloyd2 > binary order flips, so a 2-bit codec is not a safe fallback for a model where binary fails.
findings.evidence: Spearman between lloyd2 and binary retention is 0.734 (p=4e-16, n=88). Of 15 units with lloyd2 < 0.97, 10 also have binary < 0.95; 72 of 73 units with lloyd2 >= 0.97 have binary >= 0.95 (Fisher OR about 144, p=6.9e-9). Examples (binary, lloyd2): mxbai-edge-17m 0.285, 0.268; mxbai-edge-32m 0.748, 0.647; mLateOn 0.711, 0.935; LFM2.5-ColBERT 0.769, 0.847; GTE-ModernColBERT 0.882, 0.750. 8 units have lloyd2 worse than binary by more than 0.005, including LateOn (lloyd2 0.821, binary 0.981) and colpali-v1.3-hf DocVQA (0.949 vs 0.964). Share of units with retention >= 0.99: binary 0.27/0.51/0.14 and lloyd2 0.59/0.92/0.21 on DocVQA/InfoVQA/SciFact.
findings.method: Spearman, 2x2 Fisher exact test with arbitrary thresholds, and unit listings.
findings.confounds: The thresholds are post-hoc. 8 of the 10 co-failures are SciFact units, so this is partly dataset or text-model. Both codecs share a fitted mean and rotation or sign structure, so correlated failure is expected.
findings.practical_implication: Measure the model first. Do not assume that lloyd2 is safe where binary fails, and treat text ColBERT models as higher risk for both.
findings.question: codec-ladder

verdict.recomputed: Own script on measured.json, labels 'binary' and 'lloyd2(7)': 88 units (model x dataset; 21 orgs). Spearman 0.745 (p=9e-17), against the claimed 0.734; the difference is probably row or label selection. Cluster bootstrap over models gives a 95% CI of 0.61 to 0.84. One random unit per org gives a mean of 0.83 (CI 0.70 to 0.91, 300 draws). Dropping the extreme unit (mxbai-17m, binary ~0.3) gives 0.736. Within-dataset Spearman: SciFact 0.70 (n=14), DocVQA 0.69 (n=37), InfoVQA 0.68 (n=37). So the association is not just a dataset or modality artefact. 2x2 table (lloyd2<0.97 vs binary<0.95): 9 both, 5 lloyd2-only, 2 binary-only, 72 neither. Fisher OR 65, p=1.7e-7. The claim said 10 of 15, OR ~144. My counts are 9 of 14, which is weaker, and the thresholds are post-hoc. Per dataset, the table is only informative on DocVQA (OR 21, p=0.04) and SciFact (7,2,1,4; p=0.09), and it is empty on InfoVQA (0 failures). Units with retention >=0.99: binary 0.27 / 0.51 / 0.14 and lloyd2 0.59 / 0.92 / 0.29 on DocVQA / InfoVQA / SciFact. The lloyd2 SciFact share is 0.29 for me against 0.21 claimed. Flips: 7 units have lloyd2 < binary - 0.005 (the claim says 8). Only 3 have a gap above 0.02: LateOn (0.835 vs 0.977), GTE-ModernColBERT (0.772 vs 0.892) and mxbai-edge-32m (0.665 vs 0.753). Query-bootstrap CIs separate only LateOn and GTE. The other four flips are 0.006 to 0.018 with overlapping CIs, which is noise-level. colpali-v1.3-hf (0.949 vs 0.964) overlaps. Overall lloyd2 > binary in 84% of units.
verdict.issues:
1. The headline, "where lloyd2 collapses binary usually does too", rests partly on loosely defined collapses. Of the 14 units with lloyd2<0.97, several are mild (0.949 to 0.969, mostly colpali-family DocVQA units). The marginal lloyd2 failures (>=0.93) are also mostly not co-failures with a severe binary failure.
2. The listed examples mislead. mLateOn (binary 0.73, lloyd2 0.94) and LFM2.5 (0.79 vs 0.86) show lloyd2 rescuing binary, not co-failing. Among the 11 units with binary<0.95, lloyd2 is higher in 7 (including 2 rescued to >=0.97), roughly equal in 1 (17m, 0.298 vs 0.304) and clearly lower in 2 (GTE, 32m). The claim "not a safe fallback" therefore applies to about 3 of 11 binary-failing units, all SciFact.
3. A quantitative gap in the second sentence: only 2 to 3 flips are beyond noise (LateOn, GTE, probably 32m). Seven flips were counted, but 4 are CI-overlapping differences of 0.006 to 0.018. Retention above 1 is noise, so VultronRetriever and colbertv2 are not real flips.
4. Siblings are correlated: the colpali family, mxbai-edge 17m/32m, LateOn/mLateOn/GTE (lightonai), and Vultron. The Spearman p of 4e-16 treats the 88 units as independent, which is overstated. The cluster-bootstrap CI of 0.61 to 0.84 is the honest uncertainty.
5. The thresholds (0.97, 0.95) were chosen post hoc, and the Fisher p-values are descriptive. The "mostly SciFact" part holds in raw counts but is confounded with dataset and modality. The SciFact failures are 7 of the 9 co-failures in my count (vs 8 of 10 claimed).
6. The numbers could not be reproduced exactly: rho 0.745 vs 0.734, the Fisher table, the flip count, and a couple of unit values (mxbai-17m binary 0.298 vs 0.285; LateOn 0.835 vs 0.821; GTE 0.772 vs 0.750; colbertv2 appears as a flip for me). The claimed values may come from the wide/ per-model files rather than the measured.json rows I used.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory, post hoc. Across 88 model-by-dataset units, binary and lloyd2(7) retention are strongly rank-correlated (Spearman ~0.74, cluster-bootstrap 95% CI ~0.61 to 0.84). The correlation is also seen within each dataset (0.68 to 0.70), so it is not only the dataset/modality confound. Severe failures at the 0.95/0.97 thresholds overlap (9 units fail both), but lloyd2 is usually the more robust codec: it is higher than binary in 84% of units and rescues binary in about 7 of the 11 binary-failing units. A reversal beyond query-bootstrap noise exists in only 2 to 3 SciFact units (LateOn, GTE-ModernColBERT, probably mxbai-edge-32m), with mxbai-edge-17m failing both. So 2-bit is not a safe fallback for those specific models. This is not a general rule, and the "usually collapses together" wording should be softened to "failures are positively associated, with a few reversals". Sibling dependence and the post-hoc thresholds mean the p-values should not be taken at face value.

findings.title: Binary loss is a repeatable model property; the best-codec choice is mostly noise
findings.claim: Binary retention correlates across datasets for the same model (rho 0.59), while lloyd2 and int4(mean) residuals do not. The cheapest codec above a retention threshold therefore changes between DocVQA and InfoVQA for most models. Binary is also systematically worse on DocVQA than InfoVQA.
findings.evidence: Cross-dataset Spearman over 37 image models: binary 0.591 (boot 0.33 to 0.78), lloyd2 0.144 (-0.20 to 0.48), int4(mean) -0.248 (-0.54 to 0.09), int4 0.206 (-0.15 to 0.54). Cheapest codec with retention >= 0.99 agrees between datasets for 10/37 models (27%; Spearman of choice rank 0.285, p=0.087). At tau=0.99 by point estimate the picks are binary 31, lloyd2 28, int4 16, int4(mean) 8, int8 5; with the CI lower bound >= 0.99 they shift to int4 31, int8 20, int4(mean) 12, binary 11, lloyd2 9, float16 5. Median compression at the selected codec: 7.8x (tau 0.995), 16x (0.99), 32x (0.98 and 0.95). Binary loss is 0.0248 on DocVQA vs 0.0098 on InfoVQA, paired difference 0.0151 (boot 0.0105 to 0.0199), 33/37 models worse on DocVQA (Wilcoxon p=4.7e-8). Sibling pairs agree closely, e.g. tsystems colqwen2.5-3b and its merged copy have binary 0.9921 vs 0.9934 on DocVQA.
findings.method: Cross-dataset Spearman with bootstrap over models, a selection rule applied per unit (cheapest codec with point estimate or CI lower bound >= tau), agreement counts, and a paired Wilcoxon test with a bootstrap CI.
findings.confounds: Only 37 models, and many are siblings (this inflates the cross-dataset correlation for binary if siblings share a weakness). The near-1 codecs have small true differences relative to noise, which mechanically lowers repeatability. DocVQA vs InfoVQA differ in baseline level, text density and vectors per doc. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling.
findings.practical_implication: Quote the binary penalty per model and dataset family rather than a global number. Pick among int4(mean), lloyd2 and binary by measuring on the target corpus, not by transferring a choice from another dataset. Use a CI-aware rule if the choice must be stable.
findings.question: codec-ladder

verdict.recomputed: From measured.json, 37 image models have docvqa+infovqa with all six single codecs. Cross-dataset Spearman (bootstrap over models, 2000 draws): binary 0.584 [0.32, 0.79]; lloyd2 0.139 [-0.20, 0.47]; int4(mean) -0.251 [-0.54, 0.08]; int4 0.215 [-0.14, 0.54]; int8 -0.045 [-0.43, 0.34]. These match the claim within bootstrap noise. Binary loss: DocVQA 0.0248, InfoVQA 0.0098, paired difference 0.0151, 33/37 worse on DocVQA, Wilcoxon p=4.7e-8. Leave-one-model-out binary rho ranges 0.548 to 0.635, so no single model drives it. At tau=0.99 by point estimate (cheapest codec by compression among the six singles), the same pick appears in both datasets for 11/37 models, against the claimed 10/37. My pick counts differ from the claimed ones, probably because of tie-breaking or the codec set, and the claimed counts sum to 88 for 74 picks, which looks inconsistent. One model per organisation (15 models): binary rho 0.454 [-0.12, 0.87], int4 0.423, lloyd2 -0.018, int4(mean) -0.177. Binary's median half-width of the DocVQA query-bootstrap CI is 0.024, and its across-model SD is 0.018 on DocVQA and 0.0078 on InfoVQA.
verdict.issues: 1) Sibling inflation, which the claim itself flags. 13 of the 37 models come from the vidore org, and tsystems, nomic, nvidia, tencent and others each have pairs. With one model per org, binary rho falls to 0.45 and its CI includes 0 (-0.12 to 0.87). So 'repeatable model property' is moderately supported at best, and the CI-based evidence leans on correlated checkpoints. 2) Binary's between-model spread on DocVQA (SD 0.018) is about the same size as the per-estimate query-bootstrap half-CI (0.024), so even the repeatable part is only partly separated from noise. 3) The comparison with lloyd2 and int4(mean) is by CI overlap only. Their near-zero rho is consistent with small true differences, but the data cannot distinguish 'no repeatability' from 'low signal-to-noise'. Their CIs also include the binary estimate for lloyd2 and int4 (0.14 and 0.21 against 0.58 is not a tested difference). 4) 'Systematically worse on DocVQA' is confounded with dataset: baseline level, text density, vectors per page. It is a dataset property, not a codec property. 5) The 'cheapest codec flips for most models' conclusion depends on the sharp tau=0.99 cutoff. Many models sit near the threshold, so most of the disagreement is threshold noise, not a real change in the best codec. Agreement is about 30% (11/37). 6) The Spearman for float16 is not meaningful because retention values are heavily tied near 1.0 (the code warned of constant input in bootstrap draws). 7) About 8 or more comparisons were made and no multiplicity correction was applied. This is exploratory analysis. Float16-inference baselines were not separately excluded.
verdict.corrected_claim: Across 37 image models, binary retention at ndcg@5 correlates between DocVQA and InfoVQA (Spearman about 0.58, CI 0.32 to 0.79; leave-one-out 0.55 to 0.64). The lloyd2, int4 and int4(mean) correlations are near zero with CIs spanning 0, which is consistent with small true differences relative to noise. The binary correlation weakens to 0.45 with a CI that includes 0 when only one model per organisation is kept (n=15), so it is moderate and partly driven by sibling checkpoints. The cheapest codec above tau=0.99 agrees between datasets for only about 11 of 37 models, but this is sensitive to threshold noise. Binary is worse on DocVQA than InfoVQA in 33/37 models (mean loss 0.025 vs 0.010; paired difference 0.015), but this is confounded with dataset characteristics and cannot be attributed to the codec or to modality.

findings.title: Binary loss falls with native dimension, but the evidence for a causal width effect is mixed
findings.claim: Models with larger native dimension lose less to binary. Family explains much of this, and PCA-width experiments show width matters inside the 128-d population but high-dimension models are cheap at 128 bits too.
findings.evidence: Spearman of binary loss vs log2(dim): DocVQA -0.60 (cluster boot -0.76 to -0.37), InfoVQA -0.73 (-0.82 to -0.56), text -0.56 (p=0.036, n=14). Median loss by dim: 128 0.0191 (62 units, 37 models), 320 0.0045 (12), 640 0.0045 (4), 2048 0.0017 (2), 2560 0.0066, 4096 0.0045. Text outliers at dim 48 (0.715) and 64 (0.252) are single models. Family eta-squared of dataset-standardised log loss is 0.506 over 37 image models in 10 families (permutation p=0.001; model identity ceiling 0.80). Matched PCA test (project(k)>binary normalised by project(k)>float16): native 128 to PCA-64 raises binary's incremental loss by 0.0176 on DocVQA (Wilcoxon p=0.0002, 80% of 25 models worse) and 0.0041 on InfoVQA (p=0.011). For 12 models of native dimension 320 to 4096, going to PCA-128 changes the incremental loss from 0.0112 to 0.0164 on DocVQA (p=0.57) and from 0.0020 to -0.0049 on InfoVQA (p=0.064). At 128 bits, native-128 models lose 0.0313 (DocVQA) and 0.0135 (InfoVQA) vs 0.0100 and -0.0135 for the PCA-128 high-dimension models (Mann-Whitney p=0.031 and 1.1e-5). In PCA rows binary exceeds float16 by more than 0.002 in 30% of InfoVQA cases and 10% of DocVQA cases, and the gap shrinks as k grows (rho of loss vs log2 k -0.60 on InfoVQA).
findings.method: Spearman with model-cluster bootstrap, permutation test of family eta-squared, OLS on log loss with cluster bootstrap (image: ldim -0.52 per standardised unit, CI -0.87 to -0.37, R2 0.54), and paired Wilcoxon contrasts from project(k) > codec rows.
findings.confounds: Native dimension is almost perfectly confounded with family (nemotron, EVIE, colvec, colqwen3.5 are the high-dimension families; the 128-d group is 37 models). Newer high-dimension models also have different training and baselines. Within-family dimension contrasts (colqwen3: 128 vs 320, n=2+2) are too small. The PCA rows share projections and are not independent, and the normalisation by the float16 projection can exceed 1. I could not test rotation vs redundancy as mechanisms without raw vectors. Dimension was not manipulated for the native models.
findings.practical_implication: Expect binary to be cheapest on wide-embedding families, but do not state that dimension itself protects binary; measure per family. PCA-then-binary is an untested lever for 128-d models only if the gain survives validation.
findings.question: codec-ladder

verdict.recomputed:
From measured.json "binary" rows, loss = 1 - retention. Dimension is taken from the optivision.adapters registry.

**Spearman of loss vs log2(dim)**
- DocVQA: n=37, rho -0.604, p=7.6e-5, model-cluster bootstrap CI [-0.77, -0.37]. This matches the claim.
- InfoVQA: n=37, rho -0.728, CI [-0.82, -0.56]. This matches.
- Text: n=14, rho -0.563, p=0.036, CI [-0.81, -0.31]. This matches.
- Leave-one-family-out on image: rho stays between -0.48 and -0.70 on DocVQA and between -0.63 and -0.80 on InfoVQA.
- Family-level medians (10 families): rho -0.80 on DocVQA and -0.85 on InfoVQA.

**Median loss by native dimension (image)**
- DocVQA: 128 is 0.030 (n=25), 320 is 0.0137 (6), 640 is 0.0078 (2), 2048 is 0.0019 (1), 2560 is 0.011 (1), 4096 is 0.0082 (2).
- InfoVQA: 128 is 0.014, 320 is 0.0026, 640 is 0.0010, 2048 is 0.0015, 2560 is 0.0023, 4096 is 0.0019.
- The pooled medians in the claim (0.0191 at 128, 0.0045 at 320) are not reproduced per dataset, but they are plausible as pooled values.

**128-d vs wider native models**
- DocVQA: the median gap is 0.021 (bootstrap CI 0.011 to 0.028, Mann-Whitney p=4e-4).
- InfoVQA: the gap is 0.012 (CI 0.009 to 0.015, p=9e-6).
- Image models split 25 (128-d) vs 12 (wider), and the wider ones come from only 5 families.

**Matched PCA contrast**
I used a difference (project(k)>float16 minus project(k)>binary) rather than the claim's ratio. The two versions give similar numbers.
- Native 128 to PCA-64, 25 models: incremental binary loss rises by 0.0162 on DocVQA (Wilcoxon p=0.0012, 72% worse) and by 0.0037 on InfoVQA (p=0.019, 64% worse). The claim reports 0.0176 and 0.0041.
- Dropping the 3 largest increases leaves about 0.011 (DocVQA) and 0.002 (InfoVQA).
- Wider native models to PCA-128 (12 models): DocVQA incremental loss goes from 0.0112 to 0.0161 (p=0.57). InfoVQA goes from 0.0020 to -0.0048 (p=0.064). This matches the claim.

**Registry facts**
- 13 DocVQA models used float16 inference, including nearly all the wide-dimension models (the EVIE pair, nemotron-8b, ColVec1.1, tomoro-8b, Vultron Prime). Their baseline is therefore not float32.
- The registry puts the colqwen3.5 family at 320 (4 models) and 2048/4096 (EVIE). It puts colqwen3 at 128 (2 models) and 320 (2 models).

**Text**
- 12 of the 14 text models are 128-d. The other two are mxbai-edge-colbert 17m (dim 48, loss 0.70) and 32m (dim 64, loss 0.25).
- Dropping the dim-48 model takes rho from -0.56 to -0.39 (p=0.19).
verdict.issues:
1. The text correlation is carried by two sibling checkpoints from one family (mxbai-edge-colbert) that are unusually lossy. They are probably weak or tiny models, so this is a model-quality effect and says nothing about dimension. Among the 12 text models at 128-d there is no dimension variation, so text gives no independent support. Without the dim-48 model the result is not significant.

2. Native dimension is almost fully confounded with family. Wider native models come from 5 families (colqwen3 at 320, colqwen3.5 at 320 plus EVIE, nemotron, colvec). The 128-d group is mostly colqwen/colpali siblings, many of them merged or hf duplicates of the same checkpoint (colpali has 8 variants and colqwen has 12). The effective n for the 128-d group is far below 25. The model-cluster bootstrap does not remove sibling correlation, because siblings are separate clusters. Family-level rho is still strong (-0.80 and -0.85, n=10 families), but 10 families is small. The only within-family dimension contrast is colqwen3 128 vs 320 (2 models vs 2), which is too small to support a causal reading.

3. The wide-dimension models are newer and are mostly float16-inference models measured against a float16 baseline. Their binary retention is therefore not directly comparable to the float32-baseline 128-d models. The claim does not list this confound.

4. The dimension dependence is not monotone: DocVQA at 2560 (0.011) is higher than at 320 or 640 and about the same as at 4096. Each of the 2048, 2560 and 640 bins has 1 or 2 units. So the picture is "128-d loses more", not "loss falls with dimension".

5. The PCA evidence is of mixed strength. For native 128 to PCA-64, the InfoVQA effect is small (0.004) and not robust to dropping the top 3. The wider-model PCA-128 tests are not significant. This supports the claim's own "mixed" label, and the PCA rows share projections.

6. Retention above 1 is noise, and the query bootstrap ignores corpus sampling. I did not retest p-values for these, and I did not rerun the family eta-squared permutation test or the OLS.

7. The claimed pooled median-by-dim figures (62 units) mix text and image data, so they conflate modality with dimension. Per-dataset medians are the cleaner view.

8. Test count: I ran 3 Spearman tests plus 2 bootstraps, 2 Mann-Whitney, 4 Wilcoxon, and 2 leave-one-out or family-level checks. None are corrected for multiple comparisons. This is post-hoc exploration.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among 37 image models, those with native dimension of 320 or more lose less to binary than 128-d models. The median difference is about 0.02 on DocVQA and 0.012 on InfoVQA, and Spearman rho is about -0.6 to -0.7, surviving leave-one-family-out. Dimension is almost fully confounded with family and with the newer, mostly float16-inference models, and the 128-d group is dominated by near-duplicate colpali and colqwen siblings. So the pattern is a weak-to-moderate association, not evidence of a width effect. The text result (rho -0.56, p=0.036) comes from two sibling mxbai-edge checkpoints at dim 48 and 64, and it is not significant without the 48-d model (rho -0.39, p=0.19). The matched PCA test shows that shrinking a 128-d model to 64 dimensions modestly raises binary's incremental loss, by about 0.016 on DocVQA and 0.004 on InfoVQA. The test does not show that wide native models are intrinsically robust, because PCA-128 changes for the wide models are not significant (p=0.57 and 0.064).

findings.title: Baseline strength and vectors per doc do not independently predict binary loss
findings.claim: The apparent link between baseline ndcg and binary loss is mostly the dataset and dimension effect. Within dataset and dim=128 it is weak, and vectors per doc is not a predictor for image models.
findings.evidence: Pooled over both image datasets, rho(loss, base)=-0.66, but this is the dataset effect (InfoVQA baselines are higher and binary loses less). Within dataset: DocVQA -0.51 (p=0.001), InfoVQA -0.62 (p=5e-5), SciFact +0.29 (p=0.31). Restricted to dim=128 within dataset: DocVQA -0.12 (p=0.57, n=25), InfoVQA -0.35 (p=0.085, n=25); absolute ndcg drop gives -0.03 and -0.32. Vectors per doc: image rho +0.04 (cluster boot -0.18 to 0.29), text +0.44 (p=0.11, n=14), OLS lvpd coefficient -0.15 (CI -0.38 to 0.06). fp16-inference vs fp32-inference image models: binary loss 0.0196 vs 0.0277 on DocVQA (p=0.25) and 0.0060 vs 0.0118 on InfoVQA (p=0.050).
findings.method: Spearman within dataset and within a dimension stratum, absolute vs relative drop, Mann-Whitney on inference dtype, and OLS with cluster bootstrap.
findings.confounds: Baseline is correlated with dimension, family and model size. The dim=128 strata have 25 models, so power is low. fp16-inference is confounded with family and dimension (12 of 26 fp16 units are above 128). The text n=14 result uses 3 predictors.

verdict.recomputed: From measured.json (row label 'binary', loss = 1 - retention; dim from the MODELS registry), I reproduced almost all of the quoted figures. Pooled image Spearman rho(loss, base) = -0.662. Within dataset: DocVQA -0.514 (p=0.0011, n=37), InfoVQA -0.618 (p<1e-4, n=37). At dim=128 only: DocVQA -0.121 (p=0.56, n=25), InfoVQA -0.354 (p=0.083, n=25). Absolute drop at dim=128: -0.025 and -0.315 (p=0.125). Vectors per doc, within dataset: DocVQA -0.008, InfoVQA -0.146 (p=0.39). fp16 vs fp32 inference, binary loss: DocVQA 0.0196 vs 0.0277 (Mann-Whitney p=0.246); InfoVQA 0.0060 vs 0.0118 (p=0.052). Not reproduced exactly: SciFact rho is +0.24 (p=0.41, n=14) here, versus +0.29 (p=0.31) claimed; SciFact vpd rho is +0.44 (p=0.114), as claimed. Extra checks. Within dim=128, leave-one-out rho ranges from -0.25 to -0.03 on DocVQA and from -0.50 to -0.30 on InfoVQA, so no single model drives the result. Bootstrap 95% CI over models at dim=128: DocVQA [-0.55, 0.36], InfoVQA [-0.78, 0.13]. Dimension strongly structures both quantities: mean binary loss on DocVQA is 0.031 at dim 128 and 0.002-0.015 at dim 320 and above, and mean baseline rises with dimension. The dim=128 stratum is 10 colqwen and 7 colpali checkpoints out of 25, so siblings dominate it. I ran about 20 tests, all exploratory and post hoc. The only test I did not repeat is the OLS with cluster bootstrap.
verdict.issues: 1) The claim leans on non-significance at n=25 as if it showed absence. The InfoVQA dim=128 rho is -0.35 with a bootstrap CI of [-0.78, 0.13] and a negative sign in every leave-one-out run. That is a weak-to-moderate negative link that was not excluded, not "no link". DocVQA is closer to null, with a CI spanning zero in both directions. 2) The InfoVQA baselines are near ceiling (mean about 0.88 at dim 128), so the within-stratum relationship may be a ceiling effect on a bounded metric. 3) The claim says the link is "mostly the dataset and dimension effect". I did not test that decomposition. The dataset effect is clear, and dimension co-varies strongly with both baseline and loss, but the dim=128 stratum is also dominated by two sibling families, so the within-stratum estimates are not independent. 4) fp16 evidence is weak: p=0.25 and p=0.052 are unadjusted, and fp16 is confounded with family and dimension, as the analyst noted. The direction (fp16 loses less) is consistent across both datasets, but a causal reading is not supported. 5) The SciFact rho differs slightly from the quoted value (+0.24 vs +0.29), probably because the analyst used a slightly different row or sample. This does not change the conclusion, since all SciFact results are non-significant and the dataset and modality are fully confounded. 6) Query-bootstrap CIs on retention ignore corpus sampling, and all conclusions are exploratory.
verdict.corrected_claim: Pooled across the two image datasets, the baseline-ndcg vs binary-loss correlation (-0.66) is largely a dataset effect, because InfoVQA has higher baselines and lower binary loss. Within a dataset the correlation is still moderately negative (-0.51 and -0.62), and dimension is a strong shared driver of both baseline and loss. Restricted to dim=128 (25 models, mostly colqwen/colpali siblings), the correlation is not detectable on DocVQA (-0.12, CI about -0.55 to 0.36) and weakly negative on InfoVQA (-0.35, CI about -0.78 to 0.13), so a modest independent link cannot be excluded. Vectors per doc shows no detectable association for image models (rho about 0 to -0.15 within dataset), and the SciFact result (n=14) is uninformative. The fp16-inference difference (lower loss, p=0.25 on DocVQA and p=0.052 on InfoVQA) is suggestive but confounded with family and dimension.

results.summary: Exploratory, post-hoc analysis of token reduction (hierarchical_merge at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1, adaptive_merge radius 0.6) over 55 models and 95 model x dataset cells (40 DocVQA, 40 InfoVQA, 15 SciFact). About 110 p-values or intervals were computed, uncorrected for multiplicity. The main result is that loss accelerates as the keep fraction falls, with no sharp knee. The practical bend is between keep 0.25 and 0.1. Loss tracks the absolute number of vectors kept better than the keep fraction. Differences between models at mild reduction are mostly sampling noise, and a model's tolerance on DocVQA does not predict its tolerance on InfoVQA. The redundancy hypothesis (pages with more vectors tolerate merging better) is only a weak, family-confounded pattern. Modality is fully confounded with dataset, corpus size and vectors per page. The Write tool refused the requested REPORT.md (it rejected report files from subagents), so no REPORT.md exists at the requested path. This structured output carries the full content instead, and the scripts and .out files are in the folder. Merge stage behaviour (src/optivision/stages/merge.py): hierarchical_merge Ward-clusters each page's unit vectors to ceil(r*n) clusters and replaces each cluster by its rescaled mean; the achieved keep fraction was 0.500/0.331/0.251/0.101. adaptive_merge does a greedy farthest-point cover until every vector has cosine >= radius to a centre, so the count adapts per page; its achieved keep fraction was 0.04-0.47. findings.title: Loss accelerates as the keep fraction falls; no sharp knee, practical bend between keep 0.25 and 0.1
findings.claim: Retention loss grows roughly with the square of the number of halvings of the page. Image models stay within about 1% of baseline down to keep ~0.25 and lose 1-3% at keep 0.1. Text models lose far more.
findings.evidence: Mean retention at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1: DocVQA 0.9961/0.9929/0.9904/0.9731; InfoVQA 0.9976/0.9959/0.9944/0.9829; SciFact 0.9889/0.9714/0.9524/0.8816. Paired step 0.25->0.1 costs 1.70 pp (CI 1.18-2.34, Wilcoxon p=5e-8) on DocVQA and 1.15 pp (0.91-1.43, p=1e-7) on InfoVQA, against 0.56 pp and 0.32 pp for the whole 0.5->0.25 step. A hinge fit puts the knot at the grid boundary, so no discrete break is detected. Median image loss stays under 1% to keep ~0.22 (DocVQA) and ~0.14 (InfoVQA). Share of cells with retention >= 0.99 at keep 0.1: DocVQA 24%, InfoVQA 24%, SciFact 0%. Cells with CI upper bound < 0.99 at keep 0.1: 11/37 DocVQA, 6/37 InfoVQA, 13/14 SciFact.
