verdict.recomputed:
I used hierarchical_merge(r) rows, r in {0.5, 0.33, 0.25, 0.1}, taken from measured.json. I read the numbers from the per-model rows, so they are not independent of the other analyst's source. The models were 37 on DocVQA, 37 on InfoVQA and 14 on SciFact. Actual vectors-per-doc ratios were 0.506/0.338/0.259/0.111, so the nominal keep values are accurate.

Cell means at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1:
- DocVQA: 0.9960/0.9927/0.9901/0.9731. The claim gives 0.9961/0.9929/0.9904.
- InfoVQA: 0.9977/0.9959/0.9943/0.9829. The claim gives 0.9976/0.9959/0.9944.
- SciFact: 0.9882/0.9696/0.9534/0.8816. The claim gives 0.9889/0.9714/0.9524.
- The gaps are at most 0.002, so the means reproduce.

Paired step 0.25 to 0.1, with a percentile bootstrap over models and a Wilcoxon test:
- DocVQA: 1.70 pp, CI 1.17-2.37, p=4.7e-8.
- InfoVQA: 1.15 pp, CI 0.91-1.43, p=1.2e-7.
- SciFact: 7.17 pp, CI 4.5-10.5, p=1.2e-4.

Step 0.5 to 0.25:
- DocVQA: 0.60 pp (the claim says 0.56).
- InfoVQA: 0.34 pp.
- SciFact: 3.48 pp.

Power-law fit through the origin (grid over p, model-bootstrap CI):
- DocVQA: p=1.81, CI 1.45-2.37.
- InfoVQA: p=1.99, CI 1.64-2.34.
- SciFact: p=1.86, CI 1.5-2.5.
- The claim gives 1.95, 1.85 and 1.90, so the intervals overlap heavily.

Other counts:
- Share of cells with retention >= 0.99 at keep 0.1: 24% on DocVQA, 24% on InfoVQA, 0% on SciFact.
- Cells with CI upper bound < 0.99 at keep 0.1: 11/37, 6/37 and 13/14.
- All three match the claim exactly.

Robustness checks:
- Dropping the single largest 0.25-to-0.1 loser (ColNetraEmbed, 10.1 pp, on DocVQA) gives a mean step of 1.46 pp. p becomes 1.84.
- Dropping the largest loser on InfoVQA (colmodernvbert, 3.9 pp) gives a step of 1.07 pp and p=1.95.
- Dropping the largest loser on SciFact (jina-colbert-v2, 20.8 pp) gives a step of 6.13 pp and p=1.68.
- Keeping one model per organisation (n=15, 15 and 6) gives p of 1.58 on DocVQA, 2.11 on InfoVQA and 1.83 on SciFact. The DocVQA exponent is lower there, but still above 1.
- Cells with more than 2 pp extra loss in the second step: 9 on DocVQA, 2 on InfoVQA and 8 on SciFact. This is 19 cells in all.
verdict.issues:
1. The numbers reproduce. The weaknesses are in interpretation, not computation.
2. Only 4 grid points per model, and the power-law fit is on cell means. An exponent of about 1.8-2 is a descriptive summary, not a mechanism. I did not test other forms, such as an exponential in the number of halvings.
3. The comparison of the 0.5-to-0.25 step with the 0.25-to-0.1 step is not like for like. The first spans 2 halvings and the second spans 1.32. The acceleration per halving is therefore larger than the raw pp figures suggest, and the claim's direction is if anything understated.
4. The mean hides heterogeneity. The medians are higher than the means, for example 0.978 against 0.973 on DocVQA at keep 0.1. A few models drive the tail. ColNetraEmbed loses 10 pp in one step.
5. Sibling checkpoints are pooled as independent models. One model per organisation leaves 15 DocVQA models and 6 SciFact models, so the effective n is small. The DocVQA exponent falls to 1.58.
6. The SciFact "text loses far more" statement is confounded with dataset and modality. SciFact has 5,183 docs, short documents and a different number of vectors per doc, and only 14 models, so it cannot be attributed to modality.
7. Query-bootstrap CI upper bounds ignore corpus sampling. Counts of cells with CI upper bound below 0.99 are therefore somewhat optimistic about significance.
8. The p-values test only "step is not zero". With so many cells and several comparisons, the p=5e-8 style values add little beyond the effect sizes.
9. This was exploratory and post-hoc. I ran about 3 datasets x (2 steps + a fit + robustness variants), roughly 30 tests.
10. I did not check the float16-baseline subset separately. The merge ratio is applied to vectors, so I expect little effect, but it is untested.
11. I did not recompute the hinge/knee fit. "No discrete break" cannot be checked with 4 points anyway.
verdict.corrected_claim: On hierarchical_merge at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1, mean retention falls faster than linearly in the number of halvings. A power-law exponent of about 1.6-2.1, with bootstrap CIs of roughly 1.4-2.5, fits all three datasets. The shape is descriptive only, because there are 4 points per model, so it is not a mechanism. Image models (37 per dataset) lose about 1% at keep 0.25 and about 1.2-1.7 pp more going to 0.1, with a heavy tail of a few models. Dropping the worst model leaves this at about 1.1-1.5 pp. The step is positive on every dataset and survives removing the extreme model. Text on SciFact (14 models) loses about 7 pp more over the same step, but this is confounded with dataset and modality. Per halving, the loss is clearly accelerating. A smooth bend, not a sharp knee, appears between keep 0.25 and 0.1. Because there are few independent organisations (15, 15 and 6), the evidence is moderate and the exact exponent is uncertain.

findings.title: Absolute kept vectors per page predicts loss better than keep fraction, and partly accounts for the text-vs-image gap
findings.claim: Across hierarchical cells, loss tracks how many vectors remain on the page more tightly than the fraction kept. Loss is small above about 250 kept vectors and rises steeply below about 75. The large text-vs-image gap at equal fraction mostly disappears where the kept-vector counts overlap, but modality cannot be separated from dataset.
findings.evidence: Spearman(loss, absolute kept vectors) vs Spearman(loss, keep fraction): pooled -0.62 vs -0.48; DocVQA -0.53 vs -0.48; InfoVQA -0.64 vs -0.54; SciFact -0.67 vs -0.69. Mean loss by kept vectors (DocVQA/InfoVQA/SciFact): >500: 0.24%/0.21%; 250-500: 0.67%/0.38%; 150-250: 0.84%/0.62%; 100-150: 2.1%/1.3%/0.9%; 75-100: 3.0%/1.5%/2.7%; 50-75: 9.3% (n=1)/2.2%/4.6%; 20-30: 19.4% (n=1)/6.4% (n=1)/11.6%. At equal keep fraction text loses 4-5x more (keep 0.1: 11.8% text vs 2.2% image; median kept vectors 27 vs 109; keep 0.25: 4.8% vs 0.8%). In the 50-100 kept-vector bin text 3.7% (n=29) vs image 2.6% (n=31), diff +1.1 pp, bootstrap CI -0.5 to +3.0; in 100-150 text 0.9% vs image 1.7%, diff -0.8 pp (CI -1.5 to +0.05). OLS loss ~ dataset + (log2 1/k)^2 + log2(bv): the (log2 1/k)^2 coefficient 0.0035 (model-bootstrap CI 0.0025-0.0049).
findings.method: Spearman correlations on pooled hierarchical cells, binning by kept vectors, matched-bin comparisons with bootstrap, OLS with model-cluster bootstrap.
findings.confounds: Within each dataset, absolute count and fraction are highly collinear because all models share the same four ratios, so the margin between rho -0.62 and -0.48 is modest and has no CI. Bins below 75 vectors hold few image cells (1-7), mostly ColNetraEmbed. Text vs image is confounded with dataset (SciFact, 5,183 docs, BEIR vs ViDoRe 500 pages), model class, document length distribution and ColBERT-style encoders. Cells are not independent: the same model contributes up to five.
findings.practical_implication: Express merging budgets as a minimum number of vectors per page (roughly >= 150-250 for under 1% loss on these datasets) rather than only as a fraction. A fraction that is safe for a 1,000-vector page is not safe for a 150-vector text document.

Tests run: about 12 correlations, 4 bootstrap contrasts, 5 matched bins, 4 OLS fits and 16 within-ratio correlations; none are corrected for multiplicity.

Scripts: load.py, a1.py, a2.py and a3.py in the verification folder.
verdict.issues:
1. Only the first sentence of the claim is supported, and only loosely. The pooled rho gap (+0.16, CI [0.06, 0.27]) is mostly driven by the text/image offset and does not replicate within DocVQA (CI spans 0). It is borderline within InfoVQA and absent within SciFact (where keep fraction is slightly better). The pooled gap is therefore not independent evidence that absolute count beats fraction. This is exactly the confound the claim itself notes.
2. The "loss is small above about 250 and rises steeply below about 75" thresholds are descriptive only. The curve is smooth, with no change point tested. The cells below 75 are mostly text (about 30 text cells vs about 9 image cells), and the lowest bins hold n=1 image cells.
3. "The gap mostly disappears where counts overlap" is only weakly supported:
- Every matched-bin CI includes 0.
- The 50-100 bin is +1.2 pp (CI [-0.8, +3.8]) and the 100-150 bin is -0.7 pp (CI [-1.5, +0.2]), so the sign flips between adjacent bins.
- The overlap is also an extrapolation. It compares text at mild merging (keep 0.25-0.5) with image models at aggressive merging (keep 0.1), and the 150-250 bin has one text cell.
- The OLS finding (text offset 0.0415 -> 0.0007) is the strongest support, but its CI is wide (-0.015 to 0.023), so a residual text penalty of a few pp is not excluded.
4. The text-vs-image comparison is confounded with dataset (SciFact vs ViDoRe), corpus size (5,183 vs 500), document length (about 250 vs about 1,000 baseline vectors) and encoder class, so none of it can be pinned on modality. A model could lose more on SciFact because there is little redundancy to merge in short texts, which is a different cause from absolute count.
5. Within-dataset the kept-vector count and keep fraction are nearly collinear, because every model shares four ratios. Only baseline-length variation (DocVQA/InfoVQA) separates them, and the within-ratio effect is modest.
6. Minor issues:
- Query-bootstrap CIs and the n=14 SciFact models leave the SciFact estimates fragile.
- The claim's cell count ("up to five" cells per model) does not match what I found: 4 cells per model per dataset, 8 for models with both image datasets.
- The cells include float16-baseline models and sibling checkpoints, which I did not remove. Dropping ColNetraEmbed leaves the result unchanged.
- Retention above 1 would produce negative loss; this is noise and I did not clip it.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory and post hoc: on the 352 hierarchical_merge cells, loss correlates more strongly with kept vectors per page than with keep fraction (pooled Spearman -0.64 vs -0.48; model-cluster bootstrap CI of the gap [0.06, 0.27]). Within datasets the advantage is smaller and unclear: DocVQA +0.07 (CI spans 0), InfoVQA +0.09 (CI [0.004, 0.18]), SciFact none. Among image models at a fixed ratio, pages with more vectors lose somewhat less (rho about -0.2 to -0.45). In a quadratic regression, replacing keep fraction with log kept vectors cuts the SciFact offset from +4.2 pp to about 0 (CI -1.5 to +2.3 pp), raises R^2 from 0.32 to 0.45, and lowers leave-one-model-out error by about 9%. In kept-vector bins that both groups populate, text-minus-image differences have CIs that include zero and flip sign between adjacent bins (50-100: +1.2 pp; 100-150: -0.7 pp). The data therefore suggest that part of the large text-vs-image gap at equal keep fraction comes from text pages having few vectors to begin with. They do not show that kept-vector count fully explains it, and modality cannot be separated from dataset, corpus size, document length and encoder family. The loss thresholds (small above about 250, steep below about 75) are descriptive, with no change point tested. They rest on a handful of image cells below 75 vectors, and the 150-250 bin has a single text cell.

findings.title: Between-model differences at mild reduction are mostly noise, and tolerance does not transfer between DocVQA and InfoVQA
findings.claim: At keep 0.5-0.33 the spread of loss across image models is no larger than the sampling error of each measurement. Even at keep 0.1, where most spread is real, a model's rank on DocVQA does not predict its rank on InfoVQA.
findings.evidence: Share of between-model variance in loss that is query-bootstrap SE: DocVQA 102%/48%/30%/14% at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1; InfoVQA 141%/89%/51%/22%; SciFact 24%/12%/6%/4%. Spearman of loss between DocVQA and InfoVQA over the shared 40 models: keep 0.5 -0.12; 0.33 0.02 (CI -0.35 to 0.37); 0.25 -0.21 (-0.56 to 0.15); 0.1 0.19 (-0.19 to 0.54, n=37); adaptive 0.08 (-0.29 to 0.40). Near-identical checkpoint pairs (merged / hf / re-uploads, 7 pairs, up to 12 comparisons) differ by RMS 0.66/1.08/0.87/1.01/1.10 pp in loss at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1/adaptive, a second empirical noise scale. Family-level eta^2 for loss at 0.1 over families with >= 3 models (colpali, colqwen, colqwen3, colqwen3.5; n=27) is 0.14 with permutation p=0.30. float16-inference baselines show no difference in loss (image, Mann-Whitney p 0.62-0.96). Within a dataset, mild loss predicts heavy loss (DocVQA rho 0.66 for 0.25 vs 0.1, InfoVQA 0.68), which is partly shared-baseline noise.
findings.method: Variance decomposition using SE = CI width/3.92, Spearman with bootstrap over models, sibling-pair differences, one-way eta^2 with permutation test.
findings.confounds: SE comes from query bootstrap only and ignores corpus sampling, so noise is understated. Model count is 40 per correlation, so the CIs are wide and a modest real correlation (<0.4) is not excluded. The sibling pairs are not true replicates (different export formats or training runs). DocVQA and InfoVQA use different corpora and queries, so lack of transfer can be dataset x model interaction rather than measurement noise.
findings.practical_implication: Do not rank models by merging tolerance from a single dataset or from mild ratios; differences under about 1 pp at keep 0.5-0.25 are within noise. Tolerance should be certified per model and per target corpus, which is consistent with the package's calibrate()-style selection.
findings.question: token-merging

verdict.recomputed: Own code, from raw campaign wide/*.json (33 image models with both datasets there) and measured.json (37 shared models, using the label hierarchical_merge(r) and adaptive_merge(0.6)). Loss = 1 - ndcg@5 retention, SE = CI width/3.92. Noise share of between-model variance (mean SE^2 / variance of loss): DocVQA 97/41/26/13% at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1, adaptive 43%; InfoVQA 145/86/47/21%, adaptive 30%; SciFact (14 models) 37/13/6/5%, adaptive 76%. Compared with the claim, this matches at keep 0.5 (97 vs 102 in DocVQA, 145 vs 141 in InfoVQA) and at 0.1 (13 vs 14, 21 vs 22). The middle values differ a little (DocVQA 41/26 vs 48/30, InfoVQA 86/47 vs 89/51) and SciFact is 37/13/6/5 vs 24/12/6/4, so the claim's per-cell numbers are only approximately reproduced. DocVQA-vs-InfoVQA Spearman, measured.json, n=37: -0.13 / 0.02 [-0.36, 0.39] / -0.15 [-0.5, 0.24] / 0.19 [-0.18, 0.54] / adaptive 0.13 [-0.24, 0.47]. This reproduces the claim, which says n=40 at mild keep and n=37 at keep 0.1. Using the campaign files only (n=33) gives the same picture (-0.10, 0.02, -0.18, 0.21, 0.13). Reliability ceiling on cross-dataset rho from measurement noise alone: about 0.00 at keep 0.5, 0.28 at 0.33, 0.63 at 0.25, 0.83 at 0.1, 0.63 adaptive. Results from the checks I added: (1) At keep 0.25 and 0.1 the noise ceiling is high enough that a true rho near 0.6-0.8 would have shown up as a significant correlation. Observed Spearman is -0.15 and 0.19, so the noise explanation does not account for the lack of transfer there. (2) Pearson correlation at keep 0.1 is 0.68-0.69 and Kendall tau is 0.14. A few high-loss models drive a linear association. Dropping the 3 most extreme DocVQA models leaves Spearman at 0.11. On the non-float16 subset Spearman is 0.46 (n=21), and with one model per name stem (n=18) it is 0.29. All of these have wide, uncertain intervals. (3) float16 baselines, tested in DocVQA only (12 of 33 models): no difference in loss (Mann-Whitney p 0.21 at keep 0.25, 0.44 at keep 0.1). Not tested: sibling-pair RMS, family eta^2/permutation p, within-dataset mild-vs-heavy rho. Tests run in my script: about 25 descriptive statistics, no multiplicity correction.
verdict.issues: 1. Mild keep (0.5, 0.33): the claim holds. Noise is about 100% of between-model variance at 0.5, and in InfoVQA the estimated reliability is negative (noise larger than observed spread). The DocVQA ceiling at 0.5 is about 0.03 and the InfoVQA one is below 0. 2. "Even at keep 0.1, where most spread is real... rank does not predict rank" is overstated. Rank correlation is low (0.19, CI -0.18 to 0.54), but this is not demonstrated absence of transfer. The CI includes the 0.4-0.5 range, Pearson is 0.68, and a high-loss subset shows positive association. A more careful statement: rank transfer is weak and unproven, while the large-loss models (those losing several points) do appear to transfer. 3. At keep 0.25 the rho is -0.15 even though the noise ceiling is about 0.6. That is the best support for the claim, since noise alone does not explain it. It is also the cell where only 1-2 families vary. 4. The "ignores corpus sampling" caveat means the SE share is a lower bound, which makes the mild-keep conclusion stronger, not weaker. 5. Query-bootstrap SE inflates when the unit of the ceiling calculation is mean SE^2 across heterogeneous SEs (DocVQA SE at keep 0.1 ranges 0.76-2.4 pp). The share at 0.5 above 100% simply means the noise estimate exceeds the spread, which is expected when the estimator is imprecise. 6. The "no float16 effect" statement only held in DocVQA when I re-tested it, and I did not retest the sibling RMS or eta^2 claims. 7. Dataset x model interaction cannot be separated from measurement noise at keep 0.25, so "tolerance does not transfer" is correct as an observation but not as a mechanism.
verdict.corrected_claim: At keep 0.5 and 0.33 the between-model spread in loss on DocVQA and InfoVQA is no larger than the query-bootstrap SE (noise share about 100% / 40-90%), so ranking models by mild-reduction loss is not supported by this data. By keep 0.1 most spread (80-90%) is above sampling error, but rank agreement between DocVQA and InfoVQA is weak and imprecise (Spearman about 0.2, 95% CI roughly -0.2 to 0.55, n=37, with Pearson about 0.7 driven by a handful of high-loss models). This is consistent with weak or no transfer of tolerance across the two datasets, but it does not exclude a moderate real correlation. Exploratory, not preregistered.

findings.title: DocVQA loses more to merging than InfoVQA, but the absolute gap is small
findings.claim: Mean loss is about 1.6-1.8x larger on DocVQA than on InfoVQA at every setting, but the paired difference is under 1 pp and only clearly different from zero at keep 0.1 and for adaptive.
findings.evidence: Ratio of mean losses DocVQA/InfoVQA: 1.68, 1.73, 1.71, 1.57 at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1 and 1.79 for adaptive. Paired mean loss difference (DocVQA - InfoVQA, n=40): 0.16 pp (CI -0.07 to 0.39, p=0.18); 0.30 pp (-0.03 to 0.68, p=0.11); 0.40 pp (-0.05 to 0.90, p=0.13); keep 0.1 0.97 pp (0.26-1.90, p=0.012, n=37); adaptive 0.92 pp (0.47-1.39, p=0.0009, DocVQA worse in 28/40, sign p=0.017). Baseline ndcg@5 means are 0.62 (DocVQA) and 0.90 (InfoVQA). Spearman(baseline, loss) within dataset is not significant for hierarchical (DocVQA 0.16-0.21; InfoVQA -0.06 to -0.23), but it is -0.41 for adaptive on InfoVQA (p=0.009).
findings.method: Paired Wilcoxon, sign test and bootstrap CI over the 40 models measured on both datasets; Spearman against baseline.
findings.confounds: The datasets differ in baseline headroom (0.62 vs 0.90), so loss in relative retention is not comparable in scale. Differences in page layout, query style and corpus are not separable. DocVQA has slightly more vectors per page in 78% of models, which by the redundancy idea would predict less DocVQA loss, so vector count does not explain the gap. The 1.6-1.8x ratio of means is dominated by a few lossy models. Sibling checkpoints inflate effective n.
findings.practical_implication: Plan a small extra safety margin for document-style pages (DocVQA-like) compared with infographic-style pages; do not assume InfoVQA results transfer.
findings.question: token-merging

verdict.recomputed: Own script (v2.py) on measured.json, rows labelled hierarchical_merge(0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1) and adaptive_merge(0.6), loss = 1 - retention, paired by model. Only 37 models have both datasets and merge rows, not 40: vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged, colqwen2-v1.0-merged and colqwen2.5-v0.2 have no merge rows in measured.json or the campaign files. Ratio of mean loss DocVQA/InfoVQA: 1.73, 1.76, 1.75, 1.57, 1.70 (adaptive); this matches the claimed 1.6-1.8x. Paired mean difference in pp (bootstrap 95% CI, Wilcoxon p): 0.17 (-0.08 to 0.40, 0.17); 0.32 (-0.06 to 0.70, 0.14); 0.42 (-0.04 to 0.94, 0.13); keep 0.1 0.97 (0.28 to 1.86, 0.012); adaptive 0.84 (0.37 to 1.32, 0.003). Adaptive: DocVQA worse in 26/37, sign p=0.02. Baseline means 0.617 (DocVQA) and 0.902 (InfoVQA), as claimed. Spearman(baseline, loss) is not significant within dataset for hierarchical (DocVQA 0.17 to 0.25, InfoVQA -0.10 to -0.27), and is -0.46 (p=0.005, n=37) for adaptive on InfoVQA, as claimed. Robustness: dropping ColNetraEmbed shrinks keep 0.1 to 0.64 pp (CI 0.15 to 1.11, p=0.02) and the keep 0.33/0.25 ratios to about 1.5; adaptive is stable at 0.77 pp (p=0.004). Excluding 13 models whose note or first row mentions float16 (crude heuristic) leaves 24 models, and every comparison becomes null: keep 0.5 diff 0.01 pp, keep 0.1 0.84 pp (CI -0.11 to 2.10, p=0.17), adaptive 0.47 pp (CI -0.11 to 1.07, p=0.13), ratios 1.05 to 1.58. One model per family (about 20 families, crude name-based grouping) gives larger and clearer differences (0.47 to 1.02 pp, with keep 0.5, 0.33 and adaptive significant, keep 0.25 and 0.1 not), so sibling inflation does not manufacture the effect. Loss in absolute ndcg@5 points (relative loss times baseline) is DocVQA 0.25/0.45/0.61/1.65/1.24 pp versus InfoVQA 0.20/0.37/0.51/1.54/1.06 pp, a ratio of only about 1.07 to 1.23.
verdict.issues: 1) n is 37, not 40, for all five settings. The claim says 40 for three of them and 37 only for keep 0.1; the claimed means and p-values nevertheless closely match my n=37 numbers. 2) The 1.6-1.8x ratio is a ratio of means of relative-retention loss, and it largely reflects the baseline gap (0.62 vs 0.90). In absolute ndcg@5 the gap is about 1.1-1.2x, so the DocVQA-worse claim is mostly a scale artefact. The claim acknowledges the scale issue but still calls it a real DocVQA-loses-more pattern. 3) The adaptive and keep 0.1 significance is fragile. It disappears when the 13 possibly float16-inference models are dropped (adaptive p=0.13, keep 0.1 p=0.17, n=24), so those models carry the effect. That subset is confounded with model type and size, and my float16 detection is only a text heuristic. 4) Keep 0.1 depends on ColNetraEmbed (0.97 to 0.64 pp without it). The sign test at keep 0.1 is null (21/37 DocVQA worse). Medians of the ratio are erratic (0.9 to 2.8), so the mean ratio is dominated by a few lossy models. 5) Siblings and the dataset=modality-like confound (different layout and queries) remain unresolved. About 20 families gives roughly 20 effective units. 6) About 25 tests across settings and subsets were run, with no multiplicity correction. Exploratory, post-hoc, and the query-bootstrap CIs of the inputs ignore corpus sampling.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among the 37 models with merge results on both ViDoRe sets (not 40), the mean relative-retention loss from token merging is about 1.6-1.8x larger on DocVQA than InfoVQA, but this is largely a baseline-headroom scale effect: in absolute ndcg@5 points the gap is about 1.1-1.2x (under 0.2 pp at keep 0.5-0.25, about 0.1-0.2 pp at keep 0.1, about 0.2 pp for adaptive). Paired relative-loss differences are under 1 pp, and the CIs include zero at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25. The keep 0.1 (p=0.012) and adaptive (p=0.003) differences are weak, exploratory, and not robust: they depend on ColNetraEmbed (keep 0.1) and on the roughly 13 float16-note models, and they vanish when those are removed. They do survive one-model-per-family dedupe for adaptive. Treat as a weak, unconfirmed tendency, not a dataset effect.

findings.title: Adaptive merge versus hierarchical at matched keep fraction: slightly worse on images, better on text, collapses on an anisotropic text model
findings.claim: At the same number of vectors kept, adaptive_merge(0.6) loses about 0.2 pp more than hierarchical on image pages, but about 1.8 pp less on SciFact. With radius 0.6 and no centring it keeps only about 1 vector per document on answerai-colbert-small.
findings.evidence: Matched comparison against hierarchical loss interpolated log-linearly in keep (82 of 95 cells; 13 with adaptive keep < 0.1 excluded): DocVQA n=32, median keep 0.159, adaptive loss 2.08% vs 1.87%, diff +0.20 pp (CI -0.27 to +0.67, Wilcoxon p=0.48, adaptive worse in 18); InfoVQA n=36, median keep 0.197, 1.13% vs 0.94%, diff +0.19 pp (CI 0.03-0.36, p=0.028, adaptive worse in 24); SciFact n=14, median keep 0.323, 2.08% vs 3.85%, diff -1.77 pp (CI -3.7 to -0.4, p=0.042, adaptive worse in 5). Adaptive keep fraction varies by model: 0.038-0.316 DocVQA, 0.079-0.394 InfoVQA, 0.004-0.47 SciFact. answerai-colbert-small: 1.05 vectors/doc and retention 0.612 at radius 0.6 (0.614 at 0.5 with 1.00 vectors; 0.624 at 0.7 with 1.81 vectors); hierarchical keep 0.25 retains 0.939 for the same model. Ward max_distance rows exist for only 4 models: d=1.3 gives 5.2-8.1x compression with 0.8-3.0 pp loss on the three image models, while answerai loses 12.4 pp at d=1.3 (10.5 vectors) and 4.3 pp at d=0.8.
findings.method: Interpolate each cell's hierarchical loss-vs-log-keep curve at the adaptive keep fraction, then paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon on the differences.
findings.confounds: Interpolation between four grid points is crude, especially between 0.1 and 0.25. Adaptive keep differs per model, so the matched cells have different keep fractions. Text n=14 and p=0.042 is one of many tests. The adaptive stage had only one setting measured for most models. The answerai collapse is a configuration issue (the stage docstring recommends center='mean' for anisotropic encoders), not necessarily a flaw of the method.
findings.practical_implication: For image pages, hierarchical at a fixed ratio is at least as good as adaptive at matched size; adaptive is worth a closer look for text, where it self-adjusts per document. Never use adaptive_merge with an absolute cosine radius on text models without centring.
findings.question: token-merging

verdict.recomputed:
From measured.json I rebuilt the matched comparison. The hierarchical curve uses single-stage ratio rows with no max_distance, and the keep fraction is vectors_per_doc divided by the baseline vectors_per_doc. I interpolated hierarchical loss log-linearly in keep, excluded adaptive keep below 0.1, and excluded cells outside the hierarchical keep range. That gives 86 cells, against the claim's 82. The difference comes from 4 extra cells that use the radius 0.7 or 0.5 settings. Restricting to adaptive_merge radius 0.6 with center='mean' (the only configuration with enough cells) reproduces the claim:
- DocVQA: n=32, median keep 0.160, adaptive loss 2.08% vs hierarchical 1.87%, diff +0.20 pp (bootstrap CI -0.28 to +0.68), Wilcoxon p=0.48, adaptive worse in 18.
- InfoVQA: n=36, median keep 0.197, 1.13% vs 0.94%, diff +0.19 pp (CI 0.04 to 0.36), p=0.028, adaptive worse in 24.
- SciFact: n=14, median keep 0.323, 2.08% vs 3.85%, diff -1.77 pp (CI -3.58 to -0.35), p=0.042, adaptive worse in 5.
- Including the 4 extra cells barely changes anything: DocVQA +0.24 (p=0.33), InfoVQA +0.18 (p=0.033), SciFact unchanged.

The answerai-colbert-small numbers also match, from the same file:
- Adaptive with no centring keeps 1.05 vectors/doc at radius 0.6 (keep 0.0045), with retention 0.612. Radius 0.5 gives 1.00 vector and radius 0.7 gives 1.81 vectors.
- Hierarchical ratio 0.25 retains 0.939.
- Ward max_distance 1.3 gives 10.5 vectors and retention 0.876 (12.4 pp loss). max_distance 0.8 gives retention 0.957 (4.3 pp loss).

Leave-one-model-out on SciFact keeps the diff at -1.0 to -2.0 pp, with p between 0.013 and 0.08. The p-value rises above 0.05 in 8 of the 14 leave-outs. Dropping LFM2-ColBERT-350M, the model with the largest gain, shrinks the diff to -1.02 pp (CI -1.95 to -0.12, p=0.08).
verdict.issues:
1. The image result is a null or negligible effect, not "slightly worse". DocVQA has CI spanning 0 and p=0.48. InfoVQA has p=0.028 with a +0.19 pp difference, which is tiny. It would not survive a correction for the roughly 3 or more tests in this family.
2. The SciFact advantage is fragile. It rests on 14 models, p=0.042 uncorrected, and is not robust to leave-one-out (p up to 0.08). The adaptive loss is nearly flat at about 2% while the hierarchical baseline is a coarse log-linear interpolation between grid points (0.25 and 0.5 on text). Most of the text gap is likely interpolation and model-specific, driven by a few models such as LFM2-ColBERT-350M.
3. Modality and dataset are confounded, so "better on text" really means "better on SciFact with these 14 text models".
4. Several of the 14 SciFact models are siblings (colbertv2.0 and lightonai/colbertv2.0, LFM2 and LFM2.5, the two mxbai-edge models, ColBERT-Zero, LateOn and mLateOn), so the effective n is below 14.
5. Every matched cell uses radius 0.6 with center='mean'. The claim text says "adaptive_merge(0.6)" without mentioning centring. The setting is not matched in keep fraction across models (each model has one adaptive keep).
6. Text keep fractions are 0.2 to 0.47, so the SciFact comparison sits mostly in the 0.25 to 0.5 gap of the hierarchical grid. DocVQA and InfoVQA sit in the 0.1 to 0.25 gap, where interpolation is crudest.
7. The answerai collapse is real but is an uncentred configuration. The same stage with center='mean' is the setting used for all 14 other text models. Its only evidence is 3 uncentred rows on one model, so it shows a configuration pitfall for anisotropic encoders, not a flaw of adaptive_merge. Hierarchical on answerai also shows its largest loss at ratio 0.25.
8. The wording "keeps only about 1 vector per document" is correct (1.05).
verdict.corrected_claim: At matched keep fraction, adaptive_merge(0.6, center='mean') is indistinguishable from hierarchical_merge on image pages (DocVQA +0.20 pp, CI -0.28 to +0.68; InfoVQA +0.19 pp, CI 0.04 to 0.36, p=0.028 uncorrected). On SciFact it loses about 1.8 pp less (n=14 models, CI -3.6 to -0.35, p=0.042 uncorrected). This is a weak, exploratory pattern: it weakens to p of about 0.06 to 0.08 when dropping any of several models, sibling checkpoints are included, and the comparison rests on a coarse interpolation of the hierarchical curve. Without centring, radius 0.6 collapses to about 1 vector per document on the anisotropic answerai-colbert-small (retention 0.612). Centring is the recommended setting for anisotropic encoders and was used for all other text models.

findings.title: Weak pattern: pages with more vectors tolerate heavy merging slightly better
findings.claim: Among image models, higher baseline vectors per page goes with somewhat lower loss at keep 0.1 and 0.25, consistent in sign across all eight dataset x ratio cells, but family-confounded and not supported by two other checks.
findings.evidence: Spearman(baseline vectors/page, loss) within dataset, image models: DocVQA -0.19/-0.14/-0.28/-0.35 at keep 0.5/0.33/0.25/0.1 (p 0.25/0.37/0.078/0.031); InfoVQA -0.26/-0.43/-0.20/-0.33 (p 0.10/0.006/0.21/0.046). Pooled with dataset-demeaned ranks: keep 0.1 rho -0.34 (model-bootstrap CI -0.52 to -0.10, n=74), keep 0.25 -0.24 (-0.45 to -0.04, n=80), adaptive -0.10 (-0.35 to 0.15). Without ColNetraEmbed (the only image model under 500 vectors, loss 19.4%/6.4% at 0.1): keep 0.1 rho -0.30 (p=0.076) and -0.27 (p=0.11). Family-bootstrap CIs for the per-dataset cells reach zero in 6 of 8 hierarchical cells. Mean loss at 0.1 by vectors/page bin (DocVQA): 500-800 2.8% (n=11), 800-1100 2.1% (13), 1100+ 2.0% (10). Not supported: within-model DocVQA-InfoVQA difference in vectors vs difference in loss rho -0.22 (p=0.20, n=37), and the adaptive keep fraction as a redundancy proxy correlates positively with hierarchical loss (rho 0.15-0.28, not significant). SciFact (n=14-15): rho 0.04-0.29 at keep 0.33-0.1, no relation. OLS bv coefficient -0.0112 per doubling (CI -0.0194 to +0.001).
findings.method: Spearman correlations with family-cluster and model-cluster bootstrap, rank pooling within dataset, leave-one-out of ColNetraEmbed, within-model paired contrast, OLS.
findings.confounds: Baseline vectors per page is nearly a family constant (ColPali 1038, ColQwen2/2.5 759, ColQwen3 1222), so the effect is between families, with only 8-12 models in each large family. Higher-vector models also differ in architecture and training. Low-vector tail rests on one model. Many correlations were run (about 40 in this question alone) and none is corrected for multiplicity.
findings.practical_implication: Do not claim that more vectors per page means more redundancy. The data suggest only that what matters is vectors remaining (F2), not vectors originally present. A direct test would need controlled pages (e.g. one model, varying resolution).
findings.question: token-merging

verdict.recomputed:
I recomputed everything from measured.json. Loss is 1 minus the retention of hierarchical_merge(keep), and baseline vectors per page comes from the float32 row. There are 80 image model-dataset rows, 37 per dataset in the pooled analysis (74 pooled).

Per-dataset Spearman between vectors per page and loss:
- DocVQA: -0.18 (keep 0.5), -0.17 (0.33), -0.31 (0.25), -0.36 (0.1), with p 0.275, 0.31, 0.064, 0.029.
- InfoVQA: -0.23, -0.45, -0.16, -0.32, with p 0.173, 0.005, 0.337, 0.051.
- These are close to the claimed values but not identical; the 0.25 cells differ most (-0.31 vs -0.28, and -0.16 vs -0.20).
- The sign is negative in all 8 cells.

Pooled with dataset-demeaned ranks, n=74:
- keep 0.1: rho -0.35, model-bootstrap 95% CI -0.55 to -0.12, family-bootstrap CI -0.53 to -0.07. This matches the claimed -0.34 (-0.52 to -0.10).
- keep 0.25: rho -0.24, model-bootstrap CI -0.44 to -0.02. This matches the claimed -0.24.
- keep 0.33: rho -0.31, model-bootstrap CI -0.52 to -0.08.
- keep 0.5: rho -0.20, model-bootstrap CI -0.40 to +0.03.

Leave out ColNetraEmbed (n=72):
- keep 0.1: rho -0.29.
- keep 0.25: rho -0.17.
- keep 0.33: rho -0.26.
- keep 0.5: rho -0.18.
- The 0.25 effect shrinks by about 30% and the 0.1 effect by about 16%.

Family structure at keep 0.1 (mean vectors per page, mean loss):
- colgemma (2 rows): 269 vectors, 12.9% loss.
- colmodernvbert (2): 896 vectors, 5.6% loss.
- All other families: 1.4-2.2% loss, with no monotone relation to vectors per page.
- neomme (4): 2148 vectors, 1.35% loss.
- colvec (4): 1363 vectors, 0.8% loss.
- colpali (14): 1031 vectors, 1.4% loss.
- colqwen3 (8): 1169 vectors, 2.0% loss.
- colqwen2/2.5 (20): 839 vectors, 2.1% loss.
- colqwen3.5 (12): 955 vectors, 2.2% loss.

Within large families at keep 0.1:
- colqwen: rho +0.05.
- colqwen3.5: rho +0.06.
- colpali: rho -0.24 (p=0.42).
- colqwen3: rho +0.76 (p=0.027), the opposite sign.

I did not rerun the secondary checks (within-model difference, adaptive keep fraction, SciFact, OLS), so those are unverified.
verdict.issues:
1. The pooled effect is a between-family effect. Within the large families it is absent or reversed (colqwen3 +0.76, colqwen and colqwen3.5 about 0). Baseline vectors per page is close to a family constant, so this is a family or architecture effect, not evidence that more vectors per page cause better merging.
2. The negative correlation is driven by a few low-vector or older families (colgemma/ColNetra at 269 vectors with 12.9% loss, colmodernvbert at 896 vectors with 5.6% loss) and by the highest-vector, low-loss families (colvec, neomme). The middle of the range is flat.
3. Dropping ColNetraEmbed weakens the 0.25 result, and the model-bootstrap CI at 0.5 includes zero.
4. The model-level bootstrap treats sibling checkpoints as independent. The family bootstrap (10 families) is wider, but the pooled CIs still exclude zero. The per-dataset p-values are marginal and, with about 40 uncorrected tests, mostly would not survive correction.
5. The query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling, and each dataset has only 500 pages. Float16-inference baselines were not examined.
6. Per-cell values differ slightly from those given, but the sign pattern and magnitude are confirmed.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among image models on ViDoRe DocVQA and InfoVQA, baseline vectors per page has a weak negative rank correlation with hierarchical-merge loss (pooled rho about -0.35 at keep 0.1 and -0.24 at keep 0.25, n=74, sign negative in all 8 cells). It is almost entirely a between-family contrast: colgemma/ColNetra and colmodernvbert, with few vectors, lose more, while colvec and neomme, with many vectors, lose less. Within the large families (colqwen, colqwen3.5, colpali, colqwen3) it is absent or reversed. It shrinks without ColNetraEmbed (to -0.29 at keep 0.1 and -0.17 at keep 0.25). It was found post hoc among many uncorrected tests, so it should be treated as a hypothesis about family differences, not as a vectors-per-page effect.

results.summary:
Exploratory, post-hoc analysis, not preregistered: about 35 inferential tests (no multiplicity correction) and about 60 descriptive intervals. project(k) is an uncentred PCA fitted on the evaluation corpus itself (second-moment matrix of document token vectors, no query vectors), so results are optimistic about a separately fitted deployment. project(k, random) is a single seed-0 orthonormal Gaussian map scaled by sqrt(d/k).

Main results:
- Retention tracks the absolute number of kept dimensions much better than the fraction k/d, with a weak d dependence of roughly d^0.3.
- Wide models tolerate k=128 at a cost that grows with d: about 1% at 320-640 d, about 4% at 4096 d.
- There is no single safe k.
- PCA beats random by about 1.6 pp at k/d=0.25 (+12 pp at k=32 on 128-d models).
- Random projection collapses on the text models at k=32.
- Projection costs are almost independent of merging and codecs.

findings.title: Projection retention follows absolute k, not k/d; d enters only weakly (about d^0.3)
findings.claim: Retention after PCA projection is explained far better by the absolute number of kept dimensions than by k/d. A residual dependence on d remains: the loss scales roughly as k^-2.35 * d^0.65, so the dimension needed for a given retention grows about as d^0.3 to d^0.5, not linearly.
findings.evidence: Leave-one-model-out CV MSE: isotonic(log k) 0.0063, isotonic(log k/d) 0.0706, OLS(log k, log d) 0.0317. Wide models only (12): 0.00147 / 0.00347 / 0.00268. Retention>0.7 only: 0.0017 / 0.0059 / 0.0039. Regression log(loss) = 3.11 - 2.35 log k + 0.65 log d (n=172 unit-k points, 49 models); cluster-bootstrap 95% CI for log k [-2.64,-2.09], for log d [+0.51,+0.81]. Pure k/d would need +2.35 on log d; absolute-k would need 0. k98 medians (retention >=0.98): d=320 97 (range 48-123), d=640 136, d=2560 185, d=4096 225; at 128 d, 33 of 62 units are still below 0.98 at k=64. k95 medians: 58 (128 d), 72 (320), 80 (640), 131 (4096). Collapse example: 128 d at k=32 (k/d 0.25) keeps 0.800 [0.772,0.825]; 320 d at k=40 (k/d 0.125) keeps 0.828 [0.776,0.896]. The log-log slope of k_thr on d among uncensored units is 0.27 [0.25,0.32] at 95%, 0.38 at 98%, 0.48 at 99%. These slopes are biased because censored units are dropped; treat 0.3-0.5 as a rough range.
findings.method: Unit curves per (model, dataset, k): pure project(k) retention where available, otherwise mean over 4 merge ratios of ret(hierarchical_merge>project k)/ret(hierarchical_merge). Leave-one-model-out CV comparing isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) fits on log k vs log k/d and OLS on (log k, log d); OLS on log-loss with model-cluster bootstrap (2000 resamples); log-linear interpolation of k at thresholds 0.95/0.98/0.99.
findings.confounds: 128-d models (37, most of them siblings in the ColPali/ColQwen families) dominate the steep region. Wide models number 12, with 1-2 per d value above 640. Sibling checkpoints are correlated. Retention near 1 is noise-limited. The merge-controlled proxy was used for 128-d at k=16/32. The log-loss regression is restricted to loss between 1% and 50%, which is selection-biased. k_thr slopes are biased by censoring. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling. Whether the exponent 0.3 holds beyond the measured d values is unknown.
findings.practical_implication: Do not set a projection target as a fraction of d. Specify k in absolute dimensions and let it rise slowly with d: about 64 for 128-d, about 100-140 for 320-640-d, about 200-350 for 2.5k-4k-d, depending on the retention wanted.

verdict.recomputed:
I rebuilt the unit curves from measured.json. I used pure PCA project(k) where it exists, otherwise the mean over merge ratios of ret(hm>project k)/ret(hm). Keeping only k<d gives 292 unit-k points. Of those, 172 across 49 models have loss between 1% and 50%.
- Regression: log(loss) = 3.11 - 2.35 log k + 0.65 log d, which matches the claim exactly. The model-cluster bootstrap (2000 resamples) gives log k [-2.64,-2.10] and log d [0.51,0.80].
- Leave-one-model-out CV MSE, isotonic(log k) / isotonic(log k/d) / OLS(log k, log d):
  - All points: 0.0063 / 0.0905 / 0.0317. The claim says 0.0706 for k/d, a small mismatch, but the ranking is the same.
  - Wide models only (d>128): 0.00185 / 0.00363 / 0.00268. The claim says 0.00147 / 0.00347 / 0.00268.
  - Retention>0.7: 0.0017 / 0.0095 / 0.0039. The claim says 0.0017 / 0.0059 / 0.0039.
- Within d=128 alone, k and k/d are the same variable, so the 128-d CV is identical (0.00895) and carries no information on the question.
- The merge-controlled proxy matches pure project(k) where both exist (60 pairs at k=80 to 1024). Differences are typically within 1 point, so the proxy is not driving the result.
- Rank check at k=128, one value per wide model (12 models): loss rises with d. Spearman 0.91, bootstrap CI [0.69,0.97].
  - Mean loss is 0.5% to 1.4% at d=320, 1.7% to 2.4% at d=640, and 3.6% to 4.4% at d=2560 and 4096.
  - The one exception is EVIE-4.5B at d=2048, with 1.4% loss.
- Dropping any single d level (4096, 2560, 640 or 320) leaves the d exponent between 0.64 and 0.73, so no single level drives it.
verdict.issues:
1. The exponents are not stable across subsets, though their ratio is. The d exponent is 0.65 on the full mixed set, 0.34 [0.21,0.49] on pure-measured points only (98 points, 47 models), and 0.37 [0.17,0.48] on wide models only (56 points, 12 models). The k exponent changes with it, from -2.35 to -1.18 on pure points and -1.68 on wide models. The implied threshold scaling d^(b_d/|b_k|) is 0.28, 0.29 and 0.22 in the three cases, so the d^0.3 claim is consistent. The stated 'k^-2.35 d^0.65' is a property of the mixed proxy/pure sample, not a general law.
2. k and d are nearly separated in the design. The only points at k=16, 32 and 64 are d=128, and k>=80 is almost all wide models. The d effect rests on about 12 wide models with 1 to 6 models per d level, and the 320-d group is mostly Qwen3-based siblings (Tomoro, Vultron, athrael). Sibling-aware inference was not done and would widen the CIs.
3. The log-loss regression is selection-biased by the 1% to 50% loss window, as the claim notes. Widening the window to 0.3% to 90% gives k -2.31 and d 0.74, so the window is not decisive.
4. Retention near 1 is noise-limited, and EVIE-4.5B shows retention at or above 1, which makes loss-based estimates unreliable there.
5. 'Absolute k beats k/d' is mainly established by the wide-model subset, where the CV gap is 0.0019 vs 0.0036, about a 2x difference. The full-sample 14x gap is inflated by 128-d points where k/d is just k/128 and the two predictors differ only through the wide models. Separately, OLS(log k, log d) loses to isotonic(log k) in CV in every subset, so a d term does not improve out-of-model prediction. I did not test isotonic on k with an added d term.
6. The k_thr medians and slopes were not recomputed. The 99% slope in particular rests on censored data.
7. This is exploratory and post-hoc. I ran about 15 comparisons or regressions.
verdict.corrected_claim: Weakly to moderately supported: among the measured models, PCA-projection retention is predicted better by absolute k than by k/d. At matched k=128, loss rises with d (Spearman 0.91 across 12 wide models, CI [0.69,0.97]), so d does matter. The dimension needed for a given retention grows roughly as d^0.2 to d^0.3, not linearly (implied by exponent ratios of 0.22 to 0.29 in three subsets). The specific exponents k^-2.35 and d^0.65 hold only for the mixed proxy/pure sample. On pure-measured points the exponents are about k^-1.2 and d^0.35. Extrapolation beyond d=128 to 4096 and any per-family claims are unsupported given about 12 wide models, with sibling correlation not modelled.

findings.title: Wide models tolerate k=128 at a cost that rises with d; there is no single safe k
findings.claim: Projecting 320-640-d models to 128 dims costs about 1-2% nDCG@5 retention, and projecting 2048-4096-d models to 128 costs about 1.4-4.4%. 80 dims costs about 3.6% at 320 d and 4.7% at 640 d. A single absolute 'safe k' does not exist, but k=128 is a workable default for d<=640, and 256-512 is needed on 4096-d to reach 98%.
findings.method: Per-model mean loss at k=128 for D>128; Spearman with permutation test (20000 shuffles, treating models as exchangeable); Wilson intervals for threshold shares per k and d-group.
findings.confounds: Only 12 wide models, with 2 each at d=2048/2560 (counted by models) and 4096 and correlated siblings. 4096-d models are 8B-class float16-inference models (EVIE-8B, Nemotron-8B), so size, fp16 baseline and d are collinear. EVIE's card says shorter prefixes are usable, so EVIE-4.5B may be Matryoshka-trained (truncation not measured). k=80 was only tried on d<=640. The permutation p treats models as exchangeable despite family structure. Intervals are over small n. PCA is fitted on the scored corpus. Results are DocVQA/InfoVQA only.
findings.practical_implication: Default to project(128) for 320-640-d models and expect roughly 1-2% loss; expect about 4% on 4096-d. Use project(256) when 98% retention is needed on 2.5k-4k-d. Do not extrapolate the 128-d finding 'k=64 is fine' (only 47% of units reach 0.98).

verdict.recomputed: Recomputed from the raw wide/*.json files, using rows labelled exactly project(k). That gives 12 wide models (d>128) and 49 models with project rows overall. My permutation p is about 0.0004 (5000 shuffles), so the claimed p<0.0001 is not reproduced, though the result is still significant. Drop-one rho stays 0.88-0.92. After collapsing to the five distinct d values (320, 640, 2048, 2560, 4096), rho is 0.90 and the exact permutation p is 0.083, which is not significant. The models-as-exchangeable permutation overstates significance, as the analyst partly admitted. 2) d is collinear with model size, fp16 inference and family. The 4096-d units are only EVIE-8B and Nemotron-8B, on two datasets each, so "4096 needs 256-512" rests on 4 units from 2 models. The 2048 point is a single model (EVIE-4.5B) and may be Matryoshka-trained. 3) The 640-d group is a single family (ColVec), and the 320-d group is mostly Vultron and Tomoro siblings. 4) The relationship is not clean: Nemotron-4B at 2560 d loses 3.6% while EVIE-4.5B at 2048 d loses 1.4%, so a model-specific effect is plausible. The 2048-4096 range of "1.4-4.4%" spans a 3x spread. 5) k=80 is non-monotone for some models: Tomoro-8B loses 5.0% at k=80 but 0.7% at k=128. 6) The p value (<0.0001 from 20000 shuffles) and the 29/62 count do not reproduce exactly. 7) Retention intervals are query-bootstrap only and ignore corpus sampling. PCA is fitted on the scored corpus. Only DocVQA and InfoVQA were used. 8) "Workable default for d<=640" is supported: 16/16 units reach >=0.95 and 13/16 reach >=0.98. The Wilson lower bound for >=0.98 is only about 57%.
verdict.corrected_claim: In exploratory data from 12 wide models, k=128 projection costs about 0.5-1.4% nDCG@5 at d=320, about 1.7-2.4% at d=640 (one family), 1.4% at 2048 d (one model), 3.6% at 2560 d (one model) and about 4.2-4.4% at 4096 d (two fp16 8B models). Loss rises with d (rho 0.91 over models). Because models sharing a d value are nearly exchangeable, this is a weak-to-moderate trend: at the level of five distinct d values the exact permutation p is 0.08, and d is confounded with model size, family and fp16 baseline. k=128 met >=0.95 in all 16 units at 320-640 d, and >=0.98 in 13 of 16. k=80 was clearly worse (>=0.98 in 3/16, mean 0.964). On the two 4096-d models, k=128 gave 0.957 retention and k=256 gave 0.985. The "no single safe k" statement is reasonable, but the 4096-d figures come from 2 models and should not be generalised. Use 3.3% at 320 d for k=80, and 26/62 for the 128-d k=64 >=0.98 count.

findings.title: Fitted PCA beats random projection at equal k, modestly and with shrinking margin
findings.claim: At equal k, corpus-fitted PCA retains more than a random orthonormal projection. The advantage is about 1.6 pp at k/d=0.25 on wide models and about 12 pp at k=32 on 128-d models, and it shrinks as k grows.
findings.evidence: Equal-k pure pairs (24 units, 12 models, all at k/d=0.25): mean PCA minus random +1.61 pp, cluster-bootstrap CI [+0.57,+2.86]; PCA ahead in 16/24 units and 10/12 models; exact sign test p=0.039, Wilcoxon p=0.016. By d group: 320 d +1.5 pp (12 units), 640 d -0.3 pp (4 units), 2048-4096 d +2.7 pp (8 units; Nemotron-4B DocVQA at k=640: PCA 0.993 vs random 0.876). 128-d at k=32: PCA (merge-controlled) 0.800 vs random 0.676, +12.4 pp CI [+7.1,+18.6]; PCA ahead in 50/62 units; random wins in 12 units by up to 15.6 pp. Mean random loss at k/d=0.25: k=32 37.5% (37 models), k=80 4.8% (6), k=160 1.0% (2), k=512-1024 0.5-2.1%.
findings.method: Paired differences by (model, dataset) at identical k, cluster bootstrap over models, exact sign and Wilcoxon on model-level means; 128-d comparison uses merge-controlled PCA-32 (validated against pure PCA to within 0.5 pp) against pure random-32.
findings.confounds: A single random draw (seed 0) per (d, k) is shared by all models, so seed variance is unmeasured and model-to-model spread partly reflects one draw's alignment with each model's principal directions. All pure equal-k pairs lie at k/d=0.25, so k and d move together. 12 models, mostly siblings, and 4 of 12 had a 640/160-d random result at least as good as PCA. PCA is fit on the evaluated corpus (transductive); random is not. Wide default grid pairs PCA-64 with random-32, which is not equal k and was not used.
findings.practical_implication: Prefer fitted PCA over random projection, especially at small k or on text-like models. At k>=160 the difference is small enough (1-3 pp) that a data-free random map is a tolerable fallback, but with a single seed measured, check multiple seeds before relying on it.

verdict.recomputed:
Wide models, equal-k pure pairs, built from the raw wide JSONs and matched by pipeline stage method rather than label. The random-projection row in some files is labelled "project(640)" without ", random", so label matching misses it (it dropped Nemotron-4B and gave 22 units, 11 models).

- Families (Tomoro, colqwen3.5, Nemotron, EVIE, Vultron, webAI): family-mean +1.46 pp, bootstrap CI [+0.26, +2.96], but only 4/6 families ahead (sign p=0.69). Siblings are not independent, so the model-level p-values overstate the evidence.

With merge(0.25) it is +11.0 pp.
- The model-level mean is +16.1 pp, CI [8.6, 24.3], because the text models dominate.
- Image only: +5.2 pp (50 units, 25 models), model-bootstrap CI [+2.3, +8.3], 39/50 ahead. Text only (SciFact): +38.6 pp (12 units), CI [+21, +57]. Random-32 loses 24.9% on image models and 64.7% on text models.
- Merge cost: merge(0.33)>project(128) loses about 1.2 pp on average, so merge-controlled PCA slightly understates pure PCA. I could not recompute the claim's "within 0.5 pp" validation, because no pure PCA-32 row exists in the 128-d files.

1. Direction and size of the wide-model result reproduce exactly (+1.61, CI [0.57, 2.83], 10/12, p=0.039, Wilcoxon p=0.016), but the evidence is weak. Roughly 3/24 pairs are CI-separated. The result comes from DocVQA (+3.0 pp) and is about zero on InfoVQA (+0.2 pp). Without the single Nemotron-4B DocVQA draw (11.7 pp) the mean is +1.2 pp. The family-level sign test is not significant (4/6 families). Because Nemotron-4B and 8B, EVIE-4.5B and 8B, and the three Vultron models are siblings, the model-level tests overstate independence.
2. "Shrinks as k grows" is confounded. All pairs lie at k/d = 0.25, so k, d and modality move together. The 128-d point mixes 12 SciFact text models (+38.6 pp) with image models (+5.2 pp). The large 128-d gap is largely a text-model effect, partly because random-32 collapses far more on text than on image. The decline from 12 pp (k=32) to 1.6 pp (wide) therefore cannot be attributed to k. Within image models only, the 128-d gap (+5 pp) versus the 320-d gap (+1.5 pp) is a weak, 2-point trend.
3. Within the wide models the trend with d is non-monotone: 320 d +1.5, 640 d -0.3, 2048 d +0.5, 2560 d +6.7 (a single outlier model), 4096 d +1.9. The "2048-4096 d +2.7 pp" subgroup is only 8 units and is inflated by that outlier.
4. Single random seed (0) per (d, k). Seed variance is unmeasured, and the 11.7 pp and 15.6 pp extremes may be draw artefacts. The raw data cannot test this.
5. PCA is fit on the evaluated corpus and random is not (transductive). The 128-d comparison pairs merged PCA with unmerged random. Results are noted, but not fixable from the data.
6. Pair-matching pitfall: some wide files label the random row "project(640)" with no ", random". Anyone matching on label will silently drop or mis-assign it (my first attempt gave 22 units / 11 models). The pipeline `method` field is the reliable key.
7. Exploratory and post-hoc. Retention above 1 is noise (clipping at 1 changes nothing). No float16-baseline effect could be isolated, since the dtype field was empty in these files.
8. The tests were about 12 and none were corrected for multiplicity.
verdict.corrected_claim: At equal k (k/d = 0.25) on 12 wide image-retrieval models (ViDoRe DocVQA and InfoVQA, single seed-0 random draw), corpus-fitted PCA retains on average about 1.6 pp more ndcg@5 than a random orthonormal projection (model-cluster bootstrap CI +0.6 to +2.8). This is a weak and fragile effect. It sits mostly on DocVQA (+3.0 pp) and is near zero on InfoVQA (+0.2 pp). It is partly driven by one unit, Nemotron-4B DocVQA at k=640 (about +11.7 pp, one draw), and dropping it gives about +1.2 pp. Only 3 of 24 pairs have non-overlapping CIs, and the sibling-heavy models make the model-level p-values (0.039 sign, 0.016 Wilcoxon) optimistic. The family-level sign test is not significant. At 128-d, k=32, merge-controlled PCA beats pure random-32 by about +11.7 pp on average over 62 units. That gap is much larger on the 12 SciFact text models (+38.6 pp) than on the 25 image models (+5.2 pp, CI +2.3 to +8.3), so the 12 pp figure is not an image-model estimate. The data do not show a clean "shrinks as k grows" law. k, d, modality and dataset are confounded, and the trend is non-monotone across the wide models. A defensible statement is that PCA is rarely worse than random and is usually modestly better, with large gains concentrated at aggressive small-k compression of 128-d models.
