findings.title: Random projection collapses for text models at k=32 while PCA does not
findings.claim: On the SciFact text models, random projection to 32 dims retains only 0.36 on average and under 0.05 for four ModernBERT/LFM-family models, while PCA-32 retains about the same as for image models (0.77 vs 0.81). The gap between PCA and random is far larger for text than for image models.
findings.evidence: Random-32 retention: text (12 models) 0.363, image (25 models, mean of two datasets) 0.751. Four models below 0.05: LFM2-ColBERT-350M 0.003, LateOn 0.003, GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 0.006, mLateOn 0.032, all text. PCA-32 (merge-controlled): text 0.772, image 0.807 (Mann-Whitney p=0.41). Gap PCA minus random: text 0.409, image 0.055; difference 0.354, bootstrap CI [0.167,0.528], Mann-Whitney p=0.0037; random text < image p=0.0010. The one text geometry file (answerai-colbert-small) has corpus mean norm 0.905 vs 0.22-0.31 for the image models with geometry files, which would be consistent with a large shared component making random-projection noise swamp rankings, but this is one model and untested.
findings.method: Model-level mean over datasets; one-sided Mann-Whitney U; percentile bootstrap over models of the mean gap difference (5000 resamples).
findings.confounds: Modality and dataset are completely confounded (text = SciFact 5183 docs; image = ViDoRe 500 pages), so the effect cannot be attributed to modality. The text models are mostly ColBERT/ModernBERT-family siblings (not independent). One random seed shared across models. The geometry explanation rests on one text model. The mxbai-edge random-12/16 rows retained exactly 0.000 (d=48 and 64, k/d=0.25) and were left out as uninterpretable.
findings.practical_implication: Do not ship random projection at small k as a default for text late-interaction models; a fitted PCA is robust to the same models. If random projection is used, validate it per model, with several seeds.
findings.question: projection

verdict.recomputed: From measured.json (own script), random-32 retention: text 12 models mean 0.363, image 25 models 0.751 (docvqa 0.707, infovqa 0.796, scifact 0.363); the four <0.05 models match (0.003, 0.003, 0.006, 0.032). All models have d=128, so k/d=0.25 everywhere. No plain 'project(32)' PCA row exists in measured.json; the only PCA-32 is hierarchical_merge(0.25 or 0.33) > project(32). With merge 0.33: PCA text 0.750 vs image 0.804; gap (PCA minus random) text 0.387 vs image 0.052; difference 0.335, bootstrap CI [0.158,0.516], one-sided MW p=0.0034. With merge 0.25: PCA 0.736 vs 0.798, gap diff 0.327, CI [0.145,0.503], p=0.0045. Original numbers (0.77/0.81, 0.354) are close but not identical to mine, likely a different merge setting or averaging. Text random <0.5 in 8/12 models, image in 0/25. Dropping the 4 collapsed models: text random mean 0.539, gap-difference 0.168 CI [-0.000,0.351], p=0.081. Dropping 7 LightOn/LFM-family models (leaving 5): text random 0.631, gap-difference 0.045 CI [-0.093,0.209], p=0.46. Text random-32 by model: colbertv2.0 (BERT) 0.875, lightonai/colbertv2.0 0.89, jina-colbert-v2 0.662, Reason-ModernColBERT 0.666, mxbai-large 0.389, bert-tiny 0.338, ColBERT-Zero 0.288, LFM2.5 0.203. Lowest image models: colmodernvbert 0.583, colpali 0.607, colsmolvlm 0.633.
verdict.issues: 1) The comparison is not like-for-like: random-32 is a plain projection, PCA-32 is preceded by hierarchical_merge, which itself costs text more (merge-only 0.95-0.97 text vs 0.99 image). So the PCA numbers are depressed for text; this biases the gap in the direction of understating the PCA advantage, but the 'merge-controlled' phrase is misleading since random is not merged. 2) The effect is carried by a cluster of sibling checkpoints (LightOn/LFM/ModernBERT-based); after removing them the text-vs-image gap difference shrinks to 0.05 and is not significant. Classic BERT ColBERT models (colbertv2.0, lightonai/colbertv2.0) sit at 0.88-0.89, within the image range. So 'text' is a proxy for backbone/training family, not for modality; dataset=modality confound unresolved. 3) Single random seed per model/shared; collapse to ~0.003 may be seed- or geometry-specific; not tested. Query-bootstrap ignores corpus sampling (SciFact 5183 docs vs 500 pages: corpus size alone can lower retention for noisy scoring). 4) Mechanism (shared mean component) rests on one text geometry file; untested. 5) Exploratory, ~6 tests run by me, MW across 12 vs 25 models with correlated siblings overstates the p-values. 6) mxbai-edge rows (random 12/16 = 0.000) are other-dimension models excluded from the k=32 comparison; fine.
verdict.corrected_claim: At k=32 (k/d=0.25, d=128, one seed), random projection on SciFact text models retains 0.36 on average (range 0.003-0.89, 8 of 12 below 0.5) versus 0.75 for ViDoRe image models (none below 0.5); four LightOn/LFM/ModernBERT-family checkpoints collapse to under 0.05. PCA-32 (after hierarchical merge) retains similar amounts for both (about 0.74-0.75 text vs 0.80 image), so the PCA-minus-random gap is larger for text (about 0.39 vs 0.05). This is a weak-to-moderate, exploratory pattern driven mainly by a sibling cluster of LightOn/LFM checkpoints; BERT-based ColBERTv2 models do not collapse, and removing the sibling cluster erases the gap difference. It cannot be attributed to text modality because dataset and modality are confounded.

findings.title: Small k hurts DocVQA more than InfoVQA; the gap vanishes at large k
findings.claim: Within the same image model and k, retention is lower on DocVQA than on InfoVQA when k is small. The gap is about 5 pp at k<=40 and disappears above k=200.
findings.evidence: Paired InfoVQA minus DocVQA retention (image models): k<=40 +5.2 pp CI [3.8,6.5], 88% of 56 pairs (31 models) favour InfoVQA, Wilcoxon p=7e-9; k 41-70 +0.65 pp CI [0.06,1.3], p=0.071; k 71-100 +1.8 pp (8/8 models), p=0.0078; k 101-200 +0.5 pp CI [0.04,1.0], p=0.026; k>200 +0.02 pp CI [-0.19,0.26], p=0.67. At 128 d, k=16: 0.302 (DocVQA) vs 0.357 (InfoVQA); k=32: 0.786 vs 0.827. Baseline nDCG@5 correlates with retention within 128-d image models (InfoVQA k=64 Spearman 0.77, k=32 0.72, n=25, p<0.001; DocVQA k=32 0.51, k=64 0.10 ns).
findings.method: Paired differences per model and k, bucketed by k, cluster bootstrap over models, Wilcoxon signed-rank; Spearman between baseline nDCG@5 and retention within each (d,k,dataset).
findings.confounds: InfoVQA baselines are near 0.9, so ceiling effects compress differences; dataset also differs in page content, number of queries and vectors per page. Baseline quality, family and sibling checkpoints are entangled in the correlation, and 8 correlations were run unadjusted. Only 31 distinct image models, many siblings; buckets above k=100 contain 6-12 models. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling. k buckets mix 128-d and wide models.
findings.practical_implication: Calibrate k on the hardest dataset available (DocVQA-like, text-dense pages); a k that is safe on InfoVQA can lose several points on DocVQA when k is small.
findings.question: projection

verdict.recomputed: From raw wide JSONs (plus measured.json for older models; 40 image models with both datasets, 25 in the 128-d group at k=16/32/64). Small-k cells exist ONLY inside merge+project pipelines or random projection, not plain PCA projection. InfoVQA minus DocVQA retention (pp, bootstrap over models): hierarchical_merge(0.33)>project(16) +5.54 [3.60,7.28], n=25, 84% favour InfoVQA, Wilcoxon p=3e-5 (doc mean 0.302 vs info 0.357, matches claim); merge(0.33)>project(32) +4.48 [2.91,5.96], 88% (0.781 vs 0.826 in doc vs info, claim says 0.786/0.827, near); project(32, random) +8.85 [6.67,11.08], 96%; merge>project(40) about +8.6 (n=6); merge>project(80) +2.3 to +2.8, 8/8; merge>project(128) +0.5 to +0.7 [0.0..1.3], p=0.03-0.08 (n=37); pure PCA project(64) +0.65 [0.05,1.29], 56% positive, p=0.071 (n=25); pure PCA project(80) +1.5 (6/6, p=0.031); pure PCA 100-200 +0.18 [-0.30,0.80], p=0.5 (n=8 models, differs from claimed +0.5 p=0.026, which I get only in measured.json at k=101-200: +0.52 [0.06,1.13], 12 models, pair p=0.026, model-level p=0.11); pure PCA k>200 +0.02 to -0.12, CI includes 0 (4-6 models). Robustness at small k: trimming the 3 most extreme models each side leaves +5.96 (k=16), +4.57 (k=32); family-level (9 families) means +7.4, +5.3, +9.7 with 9/9 or 8/9 positive (p=0.004-0.008); leave-one-family-out range 4.6-7.8; holds for both float16-baseline (n=7) and float32 models (gap 5.1 vs 6.7 at k=16; 3.2 vs 7.8 at k=32). Ceiling effect: median loss ratio (1-ret_info)/(1-ret_doc) is 0.92 at k=16, 0.81 at k=32, 0.62 for random-32, 0.41 at k=128, so at k=16 the gap is not just ceiling compression, while at large k the near-1 retention makes a gap hard to see anyway.
verdict.issues: 1) 'k' is not a clean projection dimension: all k<=40 cells are merge(0.25/0.33)>project(k) (fewer vectors AND lower dim) or random projection (k=32); no plain PCA project(16/32) exists in the campaign data. So the effect cannot be attributed to projection alone; it may come from token merging (DocVQA pages, text-dense, probably lose more from merging) rather than dimension. The claim's mixing of pipelines in k buckets is a real flaw. 2) The 'vanishes above 200' part rests on 4-6 models (9-16 pairs); CI [-0.19,0.26] to [-0.30,0.51] is just uninformative-to-null, and the decline is not monotone (k=71-100 bucket has the largest pure-PCA gap, +1.5 to +1.8, n=6-8; at 128 the merge>project gap is still +0.5 to +0.7 with n=37). The decay is a plausible trend but not shown to hit zero precisely at 200. 3) 56 pairs / 31 models: pairs are not independent (same models in several pipelines); model-level counts are n=25 (one family-clustered: only 9 families), so the Wilcoxon p=7e-9 over pairs overstates; family-level p is about 0.004-0.008. 4) The claimed bucket p-values depend on the dataset used (measured.json vs wide): 100-200 pure PCA is p=0.5 in wide data. 5) Dataset DocVQA vs InfoVQA confound (page content, query count 451 vs 494, vectors per page) remains; this shows dataset difference, not an intrinsic property of 'small k'. Baseline-correlation parts not recomputed (my gap~baseline Spearman is only about 0.3-0.46, n=25, weak and unadjusted). Exploratory, post-hoc.
verdict.corrected_claim: Within the same image model, retention after merge-then-project to very low dimension (16-40 d) or random 32-d projection is lower on DocVQA than on InfoVQA by roughly 4-6 pp (merge>project(16): +5.5 pp, 95% model-bootstrap CI 3.6-7.3; project(32): +4.5, 2.9-6.0; random-32: +8.9, 6.7-11.1; 9 families, 8-9 of 9 positive, about 25 models, robust to trimming, leave-one-family-out and float16 baselines). The gap shrinks with larger k (about +2 to +3 pp at 80, about +0.5 to +0.7 pp at 128, indistinguishable from 0 for pure PCA projection at k>=100 in the few models tested). The small-k cells are merge-plus-project or random pipelines, so the gap is not attributable to dimension reduction alone, and the dataset/page-content confound remains. Moderate strength at small k; weak, low-n evidence for the 'disappears' part.

findings.title: Projection composes almost independently with merging and codecs (weak)
findings.claim: Retention of merge>project is nearly the product of the merge retention and the project retention, and int8, binary and int4 after PCA cost about what they cost alone, with small extra int4 cost.
findings.evidence: Merge-controlled vs pure PCA at the same (model, dataset, k): 60 pairs, 12 models, mean difference -0.19 pp, cluster CI [-0.45,+0.06] pp, mean absolute 0.51 pp, max 2.1 pp, correlation 0.94. Sanity: project(128) on 128-d (pure rotation) gives rel 0.9984-1.0000 (mean 0.99997, n=124). Codec after PCA minus codec alone: int8 +0.01 pp [-0.06,+0.09] (128 d, k=64), +0.06 pp wide; binary 0.0 pp [-0.9,+1.1] at 128 d, -0.67 pp [-1.64,+0.04] for d>=2048 (4 models), with Nemotron-4B about 2% worse after projection at every k from 128 to 1280; int4(mean) -0.47 pp [-0.64,-0.28] at 128 d, -0.47 pp wide [-0.83,-0.14], -0.91 pp for d>=2048 [-1.45,-0.32].
findings.method: Paired differences between multi-stage and single-stage rows, cluster bootstrap over models; codec excess defined as ret(project>codec)/ret(project) minus ret(codec alone).
findings.confounds: These are the pairs that happen to be in the grid, not interventions. Differences are small compared with the query-bootstrap intervals on single units. The wide-d binary/int4 effect rests on 4 models (Nemotron-4B drives it) and the PCA-rotation explanation is untested. float16-inference baselines for several wide models. Multiplicativity checked only for hierarchical_merge, not other stages.
findings.practical_implication: Per-stage losses can be multiplied to predict a pipeline's retention within about 1 pp for projection plus merge, int8, and binary at d<=640. Check binary and int4 directly on 2.5k-4k-d models after PCA.
findings.question: projection

verdict.recomputed:
I recomputed everything from measured.json with my own code. The merge-by-project result matches. For the codec after PCA, the 128-d numbers match and the wide-d numbers differ in the details.

Merge then project, compared with pure PCA at the same (model, dataset, k):
- I get 116 pairs from 12 models, not 60. I did not reconstruct the 60-pair subset. It may be one merge ratio, or only the pairs where the rows existed in the other analyst's grid.
- Mean difference is -0.20 pp, with a cluster CI over models of [-0.48, +0.06].
- Mean absolute difference is 0.57 pp and the maximum is 2.36 pp.
- The correlation between the product ret(merge)*ret(project) and the observed ret(merge>project) is 0.93.
- Dropping any one model keeps the mean between -0.12 and -0.25 pp.

Codec after PCA minus codec alone (project(k)>codec relative to project(k), minus the codec alone):
- Int8 gives +0.04 pp [-0.03, +0.12] over all 150 pairs from 49 models. At d<=128 it is +0.01 pp [-0.06, +0.09], which matches the claim.
- Binary at d<=128 gives 0.00 pp [-0.89, +1.07], which matches the claim.
- Binary at d>=2048 (4 models, 36 pairs) gives -0.63 pp [-1.67, +0.04], close to the claimed -0.67.
- Nemotron-4B drives the wide-d binary result at -2.2 pp per-model mean. The other three wide models are about 0 to -0.4 pp (Nemotron-8B +0.18, both EVIE models about -0.4).
- Int4(mean) at d<=128 gives -0.47 pp [-0.64, -0.28], which matches.
- Int4(mean) at d>=2048 gives -0.97 pp [-1.63, -0.32], versus the claimed -0.91. The 4 wide models split into two groups. The two Nemotron models are at about -1.5 to -1.7 pp. The two EVIE models are at about -0.3 pp.
- Int4(mean) at 128<d<2048 (8 models) gives -0.14 pp [-0.30, +0.03].

I could not run the check of Nemotron-4B binary excess at every k from 128 to 1280. My script hit a KeyError there, because the project(k) rows are missing for some of those k. I did not fix it, so the "about 2% worse at every k" claim is only supported by the per-model mean above.
verdict.issues:
1. The test has low power for what it claims. In the merge pairs, project retention is 0.93 to 1.00 (median 0.986) and merge retention is 0.98 to 1.00 (median 0.996). Any combination stays close to 1, so a product law is hard to tell apart from "everything is near 1". The shortfall subset (product below 0.97, 33 pairs) shows a mean error of -0.34 pp and a mean absolute error of 0.75 pp. The shortfalls correlate at 0.84 there. That supports approximate multiplicativity but with a small, systematic under-prediction, so "nearly" fits better than "independently".
2. The merge-by-project grid has only 12 models. All are large image models (the 4B to 8B Qwen-derived families, with sibling pairs such as EVIE 4.5B/8B, Tomoro 4B/8B, Nemotron 4B/8B, ColVec1 4B/1.1-8B, and three Vultron sizes). All are on DocVQA and InfoVQA, and the models are correlated siblings. The cluster bootstrap treats them as independent. The sign of the mean (-0.2 pp, CI touching 0) is stable but not firm.
3. Only hierarchical_merge was checked, as the other analyst noted.
4. The d>=2048 binary and int4 effects rest on 4 models, and the only model with a large binary penalty is Nemotron-4B. For int4 the wide-d penalty comes from the two Nemotron siblings. The EVIE models show about -0.3 pp. So -0.9 pp for "wide models" overstates the typical case.
5. The cluster-bootstrap CIs for the wide groups come from only 4 resampling units, so they are not reliable.
6. The query-bootstrap noise on single units is larger than these differences. Retention above 1 is noise, and some of the wide models use float16-inference baselines.
7. This is exploratory post-hoc analysis with no multiplicity control. I ran about 10 CI comparisons here.
verdict.corrected_claim: In the 12 large image models with merge and PCA rows, hierarchical_merge followed by project(k) tracks the product of the separate retentions within about 0.6 pp on average (max about 2.4 pp, mean difference -0.2 pp, CI [-0.5, +0.06]). At these retention levels (0.93 to 1.0) that is a weak test of independence. After PCA, int8 and binary cost about the same as alone at small d (within about 0.1 pp for int8 and about 1 pp CI for binary). Int4(mean) costs about 0.5 pp extra at d<=128 (CI [-0.64, -0.28]). At d>=2048 there are only 4 models and the extra cost is dominated by the two Nemotron models. Nemotron-4B has an extra binary cost of about 2 pp, and the Nemotron pair has an int4 cost of about 1.5 to 1.7 pp. The EVIE pair is nearer 0.3 to 0.4 pp. Label it weak and approximate, not independent.

results.summary: Exploratory, post-hoc test of a multiplicative composition model using measured.json. The product of single-stage retentions predicts combined retention well on average (MAE 0.0091, median 0.0037, n=1794 excluding float16 rows) with a slight optimistic bias (-0.0046). It is no better than an additive-loss predictor in this mostly small-loss regime. Tail failures are large and concentrated in uncentred int4/binary/lloyd2 after merging on small text ColBERT models, and in pipelines whose single stages already lose >10%. Screening from singles is useful as a pre-filter and not as a certificate. Report is at REPORT.md in the composition folder.
data_issues: project(16) and project(32) are never measured alone (and project(32)>codec is absent), so merge>project(32/16) and their codec chains can only be predicted via the measured merge>project sub-pipeline times the codec.
project(k) single exists at one k per model (k=64 for 128-d models, 128/80/160/etc. for others), so only 116 merge>project rows (12 models) support the all-singles test.
Seven model-datasets carry a legacy label scheme (ward ratio, adaptive r, int8/vec, none) alongside canonical labels; excluded as duplicates.
1584 rows (702 in the all_singles set) use float16-inference baselines; float16 stage rows are no-ops and were excluded from headline numbers.
retention > 1 in 7.7% of all rows (4.7% of combined rows): noise.
Text = SciFact only and image = ViDoRe DocVQA/InfoVQA, so modality/dataset are fully confounded.
The uncentred int4 is used in merge>int4 but int4(mean) in project chains, so codec type partly varies with chain position.
Retention CIs bootstrap queries only; singles and combos share queries, so the inside-CI metric is approximate.

findings.title: Product of single-stage retentions predicts combined retention to ~1 point on average, but not better than additive
findings.claim: Excluding float16 no-op rows, all_singles pipelines (n=1794, 51 models): MAE 0.0091, median abs error 0.0037, 90.8% within 0.02, bias -0.0046 (slightly optimistic), worst -0.357. Near-no-op controls give MAE 0.0016. Additive and min predictors are nearly as good (MAE 0.0076 additive, 0.0077 product, 0.0092 min, 0.0220 first-stage-only, n=2120 incl float16).
findings.evidence: all_singles excl f16: MAE 0.0091, RMSE 0.0230, bias -0.0046 cluster-bootstrap CI [-0.0071,-0.0027]; |e|<.01 76.7%, <.02 90.8%, <.05 97.5%; 3-stage (m>p)x codec n=1584 MAE 0.0236 median 0.0055. Controls float16/int8 n=768 MAE 0.00164, 99.3% inside reported CI.
findings.method: Build every combined pipeline with all parts measured on same model/dataset; compare actual vs product; cluster bootstrap over models for bias; compare to additive, min and first-stage predictors.
findings.confounds: Mostly small-loss regime so any reasonable predictor works; CIs ignore corpus sampling; correlated sibling checkpoints; float16-inference baselines for 702 rows; singles and combos share queries so inside-CI is loose.
findings.practical_implication: Single-stage numbers are a good first-pass estimate of combined retention, but the multiplicative form itself adds little over adding losses; do not credit the model with more than that.
findings.question: composition

verdict.recomputed: Own code from raw wide/*.json, ndcg@5 retention; a pipeline counts as all_singles if every ' > ' part is itself a measured row of the same model/dataset. Excluding pipelines containing float16: n=1480 rows, 47 models (claim: 1794 / 51). Product MAE 0.0092 (claim 0.0091), median abs error 0.0037 (match), 91.6% within 0.02 (claim 90.8%). Bias (predicted minus actual) +0.0044, i.e. optimistic; cluster bootstrap over models CI [0.0024, 0.0072] (claim -0.0046 [-0.0071,-0.0027], same magnitude, opposite sign convention). Additive MAE 0.0090, min 0.0109, first-stage-only 0.0224. Including float16: n=1760, product 0.0078, additive 0.0076, min 0.0092, first 0.0189 (claim 0.0077 / 0.0076 / 0.0092 / 0.0220, matches). float16-containing rows: MAE 0.0002, all inside CI (trivial control). Largest errors: product too optimistic by 0.27 (mxbai-edge-colbert-32m, hierarchical_merge(0.25)>lloyd2(7): actual 0.358 vs predicted 0.628), too pessimistic by 0.18 (mLateOn project(64)>binary); I could not reproduce worst -0.357 as a signed error under any sign. Paired MAE difference product minus additive over a looser definition (prefix+suffix splits, n=2680): -0.0015, model-bootstrap CI [-0.0042, +0.0002], so product is not distinguishably better than additive (and in the strict set they are equal to 0.0002). Dropping the worst 1 or 3 models by MAE: product MAE 0.0087 / 0.0075, bias still positive. Regime split (min single-stage retention): >=0.95 n=1326 MAE 0.0057, 95.5% within 0.02; 0.80-0.95 n=125 MAE 0.0225, 70% within 0.02; <0.80 n=29 MAE 0.112, 7% within 0.02, bias +0.089 (product too optimistic; additive 0.102 also bad). Predicting retention=1.0 for everything gives MAE 0.0345, so the product is a real improvement over a trivial baseline. By dataset: image models (33 models, n=1304) MAE 0.0058, 95.2% within 0.02; text/SciFact models (14 models, n=176) MAE 0.0343, median 0.0109, 64% within 0.02, bias +0.022 (dataset and modality confounded; text rows include the worst cases). Keeping one model per organisation (19 orgs, 1092 rows in the looser set): product 0.0167 vs additive 0.0170, same ordering.
verdict.issues: 1) The headline MAE is an average over a mostly small-loss regime: 90% of rows have min single retention >=0.95, where any predictor works; the claim 'about 1 point on average' hides that accuracy collapses once any stage loses >5% (MAE 0.022 at 0.80-0.95, 0.11 below 0.80, systematically optimistic). 2) The error is concentrated in SciFact text models (MAE 0.034, only 64% within 0.02) versus image models (0.0058); this is dataset-confounded and 14 models, but it means the pooled 0.0091 is not representative of text. 3) Not-better-than-additive is supported: strict-set MAE 0.0092 vs 0.0090; looser set product slightly better but the CI includes 0. 4) My row/model counts (1480/47, 1760/47) are below the claimed 1794/51 and 2120; the extra rows presumably come from a broader part definition or other source; I could not reproduce n. Core MAE/median/within-0.02 numbers did match closely, so the gap does not alter conclusions. 5) Signed worst-case -0.357 not reproducible as stated; actual extreme is +0.27 (product optimistic) and -0.18. 6) Bias sign convention is inverted vs the claim; 'slightly optimistic' is correct in my convention (predicted > actual). 7) Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling; singles and combos share queries, so the 'inside CI' control is loose. Exploratory and post-hoc; tests run: few (about 8 subsets, 2 bootstraps).
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory: for combined pipelines whose stages were each measured alone, the product of single-stage ndcg@5 retentions has MAE about 0.009 (median 0.004, about 91% within 0.02, mean over-prediction of about 0.004, CI roughly 0.002 to 0.007) across 47 models, comparable to the additive predictor (0.009) and better than min (0.011) or first-stage-only (0.022). This holds mainly where every single stage keeps >=95% (n about 1330, MAE 0.006); when any stage drops below 0.95 error grows (MAE 0.022) and below 0.80 the product is badly optimistic (MAE 0.11). SciFact text models fit worse (MAE 0.034) than image models (0.006), with dataset and modality confounded. Product is not shown to beat additive.

findings.title: Uncentred int4/binary/lloyd2 after merge are sub-multiplicative on text models; centred and int8 codecs compose
findings.claim: After hierarchical_merge, actual retention is below the product by 3.6-7.4 points for binary/int4/lloyd2 on text (14 models) but by ~0.2 points on image (37 models). int4(mean) and int8 compose near-multiplicatively.
findings.evidence: merge>codec bias text: binary -0.036 [-0.058,-0.017], int4 -0.053 [-0.100,-0.017], lloyd2 -0.074 [-0.111,-0.039]; image: binary -0.0024, int4 -0.0002 n.s., lloyd2 -0.0020; int8 text -0.0001, image -0.0001. Paired int4(mean)-int4 error text +0.049 [0.015,0.095] Wilcoxon p=0.0085 (14 models), image -0.001 [-0.002,0.0004]. Slope beta (1=multiplicative): lloyd2 text 1.62 [1.48,2.10], binary text 1.26, int4 text 1.27, image 0.97-1.02.
findings.method: Cluster bootstrap (models) of signed error by pipeline kind, codec and dataset group; paired Wilcoxon on model-level means; through-origin slope of log conditional retention on log codec retention.
findings.confounds: Text = SciFact only (modality/dataset confound), small ColBERT families, few clusters (14); 24 bias cells and 19 slope fits examined without multiplicity correction.
findings.practical_implication: If a pipeline merges then applies uncentred int4/binary/lloyd2, measure it (or use the centred codec); the product over-promises on text-like models. int8 and centred int4 can be screened from singles.
findings.question: composition

verdict.recomputed: Own script (raw campaign wide/*.json, 80 files, 800 merge>codec rows at ratios 0.25 and 0.33). Error = retention(merge>codec) minus retention(merge)*retention(codec), averaged per model, then cluster-bootstrapped over models. Text, 14 models: binary -0.0360 [-0.058,-0.016]; int4 -0.0500 [-0.096,-0.013]; lloyd2 -0.0709 [-0.111,-0.035]; int4(mean) -0.0036 [-0.009,+0.001]; int8 +0.0002 [-0.002,+0.003]. This matches the claim (lloyd2 and int4 differ by 0.003-0.004, probably a slightly different row set). Image: only 33 models are found in the wide files, not 37; binary -0.0025 [-0.005,-0.001], int4 -0.0003 n.s., lloyd2 -0.0019 [-0.004,-0.0003], int4(mean) -0.0010, int8 -0.0001. Paired int4(mean) minus int4 error on text is +0.046, median +0.020, Wilcoxon p=0.0067. Leave-one-model-out the text means stay at -0.030 to -0.040 (binary), -0.031 to -0.055 (int4), -0.057 to -0.078 (lloyd2). Medians are much smaller than the means for binary (-0.020) and int4 (-0.012), so a few models drive them. int4 text: LFM2-ColBERT-350M alone is -0.295 and 12 of 14 models are negative. Without the top model, the int4(mean) minus int4 difference is +0.028 (p=0.013). Collapsing the 14 to 10 families (mxbai-edge, LFM, LateOn/mLateOn, and colbertv2 pooled): binary -0.031 [-0.049,-0.013], p=0.027; int4 -0.037 [-0.072,-0.006], p=0.065; lloyd2 -0.060 [-0.099,-0.025], p=0.0098. Text vs image Mann-Whitney on model means: binary p=0.011, int4 p=0.017, lloyd2 p=0.0001. Not recomputed: the slope (beta) fits.
verdict.issues:
1) Main confound: codec damage is very different between the groups. The mean codec-only retention loss on text is about 15% for binary, int4 and lloyd2. On image it is 1.8% (binary), 0.09% (int4) and 0.8% (lloyd2). A product reference is expected to fail more when the codec alone already costs 15%. Image models barely lose anything from the codec, so there is almost no room to see a gap. Normalised by codec-only loss, the extra gap is about 24% (text) vs 14% (image) for binary, 49% vs 23% for lloyd2, and 33% vs 33% for int4. So the text-vs-image difference in sub-multiplicativity is largely a difference in how fragile uncentred codecs are on SciFact models, plus the dataset/modality confound. "Image composes" is better stated as "image codecs lose almost nothing".
2) Effect size is heterogeneous. Medians are 2-3 times smaller than means for binary and int4. A few models (LFM2-ColBERT -0.295 for int4, mxbai-edge -0.253 for lloyd2, mLateOn and LFM2.5 about -0.10 for binary) dominate. colbertv2.0, jina-colbert-v2, Reason-ModernColBERT and mxbai-colbert-large show about 0 or positive error. Whether it is sub-multiplicative depends on the model.
3) Sibling dependence: 14 models are about 10 families. The int4 effect is not significant at the family level (p=0.065).
4) The claim that int4(mean) and int8 "compose near-multiplicatively" is weak for int4(mean). On text the mean is -0.0036 and the CI includes 0, but the sign test is 9 of 14 negative, which is no evidence of a gap. On image it is -0.0010 (p=0.042 Wilcoxon, 21 of 33 negative). That is a tiny but nonzero shortfall. The int8 result holds trivially, since int8 is almost loss-free.
5) The image bias is not exactly "~0.2 points" for every codec. Binary and lloyd2 are small but their CIs exclude 0.
6) The model count of 37 for image does not match the 33 I found. Reasons for the 37 (older models from other report folders, or models with only one merge ratio) were not checked.
7) Only merge ratios 0.25 and 0.33 provide merge>codec pairs, so the result is limited to those ratios. Hierarchical-merge retention is also noisy, and retention above 1 is noise. The bootstrap is over queries or models and ignores corpus sampling. Many cells were tested (about 20 bias cells here) without correction. Post-hoc and exploratory.
verdict.corrected_claim: On SciFact text models (14 checkpoints, about 10 families), hierarchical_merge followed by uncentred binary, int4 or lloyd2 lands 3.6, 5.0 and 7.1 points below the product of the separate retentions (cluster-bootstrap CIs exclude 0; the family-level int4 result is borderline, p=0.065). The effect is heterogeneous: medians are 2.0 (binary) and 1.2 (int4) points. It is driven by a minority of models (LFM2, mxbai-edge, LateOn and mLateOn); colbertv2.0, jina-colbert-v2 and Reason-ModernColBERT show about zero. Centred int4(mean) and int8 show no detectable text gap (-0.4 and +0.0 points, CIs include 0), and int4(mean) beats uncentred int4 on text by about 4.6 points mean (2.0 median) in composed error (p=0.007, n=14). On ViDoRe image models (33 found, not 37) all gaps are at most 0.25 points, but this reflects image codecs losing only 0.1-1.8% by themselves rather than better composition. Per unit of codec loss, the gap is similar for int4 (about 33% in both groups) and only about 2 times larger on text for binary and lloyd2. Text vs image is confounded with dataset (SciFact vs DocVQA/InfoVQA) and with baseline fragility. Post-hoc, exploratory; slope estimates not verified.

findings.claim: Even when merge loss <1% and codec loss <1%, text rows show bias about -0.03 vs -0.002 for image. Per-model mean error ranges from +0.0007 to -0.165; 8 of 14 text models worse than -0.04.
findings.evidence: Bias by merge-loss bin: <1% text -0.0290 (4 models) vs image -0.0023 (35); 1-3% text -0.0324 vs +0.0012. Per-model (text) LFM2-ColBERT-350M -0.165, mxbai-edge-32m -0.140, mLateOn -0.093, colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 +0.0007. Spearman err vs dim 0.39 (p=0.16), vs vpd -0.49 (p=0.078), n=14; image dim rho 0.23 p=0.05, vpd 0.03 (n=74).

verdict.recomputed:
Own script recomputed error = retention(merge>codec) - retention(merge)*retention(codec) from the 'token+codec' rows of campaign/*/wide files (960 rows, 47 models: 14 text, 33 image; modality from the MODELS registry). The row set is 168 text and 792 image rows.

When BOTH single-stage losses are <1% (the claimed condition), text bias is -0.0037 by row (-0.0042 by model mean, 95% model bootstrap CI [-0.0068, -0.0027]). That is only 11 rows from 3 models: LateOn -0.0068, GTE-ModernColBERT -0.0032, jina-colbert-v2 -0.0027. Image is -0.0014 (523 rows, 31 models). The gap is about 0.003, not 0.03.

The claimed -0.03 appears only when the merge loss is <1% and codec loss is left unrestricted: text -0.025 (24 rows, 3 models, CI [-0.050, -0.004]). That is, the loss comes from codecs that lose more than 1% (binary and lloyd2 on text). With merge loss 1-3% and codec <1%, text is -0.0010 (8 models), against -0.0216 with codec unrestricted. With merge >3% and codec <1%, text is -0.0004 (9 models).

Text overall: row mean -0.027, 14-model mean -0.027 with CI [-0.040, -0.013]. Image overall: -0.001. So text sub-multiplicativity is real but it is concentrated in lossy-codec combinations.

Per-model text means, in my definition: LFM2-ColBERT-350M -0.080, mxbai-edge-32m -0.072, mLateOn -0.052, LateOn -0.046, mxbai-edge-17m -0.041, then smaller. colbertv2.0 is +0.0008, jina-colbert-v2 +0.0004. Only 5 of 14 text models are below -0.04 (claim: 8 of 14). The claimed -0.165 and +0.0007 end-points are not reproduced; the +0.0007 is close to my +0.0008.

Spearman over model means with n=14 text: error vs dim rho 0.39 (p=0.16), vs vectors per doc rho -0.48 (p=0.083). These match the claim. Image, n=33 models: dim 0.23 (p=0.19), vpd 0.18 (p=0.33). The claim's n=74 and p=0.05 for image dim apparently pooled models and datasets, which pseudo-replicates.

Dropping the 3 worst text models moves the text mean from -0.027 to -0.015. The median text model is -0.018.
verdict.issues:
1. The headline claim (text bias -0.03 vs image -0.002 when merge AND codec loss are both <1%) fails. With both under 1% the text bias is -0.004, based on only 3 models and 11 rows. The -0.03 figure comes from rows where codec loss is not restricted.
2. The "not explained by loss size" conclusion is wrong. The text error is large mainly when codec loss is large, so it is explained, at least partly, by loss size.
3. Effect sizes and counts differ from the evidence: the per-model range is -0.080 to +0.003 here, not -0.165; the count of text models worse than -0.04 is 5, not 8. I assume the other analyst used a different error definition or included other pipelines; I could not tell which. My definition may differ from theirs.
4. The image dim/vpd correlations in the claim use n=74, which is not independent; per-model n=33 here gives non-significant values.
5. Text-vs-image rests on 14 text models versus 33 image models. Modality and dataset are fully confounded (SciFact vs ViDoRe). Text models include sibling checkpoints (LateOn/mLateOn, mxbai 17m/32m, LFM2/LFM2.5, colbertv2.0 twins). Float16-inference baselines were not examined. No mechanism was tested.
6. A model-specific pattern in text (a few models strongly sub-multiplicative, others about zero) is supported, though weakly. This is exploratory, post-hoc analysis. About 30 comparisons were run, with no multiplicity correction.
verdict.corrected_claim: In the text models (SciFact, 14 models), combining token merging with a codec scores below the product of the single-stage retentions by about 0.027 on average (model-cluster CI -0.040 to -0.013), versus about -0.001 for image models. The gap is concentrated in a few models (LFM2-ColBERT-350M, mxbai-edge, mLateOn, LateOn; roughly -0.04 to -0.08) and in pairings with lossy codecs (binary, lloyd2). When both single-stage losses are under 1%, the text shortfall is only about -0.004 (3 models, 11 rows), close to image (-0.001). So it does not persist at tiny losses. Correlations with dim and vectors per doc are weak and non-significant (n=14). Modality, dataset and family are confounded, and this is post-hoc.

findings.title: Prediction error grows with the largest single-stage loss; no clean safe zone
findings.claim: MAE rises from 0.0037 (max single loss <=1%) to 0.078 (>10%, bias -0.063). A 'max single loss <=3%' rule keeps 80% of rows but 58 of 144 rows with error < -0.02 still fall inside it.
findings.method: Binning by 1-min(parts); MAE, bias, quantiles per bin; count of large under-shoots inside the rule.
findings.confounds: Few high-loss rows concentrated in text models; loss and group are correlated.
findings.practical_implication: Use a conservative margin and re-measure shortlisted pipelines; a simple loss cutoff will not remove tail risk.
findings.question: composition

verdict.recomputed: Recomputed from measured.json with my own code (parts = stage labels split on ' > '; pred = product of single-stage retentions; err = actual - pred; 2120 combined rows, 51 models; same exclusion of ward/adaptive/random/bracketed labels). Every headline number reproduces. Bins by max single loss: <=0.01 n=935 MAE 0.0037 bias -0.0022 (41 models); 0.03-0.05 n=239 MAE 0.0093; 0.05-0.1 n=137 MAE 0.0148; >0.1 n=56 MAE 0.0783 bias -0.0626 p95 abs 0.261 worst -0.357, 10 models, fraction err<-0.01 = 66% (vs 9% in the lowest bin). Rule 'max single loss <=0.03' keeps 79.6% of rows; 144 rows have err<-0.02, 58 of them inside the rule. Extra checks: (1) Model-clustered bootstrap (2000 resamples) MAE 95% CI: <=1% bin [0.0031, 0.0044]; >10% bin [0.049, 0.105]. (2) Dropping the most extreme model (LFM2-ColBERT-350M) leaves the >10% MAE at 0.076. (3) Excluding float16-inference models: >10% MAE 0.084 (n=52), low bin 0.0038, so no change. (4) The >10% bin is 48 SciFact text rows (MAE 0.091, bias -0.073, 8 models) and only 8 image rows (MAE 0.002, bias +0.001, 2 models: the nemotron colembed pair). So the blow-up in the top bin is entirely a text/SciFact phenomenon; image models with a large single-stage loss show no composition error in this data. (5) In the other bins the image and text MAEs are similar (e.g. <=1%: 0.0037 vs 0.0037; 0.05-0.1: 0.0117 vs 0.0240), so the gradual rise to ~0.01-0.015 is not a modality artefact, though it is mostly image rows. (6) The 58 under-shoots inside the rule: 55 image rows, 3 text rows, spread over 18 models; conditional rate is 3.4% inside the rule vs 19.9% outside (err<-0.02). Most extreme per-model: top-bin errors come from LFM2-ColBERT (12 rows), mxbai-edge-32m (6, mean -0.14), LateOn (4, -0.12). Tests run: about 6 binned summaries plus the above checks; exploratory, post hoc, not preregistered.
verdict.issues: 1) The headline 'MAE 0.078 for >10%' rests on 56 rows from 10 models, of which 48 rows (8 models) are SciFact text and 8 image rows have near-zero error; the high-loss effect is confounded with dataset/modality and cannot be assigned to loss size alone. 2) Rows are not independent: the same pipelines repeat across sibling checkpoints (LFM2 and LFM2.5, mxbai-edge 17m/32m, LateOn/mLateOn, nemotron 4b/8b), so row-level n overstates evidence; model-clustered CI for the top bin is wide (0.049-0.105). 3) Max single loss and pipeline group (binary/int4 codecs, heavy merge) are correlated, so 'largest single-stage loss' may proxy for the stage type. 4) Retention >1 noise and query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling; errors below about 0.01 are within measurement noise, so the 9% 'frac err<-0.01' in the bottom bin is partly noise. 5) 'No clean safe zone' is slightly strong: inside the <=3% rule only 3.4% of rows have err<-0.02 (58/1694, versus 19.9% outside), the worst in-rule error is -0.071 at most in the 0.03 neighbourhood bins and -0.053 within <=3% (bin worst -0.053), and the in-rule under-shoots are small in absolute terms. The rule does enrich safely but not eliminate misses.
verdict.corrected_claim: Prediction error (actual minus product of single-stage retentions) rises with the largest single-stage loss: MAE 0.0037 at <=1% (n=935, 41 models), 0.009 at 3-5%, 0.015 at 5-10%. The jump to MAE 0.078 (bias -0.063) at >10% comes from 56 rows in 10 models and is driven by SciFact text models (48 rows, MAE 0.091); the 8 image rows with >10% loss have essentially no error, so loss size and dataset/modality cannot be separated. A 'max single loss <=3%' rule keeps 80% of rows; 58 of 144 rows with error < -0.02 (3.4% of in-rule rows, versus 19.9% outside the rule, worst in-rule error about -0.053) still fall inside it, mostly in image models, so the rule reduces but does not remove under-shoots. Exploratory, post hoc, with sibling-correlated rows; the top-bin MAE has a model-clustered 95% CI of roughly 0.05 to 0.10.

findings.title: Screening from singles is a useful pre-filter with a noise-limited error rate
findings.claim: Predicted>=T classifies actual>=T with precision 0.968/recall 0.982 at T=0.95 and 0.910/0.931 at T=0.98; AUC 0.97/0.955/0.948; 91-94% of misclassifications have CIs straddling T. Best-predicted pipeline at a compression floor has mean regret 0.004-0.008 but max up to 0.139.
findings.evidence: n=2120 all_singles: T=0.95 59 FP (mean shortfall 0.012, max 0.043); T=0.98 117 FP (max 0.052); +0.01 margin at 0.98 gives precision 0.965 recall 0.650. AUC pred 0.972/0.955/0.948 vs min 0.961/0.945/0.952 vs first-stage 0.757/0.768/0.808. Regret at compression>=10/20/40 over 88 units: mean 0.0037/0.0047/0.0077, max 0.035/0.053/0.139; within 0.005 of best 80/81/74%. Within-unit Spearman median 0.88, min 0.41.
findings.method: Confusion matrices at thresholds with margins, AUC by rank statistic, CI-straddle share, top-1 regret within model-dataset at compression floors, within-unit Spearman.
findings.confounds: Rows within a model are correlated; base rates are high so precision flatters; query-only CIs; regret tested on the fixed pipeline grid only.
findings.practical_implication: Use singles to shortlist and drop obviously bad pipelines, then measure the shortlist; do not publish a screened number as a measured retention.
findings.question: composition

verdict.recomputed:
I rebuilt the pairs from measured.json myself. Predicted retention is the product of single-stage retentions. Actual retention is the retention of the combined pipeline. I kept only combined pipelines whose every stage has its own single row, and excluded ward, adaptive, random and bracketed labels. This gives n=2120 rows, 51 models, 88 model-dataset units. All headline numbers reproduce.

- **T=0.95:** base rate 0.868, precision 0.968, recall 0.982, 59 FP, 34 FN, AUC 0.972. FP shortfall mean 0.0117, max 0.043. 93.5% of 93 misclassifications have a CI straddling T.
- **T=0.98:** base rate 0.597, precision 0.910, recall 0.931, 117 FP, 87 FN, AUC 0.955. FP shortfall max 0.052. 91.2% of 204 misclassifications straddle.
- **T=0.99:** AUC 0.948; 94% of misclassifications straddle.
- **Margin:** with +0.01 at T=0.98, precision 0.965 and recall 0.650.
- **Competing AUCs, T=0.95 / 0.98 / 0.99:** min-of-singles 0.961 / 0.945 / 0.952. First-stage-only 0.757 / 0.768 / 0.808.
- **Regret:** mean 0.0037 / 0.0047 / 0.0077 at compression floors of 10 / 20 / 40. Max 0.035 / 0.053 / 0.139. Within 0.005 of best: 80% / 81% / 74%. The worst case at the 40 floor is LFM2.5-ColBERT-350M on SciFact, with only 5 candidate pipelines.
- **Within-unit Spearman:** median 0.879, min 0.438. The claim says min 0.41; I did not reproduce that exact value (probably a different row filter), but the median matches.

My additional checks:
- **Model-cluster bootstrap (1000 resamples), 95% CI:** T=0.95 precision 0.955-0.980, recall 0.969-0.991, AUC 0.958-0.984. T=0.98 precision 0.888-0.930, recall 0.906-0.954, AUC 0.942-0.968.
- **Regret mean CIs (units bootstrap):** 0.0024-0.0051 at the 10 floor and 0.0038-0.0126 at the 40 floor.
- **Leave-one-model-out:** precision stays in 0.966-0.972 at T=0.95 and 0.907-0.915 at T=0.98. No single model drives it.
- **By dataset:**

| Dataset | T | Base rate | Precision | Recall | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DocVQA | 0.95 | 0.82 | 0.951 | 0.969 | 0.959 |
| DocVQA | 0.98 | 0.53 | 0.865 | 0.924 | 0.939 |
| InfoVQA | 0.95 | 0.98 | 0.985 | 0.996 | 0.969 |
| InfoVQA | 0.98 | 0.75 | 0.955 | 0.941 | 0.968 |
| SciFact | 0.95 | 0.59 | 0.953 | 0.953 | 0.975 |
| SciFact | 0.98 | 0.24 | 0.772 | 0.863 | 0.943 |

- **Near-threshold band (pred within ±0.03 of T):** precision 0.911 at T=0.95 and 0.909 at T=0.98, AUC 0.92-0.94. This is the honest hard-case performance.
- **Random-pick regret** at compression floors 10 / 20 / 40: 0.039 / 0.044 / 0.030. This compares with 0.004 / 0.005 / 0.008 for the best-predicted pick.
- **Candidate set sizes:** the median is 12 / 9 / 5 pipelines at floors 10 / 20 / 40, and the minimum is 10 / 5 / 3.
- **Error vs CI:** error (actual minus predicted) has mean -0.004 and SD 0.021. Median CI half-width is 0.015. 92.9% of rows have |error| inside their CI. Per-model mean error has SD 0.0146 and ranges from -0.070 to +0.003, so part of the error is systematic per model and not pure noise.

Number of tests: about 30 descriptive statistics, none corrected for multiplicity. This is exploratory and post-hoc.
verdict.issues:
1. "Precision flatters" is real and understated. At T=0.98 the base rate is 0.597 overall, and in SciFact it is 0.24 with precision 0.772. DocVQA precision is 0.865. The pooled 0.91 is driven by InfoVQA, where the base rate is high.
2. The product of singles adds little over the min of singles. AUC is 0.972 vs 0.961 at T=0.95, 0.955 vs 0.945 at T=0.98, and min is actually higher at T=0.99 (0.952 vs 0.948). The useful part is "any single stage that is already lossy predicts a lossy combination". Multiplying is not clearly better. Min has higher recall but lower precision (0.948 vs 0.968 at T=0.95, 0.841 vs 0.910 at T=0.98), so product does buy precision.
3. The straddle share (91-94%) has no null comparison. With a median CI half-width of 0.015 and an error SD of 0.021, most misclassified rows near T would straddle anyway. It shows the errors are small, not that they are irreducible noise. The per-model systematic error (SD 0.0146, down to -0.07) means "noise-limited" is partly wrong: composition has model-specific interaction loss. Rows within a model are correlated, and the CIs are query-bootstrap only.
4. Regret is best-of-a-small-grid: median 5 candidates at the 40 floor (minimum 3), chosen on the same noisy actuals. The 40-floor max regret of 0.139 (and 0.097 and 0.093 for the next two) comes from SciFact text models with 4-5 candidates. The mean CI at the 40 floor is wide (0.004-0.013). It is a fixed-grid result, not a general one.
5. The 35 of 51 models with at least one FP at T=0.98 show errors are broad. The false positives concentrate in a few ColQwen-family models (ColVec1-4b with 11, VultronPrime with 11, nemotron-8b with 9), which are sibling checkpoints.
6. Modality and dataset are confounded. Text models are SciFact only, with 216 rows, and have the worst precision at 0.98.
7. The Spearman minimum of 0.41 is not reproduced exactly (I get 0.438); this is minor.
verdict.corrected_claim:
Reproduced. Predicting the combined pipeline's retention as the product of its single-stage retentions is a useful pre-filter on this fixed grid, but it is a screen, not a guarantee.
- **Pooled results (n=2120, 51 models):** at T=0.95, precision 0.968 (model-cluster bootstrap CI 0.955-0.980) and recall 0.982. At T=0.98, precision 0.910 (0.888-0.930) and recall 0.931. AUC is 0.97 / 0.955 / 0.948 at T=0.95 / 0.98 / 0.99.
- **Where it is weaker:** precision is 0.865 on DocVQA and 0.772 on SciFact at T=0.98, and about 0.91 for rows near the threshold. The pooled figure benefits from InfoVQA's high base rate.
- **Product vs min:** the gain over a simple min-of-singles rule is small (AUC +0.01).
- **Error size:** misclassified rows are mostly within CI width of the threshold (91-94% straddle), and false positives fall short by about 0.01 on average and at most 0.05. The errors are small, but part is systematic per model, not just noise.
- **Regret:** picking the best-predicted pipeline at a compression floor has mean regret 0.004-0.008 (CI up to about 0.013) against about 0.03-0.04 for a random pick. This is over small candidate sets (median 5-12), and the worst case reaches 0.14 on SciFact text models with 4-5 candidates.
- **Scope:** exploratory and post-hoc, with correlated sibling models and query-only CIs.

findings.title: project>binary flips sign: super-multiplicative on text, slightly sub-multiplicative on image; sub-pipeline knowledge helps modestly
findings.claim: On text, project(64)>binary beats the product by +0.044 [0.011,0.082] (12 models), tracking binary-alone loss (Spearman 0.82, p=0.001); on image it is -0.0047 [-0.0091,-0.0008] (37 models). For 3-stage pipelines (m>p) x codec has MAE 0.0075 vs 0.0102 for the triple product.
findings.evidence: Text: actual > binary-alone in 50% of rows, mean gain +0.024; image: PCA+binary worse than binary alone in 91% of rows (mean -0.023). 348 rows with all predictors: (m>p)xcodec MAE 0.0075, merge x (p>c) 0.0081, triple 0.0102. (m>p)xcodec for project(16/32) n=1584: MAE 0.0236, binary MAE 0.054 with worst +0.63; k/dim 0.12-0.26 MAE 0.0285.
findings.method: Per-model comparison of project>binary vs binary alone and product; cluster bootstrap bias; Spearman; alternative sub-pipeline predictors on matched rows.
findings.confounds: 12 text models, one dataset; PCA mechanism (rotation helping sign quantisation) is a hypothesis not tested; project(k) singles exist at one k per model so most 3-stage cases rely on partial products.
findings.practical_implication: The product is pessimistic for PCA+binary on text and optimistic on image; for aggressive projections (k/dim <= 0.25) with binary, measure directly.
