verdict.recomputed:
From measured.json, matching rows project(k) > binary against project(k) singleton and binary singleton, the text numbers reproduce exactly. Text: 12 models, all at k=64, mean (actual - product) = +0.0443, model-cluster bootstrap CI [0.009, 0.081] (the claim's [0.011, 0.082] differs only by bootstrap noise). Spearman of binary-alone loss against the excess is 0.818 (p=0.0011). 6 of 12 text rows beat binary alone, mean gain +0.0237. Image: 138 rows, 37 models, mean -0.0047 [-0.0076, -0.0020] by row bootstrap. The claim's [-0.0091, -0.0008] is a different, wider cluster-by-model interval. The per-model mean is -0.0076 [-0.0114, -0.0040]. 91.3% of image rows are worse than binary alone, mean -0.0230.

What does not hold up as stated:
- Text is not robustly positive. It is 12 models, one dataset. Per-model sign: 5 negative, 7 positive. Wilcoxon p=0.11 and sign test p=0.77. The bootstrap CI excludes zero only because of the large positive models (mLateOn +0.165, LFM2.5 +0.117, bert-tiny +0.099). Leave-one-out means range 0.033 to 0.052. Dropping mLateOn, or the two LFM models, leaves a smaller effect with a wider interval.
- The sign flip is mostly explained by the size of the binary-alone loss, not by modality. Text binary loss averages 0.087 (max 0.267). Image binary loss averages 0.012 (max 0.074) and exceeds 0.05 in only 3 rows. Pooled regression of excess on binary loss with a text dummy: slope on binary loss 0.433 (model-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [0.03, 0.58]). Text dummy +0.016 (CI [-0.006, 0.056]), which includes zero. Modality and dataset are fully confounded, so the dummy cannot be separated further.
- Part of the Spearman 0.82 is mechanical. Actual retention a is roughly flat at 0.83 to 0.98 while the product p*b falls as b falls. So a - p*b rises with (1-b) by construction. Binary-alone loss is the predictor and also a component of the outcome.
- The image mean mixes project(k) with k from 64 to 2048. Rows are not independent (50 of the 138 are at k=64, plus siblings and hf/merged duplicates). At k=64 only (25 models, matching text), the image mean is -0.0106 [-0.0151, -0.0064], larger in magnitude than the pooled -0.0047. Per dataset at k=64: DocVQA -0.0173, InfoVQA -0.0040. Over all k, InfoVQA is +0.0015 [-0.0006, 0.0037], so it is indistinguishable from zero there. Removing sibling and merged duplicates gives -0.0038 [-0.0068, -0.0009].
- 13 image models have float16-inference baselines. I did not test whether these change the result.
- I did not recompute the 3-stage MAE claims (0.0075 vs 0.0102, and so on). They are unverified here.

Tests run: roughly 10 (two cluster bootstraps, Spearman, Wilcoxon, sign test, leave-one-out over 12 models, pooled regression, k=64 and per-dataset subsets, a dedupe check). This is exploratory and post hoc.
verdict.issues: 1) Text effect is driven by a few models and is not significant by sign test (7/12 positive, p=0.77) or Wilcoxon (p=0.11). The bootstrap CI barely excludes 0. 2) The sign flip is confounded with how much binary quantisation loses alone: text binary loss is about 7 times larger than image binary loss. The pooled model with a text dummy gives a dummy of +0.016 [-0.006, 0.056], so a modality effect is not supported. 3) The Spearman is partly mechanical, because the outcome contains the product p*b and a is nearly constant. 4) Image figure mixes k=64..2048 across rows. At the k=64 that matches text it is -0.0106, larger in magnitude, so the pooled -0.0047 understates the image effect. The claim's image CI [-0.0091, -0.0008] could not be reproduced exactly. 5) Dataset equals modality, and query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling (not applied here, since I used model-cluster bootstrap on point retentions). 6) The 3-stage MAE claim was not recomputed. 7) Retention > 1 noise: binary retention of 1.012 on colbertv2 and the interval widths (roughly 0.06) mean per-model excess values of 0.03 or less are within noise.
verdict.corrected_claim: On SciFact (12 text models, project(64)>binary), actual retention exceeds the product of the single-stage retentions by +0.044 (model bootstrap CI about 0.01 to 0.08). The effect is heterogeneous: 7 of 12 models are positive and 5 are negative, and the sign test and Wilcoxon are not significant. It grows with how much binary quantisation loses on its own (Spearman 0.82, partly mechanical). On ViDoRe image models (37 models, k from 64 to 2048), project>binary is slightly below the product (-0.005 pooled over rows, -0.011 at k=64), and almost always worse than binary alone, where binary loss is small (about 1%). Pooling the two groups and adjusting for binary-alone loss leaves no significant text-vs-image difference (text dummy +0.016, CI [-0.006, 0.056]). So 'flips sign by modality' is not supported; 'excess over the product grows with binary-alone loss' is the weak, better-supported statement. The 3-stage MAE comparison is unverified.

results.summary: Exploratory post-hoc analysis of wide/*.json (4520 rows; 33 image models on both DocVQA and InfoVQA; 14 text models on SciFact), roughly 100 uncorrected comparisons, none preregistered. REPORT.md was not written: the Write tool refused it as a subagent report file, so the full text is in these findings. (a) Pipeline rankings transfer well between DocVQA and InfoVQA (per-model Spearman median 0.885), but InfoVQA is the more forgiving dataset: a DocVQA-safe pipeline is InfoVQA-safe 99.3% of the time, the reverse only 78.5%. (b) recall@1 degrades first and recall@5 last in every dataset. (c) Lower baseline goes with more fragility at 32x and above on the image datasets (stronger on InfoVQA), not on text and not at mild compression. Modality and dataset are confounded throughout.
data_issues: Write of REPORT.md was refused by the tool as a subagent report file, so no REPORT.md exists; the full text of the findings is in this output. Scripts and CSV/pickle intermediates are in the transfer-metrics folder.

The 'shared pipeline' set differs by model: wide files hold 49 to 74 rows depending on the model (older models 54, newer ones up to 74), so 32 labels are common to all models per dataset and these are mostly mild pipelines (mean retention ~0.99).
Retention > 1 in 8.0% of all rows (noise); several models (EVIE, webAI ColVec, Vultron) are near saturated on the shared set, which depresses rank correlations.
Baseline dtype is mixed (36 float32 + 6 'float32' vs 16 'float16' + 8 'torch.float16' files) and the text files have no dtype recorded (None).
Bootstrap CIs are over queries only and ignore corpus sampling; mxbai-edge files have 49 rows rather than 54.

The first background run of c_perm.py (pandas spearmanr loops) was too slow and was killed; it was rewritten in numpy and rerun with the same permutation design. The Bash tool also mangles backslashes in heredocs, which broke load.py once (fixed with Edit).
Hub popularity (hubrank.json) and selection_rules/measured.json were not needed for this question and were not used.

findings.title: InfoVQA is the more forgiving dataset; the safe set transfers one way only
findings.claim: For the same model and pipeline, retention is higher on InfoVQA than DocVQA. A pipeline whose ndcg@5 retention lower bound is >= 0.95 on DocVQA is also safe on InfoVQA 99.3% of the time. The reverse holds only 78.5% of the time.
findings.evidence: 1887 paired rows, 33 models. Mean retention difference (InfoVQA minus DocVQA) is +0.0239 (median 0.009; InfoVQA higher on 70.5% of rows). 24/33 models have a positive median difference (sign test p=0.014). Model-mean difference is +0.0246, bootstrap CI (0.019, 0.030). Safe rows: 1060 DocVQA, 1341 InfoVQA, 1053 both, 7 DocVQA-only, 288 InfoVQA-only (McNemar exact p~1e-75, kappa 0.67, Jaccard 0.78). Not just CI width: with point retention >= 0.95 the counts are 3 vs 145 (1279 vs 1421 safe). The width-matched lower bound gives 14 vs 189. Where retention is below 0.97, InfoVQA loses a median 0.69x as much as DocVQA (per-model median ratio < 1 for 32/33 models, Wilcoxon p=6e-9). The gap grows with compression (mean diff 0.009 below 4x, 0.033 at 64-128x, 0.080 above 128x) and is near zero for codec-only rows (0.003).
findings.method: Row pairing on (model, label); McNemar exact test; sign and Wilcoxon tests over model medians; model-clustered bootstrap; point-estimate and width-matched sensitivity checks; loss ratio (1-ret_InfoVQA)/(1-ret_DocVQA).
findings.confounds: InfoVQA has more queries (494 vs 451), so narrower query-bootstrap CIs (ndcg@5 width 0.029 vs 0.051). This inflates the lower-bound safe set, but the point-estimate check keeps the direction. The loss ratio first conditioned on low DocVQA retention, which biases it toward regression to the mean. Symmetric selection on the mean of both datasets still gives a median ratio of 0.76 (31/32 models below 1; b_metrics.py). The same 33 models appear twice, and sibling checkpoints (colpali versions, hf/merged copies) are near duplicates. The InfoVQA baseline is far higher (0.90 vs 0.61), so dataset, baseline and ceiling effects cannot be separated. Corpus-sampling variance is ignored.
findings.practical_implication: Calibrate on DocVQA-like (harder) data for a conservative safe set. An InfoVQA-calibrated threshold would be too optimistic for DocVQA about one time in five. Do not treat safe sets as portable in the easy-to-hard direction.
findings.question: transfer-metrics

verdict.recomputed:
From measured.json, pairing on (model, label) and excluding the float32 row, I get 2306 paired rows across 40 models. The claim uses 1887 rows and 33 models, and I do not know what restriction produced that.

- **Retention difference (InfoVQA minus DocVQA):** mean +0.0234, median +0.0102, InfoVQA higher on 74.3% of rows.
- **Per-model medians:** 30 of 40 are positive (sign test p=0.0022). The model-mean difference is +0.0241, bootstrap CI (0.019, 0.029).
- **Safe sets (lower bound >= 0.95):** DocVQA 1280, InfoVQA 1717, both 1272, DocVQA-only 8, InfoVQA-only 445.
  - P(safe on InfoVQA | safe on DocVQA) = 99.4%.
  - P(safe on DocVQA | safe on InfoVQA) = 74.1%.
  - McNemar exact p is about 1e-120.
- **Point retention >= 0.95:** 4 DocVQA-only versus 215 InfoVQA-only.
- **Interval width:** median width is 0.044 on DocVQA versus 0.020 on InfoVQA, so the interval-width confound is real. Subtracting the DocVQA half-width from both point estimates still gives 15 versus 295.
- **Loss ratio:** I selected rows on the mean of the two retentions being below 0.97 and DocVQA retention below 0.999, then took per-model medians of (1-ret_InfoVQA)/(1-ret_DocVQA) for models with at least 3 such rows. The median is 0.66, 37 of 39 models are below 1, and Wilcoxon p=3e-9.
- **Sibling dedupe:** keeping one checkpoint per name stem (32 families) gives mean +0.0255 and a model mean of +0.0264, with 30 of 32 positive.
- **Leave-one-model-out:** the model-mean difference stays between 0.0231 and 0.0249.
- **Gap by compression:** +0.003 below 4x, +0.015 at 4-64x, +0.032 at 64-128x, +0.071 above 128x. It grows with compression, as claimed.
- **Float16 baselines:** the gap is similar with and without them (+0.0268 on 779 float16 rows, +0.0217 on the rest).

The direction, the asymmetry and the compression trend all reproduce.
verdict.issues:
1. I could not reproduce the exact pair count (1887 rows, 33 models) or the exact safe-set counts, because I do not know the original row or model filter. The conclusions are the same on my broader set.
2. The lower-bound safe-set asymmetry is partly a CI-width artefact. InfoVQA intervals are about half as wide. The asymmetry survives the point-estimate and width-matched checks, but the 99.3% vs 78.5% figures are not clean effect sizes.
3. The 99.3% figure is conditional on a large "both safe" block. The 7 or 8 DocVQA-only rows are mostly borderline cases.
4. The claim does not separate the dataset effect from the baseline and ceiling effect (InfoVQA baseline about 0.90, DocVQA about 0.61). Also, every model-level and row-level test treats correlated rows as independent. Rows within a model share a codec and its failure modes, and sibling checkpoints are near-duplicates. The model-level tests and the dedupe check mitigate this only partly.
5. This is exploratory, post-hoc analysis. I ran about 12 comparisons here. Corpus-sampling variance is ignored, so the p-values (1e-75 and similar) are overstated.
6. The gap is near zero for lightly compressed rows (below 4x). The finding is about aggressive compression, not about all pipelines.
7. Results are on 500-page ViDoRe V1 subsamples only.
verdict.corrected_claim: On ViDoRe V1 subsamples, the same model and pipeline retain ndcg@5 better on InfoVQA than on DocVQA. The mean difference is about +0.024, with model-level bootstrap CI roughly (0.019, 0.029), and InfoVQA is higher on about 74% of paired rows. The gap is about 0.003 below 4x compression and about 0.07 above 128x. Pipelines whose retention lower bound is >= 0.95 on DocVQA are almost always (about 99%) also safe on InfoVQA. The reverse holds about 74-78% of the time. The direction survives point-estimate and width-matched checks, sibling dedupe, and leave-one-model-out. Part of the lower-bound gap comes from InfoVQA's narrower intervals. The effect cannot be separated from InfoVQA's higher baseline (ceiling effect). Treat it as a moderate, exploratory, dataset-specific pattern. It is not evidence that InfoVQA is intrinsically easier to compress, and it should not be assumed to transfer to other corpora.

findings.title: Pipeline ranks transfer across datasets; other models' pipeline behaviour is as good a predictor as the model's own other-dataset behaviour
findings.claim: The order of pipelines by retention is largely preserved across DocVQA and InfoVQA within a model. Pipeline identity explains more than model identity: the median over other models of the same pipeline's InfoVQA retention predicts a model's own InfoVQA retention at least as well as its own DocVQA retention.
findings.evidence: Per-model Spearman of ndcg@5 retention over shared pipelines: median 0.885 (model bootstrap CI 0.862 to 0.909; range 0.435 to 0.964; 0.924 median after dropping rows where both retentions >= 0.99). Lowest: EVIE-4.5B and EVIE-8B (0.435 each; rows nearly all saturated near 1.0), VultronFlash 0.745, webAI-ColVec1-4b 0.775. Pooled Spearman 0.82. By compression bin the rank correlation rises from 0.48 to 0.70 below 16x (saturated rows) to 0.90 to 0.96 above 64x. Leave-one-model-out over 31 models: rho 0.907 (other models' InfoVQA) vs 0.882 (own DocVQA), Wilcoxon p=0.055. MAE 0.0227 vs 0.0307, p=0.019. Own-DocVQA wins on rho in only 12/31 models.
findings.method: Per-model Spearman, model bootstrap, leave-one-model-out label-median prediction with a Wilcoxon comparison.
findings.confounds: Rank correlation is dominated by the compression level (the retention range is wide: mean 0.82 to 0.99 per model), so a high rho largely reflects that heavy pipelines are bad on both datasets. Within a narrow compression band it is lower. Saturated or near-ceiling models (EVIE, Vultron, webAI) have noisy ranks. The leave-one-out p-value for rho is borderline. Cross-model prediction uses sibling checkpoints that are near duplicates. Retention > 1 is noise.
findings.practical_implication: A pre-computed per-pipeline prior from the measured catalogue is a reasonable first guess for a new model on a new image dataset, and generally better for ranking than a single-dataset own measurement. Absolute levels still shift by dataset (F1).
findings.question: transfer-metrics

verdict.recomputed: From measured.json, 40 models have both DocVQA and InfoVQA, not 31 (the other analyst's 31 may be a subset, which I could not check). Per-model Spearman over shared labels has median 0.879, range 0.43 to 0.97, model-bootstrap 95% CI 0.855 to 0.899. This matches the claim of 0.885 (0.862 to 0.909). Leave-one-model-out label-median prediction of InfoVQA retention, over 40 models: median rho 0.914 for other models' InfoVQA versus 0.881 for own DocVQA (Wilcoxon p=0.058). Own DocVQA wins on rho in 16/40 models. Median MAE is 0.0173 versus 0.0267 (p=0.022). After crude removal of sibling checkpoints by name stem (33 models left), rho is 0.911 vs 0.885 (p=0.26), MAE 0.0181 vs 0.0251 (p=0.029). Without the lowest-rho models (38 left), rho is 0.920 vs 0.886 (p=0.13), MAE 0.0174 vs 0.0278 (p=0.037). Median within-model rank correlation by compression band: below 16x 0.71, 16 to 64x 0.79, above 64x 0.91. Compression alone ranks pipelines at median rho -0.66 against InfoVQA retention, so much of the rank agreement comes from the compression level.
verdict.issues:
1. The rank-preservation result reproduces, and the bin trend matches in direction. The below-16x band is 0.71 in my run versus the claimed 0.48 to 0.70, so I did not reproduce the lower end.
2. The claim that other models predict at least as well as the model's own DocVQA holds, but only as a weak pattern. The rho difference is borderline (p=0.058 on 40 models, p=0.26 after sibling dedup). Only the MAE advantage is moderately supported (p about 0.02 to 0.04), and it survived dedup.
3. The "explains more than model identity" wording overreaches. Rank correlations are inflated by the wide compression range, since heavy pipelines are bad on both datasets. Within a band they fall to 0.7 to 0.8 below 64x.
4. The MAE edge is partly expected. The other-model median pools many models and shrinks noise, whereas a single model's own DocVQA retention carries a dataset-specific offset.
5. Both metrics are post-hoc tests, I ran about 8 comparisons and did not correct for them. Sibling checkpoints remain correlated because my dedup was by name stem only. Retention above 1 is noise. Dataset and modality are not confounded here, since all of these are image models on the same two datasets. Float16 baselines were not examined.
6. The 31 versus 40 model count could not be reconciled from the data.
verdict.corrected_claim: Within a model, the order of pipelines by retention is largely preserved between DocVQA and InfoVQA. Median Spearman is about 0.88 (CI 0.86 to 0.90) over 40 models, and it is lower in the low-compression, near-saturated range (about 0.7 below 16x) than above 64x (about 0.9). A leave-one-model-out label-median of other models' InfoVQA retention predicts a model's own InfoVQA retention about as well as the model's own DocVQA retention on rank (0.91 vs 0.88, p=0.06, not significant after dedup) and somewhat better on absolute error (MAE about 0.017 vs 0.027, p<0.05 even after dedup). This is a weak, exploratory pattern, not evidence that pipeline identity dominates model identity.

findings.title: recall@1 degrades first, recall@5 last; ndcg@5-safe does not imply recall@1-safe
findings.claim: Under compression the ordering of metric retention is consistently recall@1 < ndcg@5 < ndcg@10 < recall@5, in every dataset.
findings.evidence: On non-saturated rows (min metric retention < 0.97), model-mean recall@1 minus ndcg@5 is -0.037 (CI -0.043,-0.030; DocVQA, positive in 1/33 models), -0.062 (CI -0.070,-0.054; InfoVQA, 0/33) and -0.018 (SciFact, 2/14). recall@5 minus ndcg@5 is +0.026 / +0.051 / +0.015 (positive in 32/33, 33/33, 14/14). ndcg@5 minus ndcg@10 is -0.013 / -0.017 / -0.010. recall@1 is the lowest of the four on 82% (DocVQA), 99% (InfoVQA) and 75% (SciFact) of non-saturated rows. Loss ratio (1-ret_recall@1)/(1-ret_ndcg@5) has median 1.18 / 1.29 / 1.06 (rows with min retention < 0.9; per-model medians 1.06 to 1.59). The gap grows with compression (InfoVQA recall@1-ndcg@5: -0.007 below 4x, -0.024 at 16-64x, -0.069 above 256x) and is about zero for codec-only and token-only groups (-0.001 to -0.003), but -0.04 to -0.05 for token+dim and token+dim+codec. Safe-set consequence: of 1341 InfoVQA rows with ndcg@5 lower bound >= 0.95, 171 have another metric whose lower bound is < 0.95 (392 of 1060 on DocVQA; 106 of 207 on SciFact). Only 12, 13 and 1 have a point retention < 0.95 on another metric, and the minimum point retention among them is 0.938 to 0.948. 18 paired comparisons, all model Wilcoxon p<0.006.
findings.method: Paired differences averaged per model then bootstrapped over models (2000 resamples); Wilcoxon over models; per-row argmin metric counts; loss ratios; safe-set cross-tabulation.
findings.confounds: Mostly a mechanical consequence of metric definition: recall@1 is a stricter, more discrete cutoff than ndcg@5, and with one relevant page per query a demotion from rank 1 to rank 2 costs recall@1 fully but ndcg only partly. So the ordering is expected, and the size is the useful number. recall@1 CIs are 1.5x wider than ndcg@5 (0.045 to 0.099 vs 0.029 to 0.066), which drives most of the safe-set shortfall (the point-estimate shortfall is small). Selection to non-saturated rows excludes about 40% of rows. Ties are rare (under 1%). Float16-baseline models are included. Models are not independent within family.
findings.practical_implication: If the downstream use depends on the top hit (recall@1), apply a margin to the ndcg@5 criterion: at the point-estimate level a pipeline that meets 0.95 on ndcg@5 still keeps at least about 0.94 on every other metric in this data. At the lower-bound level, 13 to 50% of ndcg@5-safe rows fail another metric. Report recall@1 retention next to ndcg@5.
findings.question: transfer-metrics

verdict.recomputed: From the raw wide/*.json files (campaign dir, 33 DocVQA, 33 InfoVQA, 14 SciFact models), on non-saturated rows (min of the 4 metric retentions < 0.97, at least 3 such rows per model), I got model-mean retention (recall@1, ndcg@5, ndcg@10, recall@5): DocVQA 0.727/0.764/0.777/0.790, InfoVQA 0.689/0.752/0.768/0.802, SciFact 0.644/0.662/0.672/0.677. This matches the claimed ordering in all three datasets. Recall@1 minus ndcg@5, bootstrapped over models: -0.037 (CI -0.043,-0.030; positive in 1/33), -0.062 (-0.070,-0.054; 0/33), -0.018 (-0.022,-0.013; 2/14). Recall@5 minus ndcg@5: +0.026 (32/33), +0.051 (33/33), +0.015 (14/14). ndcg@5 minus ndcg@10: -0.013/-0.017/-0.010, with 0 or 1 model positive in each dataset. Per-row recall@1 is the lowest metric on 82.4% (DocVQA), 98.8% (InfoVQA) and 75.9% (SciFact) of non-saturated rows. Wilcoxon p-values over models are at most 6e-4 in all three datasets. Gaps grow with compression: InfoVQA recall@1 minus ndcg@5 goes from -0.046 (4-16x) to -0.078 (16-64x) to -0.090 (above 256x). It is larger for token+dim groups (-0.06 to -0.09) than for token-only or codec-only groups (-0.015 to -0.019). Robustness: dropping the most extreme model barely moves the mean (-0.036, -0.061, -0.017). Restricting to the 21 models with a non-float16 baseline gives -0.040 and -0.065; the float16 models do not drive the effect. Using all rows instead of only non-saturated ones gives the same sign with a smaller size (-0.019, -0.026, -0.013). I did not recompute the safe-set cross-tabulation or the loss ratios.
verdict.issues: 1) The strict four-way ordering recall@1 < ndcg@5 < ndcg@10 < recall@5 holds for the model-mean in every dataset, but not for every model. The share of models with the full strict ordering on non-saturated rows is 82% on DocVQA, 100% on InfoVQA and 71% on SciFact (70%, 97%, 64% on all rows). The weakest link is ndcg@10 vs recall@5: recall@5 exceeds ndcg@10 in 28/33, 33/33 and 11/14 models. On SciFact the gap is only +0.005 (CI +0.002,+0.009), and on all rows its Wilcoxon p is 0.049, so "consistently" is overstated there. 2) The recall@1 versus ndcg@5 gap is small on SciFact (-0.018). Recall@1 is lowest on only 75% of SciFact rows. 3) The "about zero for codec-only" claim could not be checked on the image datasets, because no model has 3 or more non-saturated codec rows there. On SciFact, codec-only is -0.015 (n=6 models), not near zero, and token-only is -0.013. The group pattern is therefore weak and rests on few models per cell. 4) The gap is also small at low compression (about -0.004 on SciFact below 4x), so the ordering is largely a high-compression phenomenon. 5) Selecting rows by min retention < 0.97 conditions on the outcome, and each model's rows are weighted equally within it. The sign of the effect survives using all rows, but the size depends on the selection. 6) This is post-hoc and I ran about 30 paired comparisons. The model-level CIs treat models as independent, but sibling checkpoints are correlated, and the DocVQA and InfoVQA models are the same 33 models. Dataset and modality are confounded, so SciFact vs image differences must not be attributed to modality. The ordering is largely mechanical from the metric definitions, as the finding already says.
verdict.corrected_claim: On average across models, retention under compression ranks recall@1 < ndcg@5 < ndcg@10 < recall@5 in DocVQA, InfoVQA and SciFact. Recall@1 sits about 0.02 to 0.06 below ndcg@5 on non-saturated rows, with CIs excluding zero, and this holds without float16-baseline models or the most extreme model. The full four-way ordering holds per model in 82%, 100% and 71% of models. The ndcg@10 vs recall@5 step is weak, especially on SciFact (+0.005). The gap grows with compression and is near zero at under 4x compression, and it is largest for token+dim pipelines. This is post-hoc, partly mechanical from metric definitions, and the models and datasets are confounded. The safe-set counts were not rechecked.

findings.title: Lower baseline goes with more fragility at high compression on image datasets
findings.claim: Among shared pipelines at 32x and above, models with lower baseline ndcg@5 lose more retention. The relation is clear on InfoVQA, weaker on DocVQA, absent at mild compression and absent on text.
findings.evidence: Mean over shared pipelines (present in >= 10 models) of the Spearman correlation between baseline and retention: InfoVQA 32-128x rho=0.56 (model-bootstrap CI 0.39 to 0.67, permutation p=0.002, 14 pipelines, 33 models), >= 128x 0.54 (0.23 to 0.73, p=0.004, 6 pipelines, 25 models), 8-32x 0.25 (p=0.04), 1-8x 0.25 (p=0.026). DocVQA 32-128x 0.36 (0.15 to 0.53, p=0.004), >= 128x 0.41 (0.06 to 0.69, p=0.010), 8-32x 0.09 (p=0.44), 1-8x 0.02 (p=0.85). With family fixed effects (baseline and retention demeaned within 8 families, within-family permutation): InfoVQA 0.41 (p=0.002) at 32-128x and 0.45 (p=0.024) at >= 128x, while DocVQA drops to 0.27 (p=0.15) and 0.35 (p=0.056). Text (SciFact, 14 models): rho -0.07 at 32-128x and -0.12 at >= 128x, all p > 0.5. Model-level aggregates show little: mean retention over the 32 shared (mostly mild) pipelines vs baseline rho=-0.05 (DocVQA) and 0.02 (InfoVQA); retention at >= 32x gives rho 0.19 (p=0.28) and 0.38 (p=0.028, CI 0.03 to 0.66).
findings.method: Per-pipeline Spearman (baseline vs retention) across models, averaged over pipelines; permutation of baselines across models (same permutation for all pipelines, 500 permutations); model-cluster bootstrap; family fixed effects with within-family permutation; model-level Spearman.
findings.confounds: Baseline is correlated with model generation, size and vectors per doc (not controlled in c_perm.py; a partial correlation on log vectors/doc in c_baseline.py leaves the model-level ret32 rho at 0.37 for InfoVQA and 0.18 for DocVQA). Only 8 families, with colpali and colqwen sibling checkpoints near duplicates. Shared pipelines are only 14 (32-128x) and 6 (>= 128x), and they are mostly pipelines that every model has run, so they are selection-biased toward the standard fixed set. Retention > 1 noise. 24 of 80 files use float16 baselines. Permutation p-values are uncorrected across about 30 tests. The direction is plausible (low-baseline models have less margin for relevant pages) but could also reflect weaker or older architectures. Baseline range on InfoVQA is narrower (0.79 to 0.95) so the extremes (colpali v1.0, NeoMME-260M) drive much of it.
findings.practical_implication: A model's baseline is a weak but usable hint that it will need milder pipelines at 32x and above on image data (about 0.4 to 0.55 rank correlation per pipeline). Do not use it for mild compression, where there is no relation. Do not extend it to text.
findings.question: transfer-metrics

verdict.recomputed: Own code from measured.json (pipelines keyed by stage JSON, banded by per-row compression, pipelines with >=10 models, mean per-pipeline Spearman of baseline vs retention across models, permutation of baselines with the same permutation for all pipelines, 300 perms; model-cluster bootstrap 100 resamples). I got 40 models per image dataset, not 33/25 as in the claim, so band membership differs somewhat. InfoVQA (40 models, 10 registry families): 8-32x rho=0.25 (p=0.017, CI 0.04 to 0.47), 32-128x rho=0.58 (14 pipelines, p=0.003, CI 0.42 to 0.67), >=128x rho=0.37 (8 pipelines, p=0.010, CI 0.04 to 0.62). Robustness on InfoVQA: dropping the 2 lowest-baseline models gives 0.58 and 0.42; dropping min and max baseline gives 0.58 and 0.34; dropping the 13 float16-baseline models (27 left) gives 0.50 (p=0.003) and 0.54 (6 pipelines, p=0.007); one best model per family (n=10, 5 pipelines) gives 0.72 (p=0.007) at 32-128x but is noisy. DocVQA: 8-32x 0.04 (p=0.69), 32-128x 0.35 (p=0.003, CI 0.18 to 0.49), >=128x 0.27 (p=0.073, CI -0.03 to 0.50). Dropping the 2 lowest DocVQA baselines leaves 32-128x at 0.36 and >=128x at 0.30 (earlier run). SciFact (15 models, all in one family 'colbert', no float16): 8-32x 0.01, 32-128x -0.04 (CI -0.45 to 0.30), >=128x -0.15 (CI -0.59 to 0.30), all p>0.5; dropping the lowest 2 baselines gives negative values (-0.21, -0.33) but with p>0.2. The 1-8x band returned NaN in my script because some pipelines have constant retention (e.g. all 1.0), so I could not reproduce the 1-8x figures. I did not recompute the family fixed-effects or model-level aggregate numbers.
verdict.issues: 1) Model counts differ (I used all 40 models with data per dataset), yet 32-128x numbers reproduce well (InfoVQA 0.58 vs 0.56, DocVQA 0.35 vs 0.36), so the core result is not sensitive to the model set. 2) At >=128x the effect is weaker and less stable than stated: InfoVQA 0.37 here (vs 0.54 claimed; 0.54 only appears after dropping float16-baseline models, 6 pipelines), DocVQA 0.27 with CI crossing zero and p=0.07, so the >=128x DocVQA claim is not supported by my recompute (the claim gave 0.41, p=0.010). 3) The InfoVQA 8-32x correlation (0.25, p=0.017) is non-zero here, so 'absent at mild compression' is only true for DocVQA and 1-8x; the claimed InfoVQA 8-32x and 1-8x rho of 0.25 are modest but present. 4) Effect survives dropping the extreme-baseline models and float16 models on InfoVQA, so extremes (colpali v1.0, NeoMME) do not drive it. 5) Not independent: sibling checkpoints (colpali v1.0/1.1/1.2/merged, colqwen) dominate the low-baseline end; one-per-family result (n=10) is directionally consistent but has few pipelines and the null sd is 0.28. 6) Text null is uninformative rather than evidence of absence: 15 SciFact models, a single family, null sd 0.17-0.23, CIs span roughly -0.5 to +0.3; text vs image is confounded with dataset. 7) Pipelines at high compression are a standard shared set, so the correlation is per-pipeline and the 14 pipelines are highly correlated with each other; effective number of independent tests is far below 14, and p-values are uncorrected post-hoc (about 12 band-variant tests here). 8) Retention is bounded near 1 and noisy; ties and constant-retention pipelines make Spearman degenerate at mild compression.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory, post-hoc: on ViDoRe InfoVQA and DocVQA, among pipelines shared by >=10 models at 32-128x compression, models with lower baseline ndcg@5 tend to retain less (mean per-pipeline Spearman about 0.58 on InfoVQA, CI 0.42-0.67; about 0.35 on DocVQA, CI 0.18-0.49; stable to dropping extreme-baseline models and, on InfoVQA, float16-baseline models). At >=128x the sign is the same but the estimate is smaller and uncertain (InfoVQA about 0.37, CI 0.04-0.62; DocVQA about 0.27, CI -0.03 to 0.50). The relation is weak or absent at 8-32x on DocVQA and weak (about 0.25) on InfoVQA. The effective sample is about 10 families with correlated sibling checkpoints, so this is a weak-to-moderate association, not evidence of a causal or general rule. Text (SciFact, 15 colbert-family models) shows no detectable relation, but with wide CIs this is a null of low power and cannot be separated from the dataset/modality confound.

findings.title: Retention is higher where the baseline is higher across datasets, but the effect size does not track the baseline gap
findings.claim: Every image model has a much higher baseline on InfoVQA than DocVQA and a higher retention at >= 32x. But the model-specific baseline gap does not predict the model-specific retention gain, so dataset-level easiness cannot be separated from baseline level.
findings.evidence: InfoVQA baseline is higher for 33/33 models (mean +0.286, from 0.611 to 0.897). Retention (shared pipelines): mean over all 32 shared pipelines +0.0067 (25/33 models positive); at >= 32x +0.0161 (27/33 positive). Spearman between model baseline gap and retention gain: 0.067 (p=0.71) for all shared pipelines, 0.133 (p=0.46) at >= 32x. Pooled over datasets, with within-dataset standardisation (n=66, not independent): baseline vs ret32 rho=0.26 (p=0.035); raw pooled rho=0.56 (p=8e-7, dataset-confounded).
findings.method: Within-model paired differences; Spearman between deltas; pooled standardised correlation.
findings.confounds: Two datasets only, so dataset is one binary factor with near-complete overlap of baseline distributions removed (every model has a baseline gap of 0.18 to 0.38, so there is little variation to regress on). n=33 models with near-duplicate siblings. Pooled analyses count each model twice. Different corpora, query styles (InfoVQA infographics vs DocVQA scanned documents) and numbers of queries.
findings.practical_implication: Do not claim that a harder dataset or lower baseline causes fragility from the cross-dataset comparison alone. The within-dataset analysis (F4) is the safer evidence, and the dataset effect (F1) should be treated as dataset-specific.

verdict.recomputed:
Recomputed from measured.json (current file, modified 2026-10-17 09:09). It now holds 40 image models with both DocVQA and InfoVQA, not 33.
- InfoVQA baseline is higher for 40/40 models. Mean gap is +0.285 (DocVQA minimum 0.542, InfoVQA maximum 0.947).
- Shared-pipeline retention gain, InfoVQA minus DocVQA, matching rows by label with equal compression:
  - All shared pipelines: mean +0.0235 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.018 to 0.029), positive for 36/40 models.
  - Pipelines at >=32x: mean +0.0431 (CI 0.034 to 0.052), positive for 38/40 models.
  - Both are much larger than the claimed +0.0067 and +0.0161. The sign and direction agree.
- Per-model baseline gap vs retention gain (Spearman): 0.129 (p=0.43) for all pipelines and 0.139 (p=0.39) at >=32x.
  - Weak and non-significant. This matches the claim of 0.067 and 0.133.
  - Baseline level vs gain is also about 0 (|rho| < 0.08, p > 0.65).
- Robustness:
  - Dropping the two extreme models changes nothing material (rho 0.17, p=0.30).
  - Keeping one model per organisation (n=15) gives rho=0.57 (p=0.027). This is a sibling or low-n sensitivity, one of several cuts, so I treat it as unstable.
- Pooled correlations differ from the claim:
  - Raw pooled rho (n=80) is 0.54 (p=2e-7).
  - Within-dataset-standardised pooled rho is 0.61 (p=2e-9), not the claimed 0.26.
  - Within DocVQA alone, baseline vs ret32 is rho=0.60 (p=4e-5). Within InfoVQA alone it is 0.65 (p=6e-6).
- Fixed-label subset (the 25 models sharing an identical 54-label set; 20 pipelines at >=32x): the gap-vs-gain rho is 0.22 (p=0.28) and 0.21 (p=0.31). Standardised pooled rho is 0.60. Within-dataset rho is 0.52 to 0.66.
- Tests run: about 25 Spearman and Wilcoxon tests, plus bootstraps. None were corrected, and this is exploratory.
verdict.issues:
1. Model count and effect sizes are stale. The data now has 40 models, not 33. The retention gains are roughly 3x larger than claimed.
2. The pooled standardised correlation of 0.26 (p=0.035) does not reproduce. I get 0.60 to 0.61 on both the full set and a fixed-label subset. This is the biggest discrepancy, and it contradicts the implication that baseline level barely matters.
3. Models differ in which labels they have (54 to 74 shared labels per model). The claimed 32 shared pipelines is hard to reproduce, and no label set is common to all 40 models. I matched labels per model and also ran a fixed-label subset of 25 models. Pipeline-set choice therefore matters for the magnitudes.
4. The main claim, that the model-specific baseline gap does not predict the model-specific retention gain, holds in the full set (rho about 0.13 to 0.14, p about 0.4). Its stated reason, that the gap range is narrow, is plausible but untested. It is also true that baseline level is strongly associated with retention within each dataset.
5. A non-significant rho at n=40 has wide uncertainty. A moderate true correlation (about 0.4) cannot be excluded. In the one-per-organisation cut (n=15), rho=0.57 (p=0.027).
6. "Cannot be separated" is fair. Dataset easiness is the single binary factor here, and DocVQA vs InfoVQA also differ in corpus, queries and query count. Float16-inference baselines were not examined separately.
7. Retention values above 1 are noise and are included in these means.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory and post hoc, with about 25 uncorrected tests. In the current data, 40 image models have both datasets. InfoVQA baseline is higher for 40/40 models (mean +0.285). Retention on shared pipelines is higher on InfoVQA: mean +0.024 over all shared pipelines (36/40 models positive) and +0.043 at >=32x (38/40 positive). The model-level baseline gap does not predict the model-level retention gain (Spearman about 0.13 to 0.14, p about 0.4, n=40, wide uncertainty). Within each dataset, higher-baseline models retain more at >=32x (rho about 0.6). The standardised pooled rho is about 0.6, not 0.26. Dataset easiness and baseline level are therefore confounded, since dataset is a single binary factor. The within-dataset association is not independent of correlated sibling checkpoints.

findings.title: SciFact (text) retains less than the image sets at matched compression, but this is confounded
findings.claim: At matched compression, text models on SciFact lose more ndcg@5 than image models on DocVQA or InfoVQA, with a large spread across text models. Nothing about modality can be concluded.
findings.evidence: Mean ndcg@5 retention by compression bin (all rows): 16-64x SciFact 0.725 vs DocVQA 0.885 vs InfoVQA 0.904; 64-256x 0.506 vs 0.738 vs 0.775; >256x 0.398 vs 0.624 vs 0.719. Share of rows with ndcg@5 lower bound >= 0.95: SciFact 0.277, DocVQA 0.562, InfoVQA 0.711. Four text models (LateOn, LFM2-ColBERT-350M, mxbai-edge-17m and 32m) have minimum retention below 0.45 over the 32 shared pipelines, while the best (Reason-ModernColBERT) has 0.94. The recall@1 deficit is smaller on SciFact (-0.018) than on the image sets (F3).
findings.method: Descriptive binning by compression and per-model minima.
findings.confounds: Modality, dataset, corpus size (5183 vs 500 documents), vectors per document (157 to 313 vs 270 to 2920), query count (300), 2 to 8 families and 14 models are all confounded. Compression in the bin is defined against float32 bytes per doc, and the text models have fewer vectors to start with, so the same compression ratio means a more aggressive pipeline per vector. No attribution to modality is warranted.
findings.practical_implication: Do not transfer image-model safe sets to text models or vice versa. Treat SciFact thresholds as a separate calibration problem.

verdict.recomputed: From measured.json (15 SciFact models, 40 per image set; 806/2343/2343 rows). Row-mean ndcg@5 retention by compression bin, SciFact / DocVQA / InfoVQA: 16-64x 0.739/0.896/0.913; 64-256x 0.565/0.787/0.823; >256x 0.418/0.692/0.776. These are close to the claimed values, but the SciFact and DocVQA figures differ in the third decimal and the claim's exact figures were not reproduced. Same ordering. Share of rows with lower CI bound >= 0.95 in the 16-64x bin: 0.192/0.599/0.784; the claimed 0.277/0.562/0.711 were not reproduced. Model-mean bin retention with a bootstrap over models gives SciFact 0.741 [0.667,0.804], DocVQA 0.889 [0.870,0.907] in 16-64x; 0.560 [0.484,0.623] vs 0.776 [0.736,0.817] in 64-256x; 0.414 [0.335,0.490] vs 0.633 [0.565,0.702] in >256x. Matched-pipeline analysis, 71 shared pipelines with the same compression (within 10%) on all three sets: model-mean retention 0.780 SciFact vs 0.884 DocVQA (diff CI [-0.144,-0.062]) and 0.905 InfoVQA (diff CI [-0.165,-0.084]). With 4 sibling-like models removed (n=11): CI [-0.153,-0.052] and [-0.171,-0.075]. Permutation p<5e-5 for both (not corrected, and the models are not independent of their family). SciFact lower on 56/71 pipelines vs DocVQA and 63/71 vs InfoVQA. The gap depends on the pipeline. For project(64) the three sets are equal (0.977 vs 0.972 vs 0.978). project(64)>binary is higher on SciFact than DocVQA (0.937 vs 0.924). The gap is large for int4 (0.857 vs 0.945), lloyd2(7) (0.866 vs 0.988) and plain binary (0.858 vs 0.975/0.990). int4(mean) is near 1.0 everywhere. The SciFact worst model per pipeline is much lower (e.g. 0.27-0.30 for int4, lloyd2 and binary). Only about 10 of 15 SciFact pipelines-by-model means are below the DocVQA 5th percentile of 0.81 (SciFact model means range 0.65-0.94, a single model, Reason-ModernColBERT, at 0.94). The pipeline-count tests run were roughly 4 (bin comparisons x3 plus 2 matched permutation tests); post-hoc.
verdict.issues: 1) The compression-bin comparison is not matched. SciFact and image sets contain different pipeline mixes at a given bin: ward and adaptive_merge pipelines reach 100-7000x on SciFact (e.g. adaptive r=0.7 > binary: 4174x, retention 0.146) but only 3-200x on images, where they retain 0.93-0.98. So the high-compression SciFact bins are dominated by collapsed adaptive/ward rows. The bin means mostly reflect pipeline mix, not a like-for-like gap. Only the 71 matched-compression pipelines are a fair test, and there the gap is smaller (about -0.10 to -0.12, not -0.15 to -0.28). 2) The gap is not uniform: project-family pipelines show no SciFact deficit, so the claim 'text models lose more at matched compression' is true on average but driven by binary, int4, lloyd2, ward and adaptive stages, which interact with the model rather than compression ratio. 3) The claimed bin means and the lb>=0.95 shares did not reproduce exactly (differ by up to 0.09 in share), likely from using wide files or different row selection. The '4 text models with min <0.45 over 32 shared pipelines' and the recall@1 figure (-0.018) were not recomputed; over all 114 shared labels, 14 of 15 SciFact models have min retention below 0.35 (many at ~0.003, due to project(16) pipelines), so the 'four models' statement depends on which 32 pipelines were chosen. 4) Confounds the claim already lists remain: 15 models in about 8 families, sibling checkpoints (colbertv2.0 appears twice, LFM2 and LFM2.5, mLateOn), query-only bootstrap, float16 baselines, dataset=modality. Non-independence means the permutation p is optimistic.
verdict.corrected_claim: On a matched set of 71 pipelines with the same compression on all datasets, SciFact (text) models retain on average about 0.10 to 0.12 less ndcg@5 than DocVQA/InfoVQA models (model-mean 0.78 vs 0.88/0.91; bootstrap-over-models CI of the difference roughly -0.14 to -0.06 and -0.17 to -0.08), robust to removing four sibling models. The gap is concentrated in binary, int4, lloyd2 and ward/adaptive-merge pipelines; project(64)-based pipelines show no deficit. The larger bin gaps in the original evidence (up to 0.28) mostly reflect different pipeline mixes per bin (SciFact reaches high compression through collapsing adaptive/ward rows) and should not be read as a matched-compression effect. Dataset, corpus size, vectors per document and modality are fully confounded, so no modality attribution is possible. Exploratory post-hoc analysis.

results.summary: Exploratory, post-hoc analysis (about 100 uncorrected tests, groups hand-assigned after looking at data). Family carries a real but modest share of compression-profile variance on image data (about 21%, permutation p about 0.001), and it is a strong predictor in one respect: plain int4 collapse is shared within lineages (nemotron 4b and 8b, mxbai-edge 17m and 32m, LateOn and mLateOn) but not within backbones. Family is not a better predictor of a new image model's profile than the image-wide mean (squared-error ratio 0.96, CI 0.75-1.23), and a model's individual deviation from its family does not persist across datasets (r 0.06, p 0.27). Binary-codec loss falls with embedding dimension (128-d 2.3 points, 320-d 0.9, 640-d 0.4). Model size and float16-vs-float32 inference show no detectable consistent effect. The two colbertv2.0 copies (baseline 0.646 vs 0.692, 157 vs 236 vectors/doc) have the most similar profile of all 91 text pairs. findings.title: Plain int4 collapse follows lineage, not backbone, size, dtype or dimension
findings.claim: Plain per-vector int4 collapses for nemotron-colembed-vl 4b and 8b, mxbai-edge 17m and 32m, and LateOn and mLateOn, each pair together. Siblings predict collapse; backbone grouping does not. Centred int4 removes it everywhere.
findings.evidence: Retention on plain int4: nemotron 4b 0.004 (InfoVQA) and 0.009 (DocVQA); nemotron 8b 0.007 and 0.011; mxbai-edge 17m 0.268; 32m 0.792; LateOn 0.297; mLateOn 0.765; GTE-ModernColBERT 0.936. The other 44 models are 0.983 or higher. int4(mean) is 0.951-1.011 for all models. Fisher exact on whether a model has a collapsed group sibling: 6/6 collapsed models vs 9/39 others, p=0.0006 (n=45 with at least one sibling; backbone grouping p=0.006 but Qwen3-VL tomoro, Sauerkraut and webAI do not collapse while nemotron does). Not dimension: EVIE 2048/4096-d fine, nemotron 2560/4096-d collapses. Not size or dtype: nemotron 4b (float32) and 8b (float16) both collapse. In text, int4 retention correlates with binary (Spearman 0.65, p=0.012) and lloyd2 (0.76, p=0.0015) retention, n=14; nemotron collapses on int4 only, so its mechanism differs (an outlier component swamping the per-vector scale is inferred from the stage code, not measured).
findings.method: Per-model plain-int4 retention, collapse defined as maximum over datasets below 0.9; Fisher exact test of sibling collapse against own collapse; Spearman among 14 text models.
findings.confounds: Only three independent clusters carry the 6 events (nemotron, mxbai-edge, lightonai LateOn/mLateOn), so effective n is about 3. Groups were hand-assigned. Text and image collapse have different datasets and metric (nDCG@10 vs nDCG@5). Collapse is already documented for nemotron in the repo; the lineage-versus-backbone contrast is the new reading.
findings.practical_implication: Never ship plain int4 on a new checkpoint without testing it, even if its siblings or backbone are fine; test it when a sibling collapses. Default to int4(mean) (centred), which is 0.95-1.01 for all 55 models.

- int4 vs binary: 0.648, p=0.012. Reproduced.
- int4 vs lloyd2(7): 0.763, p=0.0015. Reproduced.

verdict.issues:
1. Effective n is 3 clusters. The model-level Fisher p=0.0006 (and my 6e-7) overstates the evidence. Only the group-level concordance (3 of 3 pairs fully collapsed) is informative.
2. Circularity: sibling groups were hand-assigned, and only pairs whose members both collapse count as "sibling collapse". The Fisher test is therefore close to a restatement of the grouping. A fixed grouping rule written before looking at the data would be needed to avoid this.
3. "Not dimension" is not established. Both mxbai-edge models are low-dimensional (48-d and 64-d), and within that pair collapse is worse at the lower dimension (0.268 vs 0.792). The EVIE counterexample involves large, image-model dimensions and does not address this. answerai-colbert-small (96-d) has no int4 row, so the low-dimension hypothesis is untested.
4. Modality and dataset are confounded. Text collapse is 4 of 14 and image collapse is 2 of 37 (p=0.04). Nemotron is the only image collapse and its mechanism differs: int4 only, with int4(mean) fine.
5. Within-lineage severity is not shared. LateOn is 0.30 and mLateOn is 0.77. mxbai-edge 17m is 0.27 and 32m is 0.79. The 0.9 threshold is arbitrary, and GTE at 0.936 sits in a gradient rather than a clean split. Only a collapse/no-collapse concordance holds, not a magnitude.
6. Query-bootstrap CIs are wide on single-dataset text models. 17m has [0.225, 0.314] and mLateOn has [0.714, 0.811]. The CIs ignore corpus sampling.
7. nemotron 8b is a float16-inference baseline. It collapses the same way as the float32 4b, so the dtype claim is consistent but rests on one pair.
8. The mechanism (an outlier component swamping the per-vector scale) is inferred from the code, not measured here.
9. The metric label in measured.json is wrong for text (ndcg@10 shown as ndcg@5), and the claim does not flag it.
10. "Centred int4 removes it everywhere" is slightly too strong. LateOn is 0.951 with CI [0.923, 0.978] and colpali-v1.3-hf on DocVQA is 0.975.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among 51 models with a plain-int4 measurement, 6 fall below 0.9 retention. They form 3 same-release pairs: nemotron-colembed-vl 4b and 8b (image, retention about 0.004 to 0.011), mxbai-edge 17m and 32m (text, 0.27 and 0.79), and LateOn and mLateOn (text, 0.30 and 0.77). Collapse is concordant within each pair (group-level permutation p about 1e-4, but only 3 independent clusters). Other models sharing a backbone or organisation do not collapse: ModernBERT-based GTE, ColBERT-Zero and Reason-ModernColBERT, and mxbai-colbert-large. A release line therefore predicts collapse better than backbone or organisation in this sample. Severity differs within pairs. Dimension, modality (and dataset) and small-model effects are not excluded: the mxbai-edge pair is low-dimensional, and text collapses more often than image (4/14 vs 2/37, confounded). The int4 mechanism may also differ between nemotron and the text models. Centred int4 restores retention to 0.95 or above in all 51 models, with small residual losses (LateOn 0.951). In text (n=14), int4 retention correlates with binary (Spearman 0.65) and lloyd2 (0.76); this survives dropping the collapsed models. The analysis is exploratory and post-hoc.

findings.title: Family explains a modest share of profile variance but does not beat the global mean as a predictor, and individual deviations do not persist across datasets
findings.claim: On image data, family accounts for about a fifth of profile variance, more than chance, but a family mean predicts a held-out model no better than the image-wide mean, and a model's own deviation from its family on DocVQA does not carry over to InfoVQA.
findings.evidence: Variance decomposition (30 image models in families of size >=2, twins de-duplicated, 17 labels, int4 excluded): dataset 18%, family 21% (bootstrap CI 15-37%), model-within-family 27%, model x dataset 34%; family share permutation p=0.0013 (null mean 0.10); standardised per label 16%, p=0.005. Within-family deviations: correlation DocVQA vs InfoVQA after removing family means 0.064, permutation p=0.27. Nearest neighbour: same-family model is the closest profile in 30% of cases vs 14% chance (n=30, both datasets); mean RMSD within vs between 0.0137 vs 0.0200 (DocVQA, perm p=0.0006) and 0.0054 vs 0.0100 (InfoVQA, p=0.0002); SciFact 0.117 vs 0.165, p=0.17, 1-NN 22% = chance 22%. Leave-one-out prediction (twins excluded): family-mean squared error is 0.96x the global-mean error (bootstrap 95% CI 0.75-1.23); family helps for qwen3vl (RMSE 0.0076 vs 0.0088), qwen3.5 (0.0064 vs 0.0082), neomme (0.0074 vs 0.0084), and hurts for colpali (0.0159 vs 0.0133), colqwen2 (0.0126 vs 0.0104), colqwen2.5 (0.0125 vs 0.0108), smolvlm (0.0115 vs 0.0088). Transplanting a model's own other-dataset deviation gives error ratio 1.90 (CI 1.52-2.40) against the global mean, matching the 2.0 expected if no individual signal persists.
findings.method: Two-way variance decomposition with permutation of family labels and model-cluster bootstrap; within-vs-between RMSD permutation tests and 1-NN; leave-one-out prediction with model-cluster bootstrap on squared-error ratios.
findings.confounds: Families hand-assigned after seeing data. Only 7 grouped families and 30 models; families of 2 to 8 members. Family partly proxies backbone generation and embedding dimension (see F3). Query-bootstrap intervals ignore corpus sampling. Text family test has 14 models on one dataset. Seven ward-label profiles excluded. Retention above 1 is noise and was not clipped.
findings.practical_implication: Use family only as a weak prior for the Qwen3-based families; for others rely on the dataset-level profile and measure the new model. Treat the shared profile as 'what compression generally costs on this dataset' plus a few measured exceptions such as int4.
findings.question: families

verdict.recomputed:
Own script rebuilt the image retention matrix from measured.json. I assigned families by name pattern (colpali, colqwen2, colqwen2.5, qwen3vl, qwen3.5, neomme, smolvlm). I dropped the -hf and -merged twins and the ungrouped models. I used the standard-label set (29 labels with int4, float32 and float16 excluded, plus a 17-label subset). That gave 26 models in 7 families, not the claimed 30. The labels and the exact family assignment are not specified in the claim, so counts differ.

Reproduced:
- **Variance shares (29 labels, twins dropped):** dataset 17%, family 21%, model-within-family 30%, model x dataset 32%. The 17-label subset gives family 20%. With twins kept, family is 17%.
- **Family share vs chance:** permutation p = 0.017 (29 labels), 0.0125 (17 labels), 0.013 (twins kept). The null mean is about 0.10-0.12. This is more than chance, but weaker than the claimed p = 0.0013.
- **Leave-one-out prediction:** family-mean squared error is 1.09x the global-mean error (bootstrap 95% CI 0.93-1.32) for 29 labels. For the 17 labels it is 1.10x (0.92-1.37). With twins kept it is 1.18x (1.01-1.38). Jackknife range 1.04-1.24. The claimed 0.96x was not reproduced. The family mean is no better than the global mean in my runs, and in one specification it is slightly worse.
- **Per-family RMSE (family vs global, 29 labels):** qwen3.5 0.0106 vs 0.0115 (family helps). colqwen2 0.0131 vs 0.0107, smolvlm 0.0114 vs 0.0099 and qwen3vl 0.0102 vs 0.0092 (family hurts). colpali, colqwen2.5 and neomme are about equal. The direction of the family-level pattern is mixed. In my runs neomme and qwen3vl do not show the claimed help, which comes from different label sets and family definitions.
- **Persistence of deviations:** the pooled correlation of DocVQA vs InfoVQA deviations from the family mean is 0.19 (29 labels) or 0.19 (17 labels), 0.12 with twins kept. Model-cluster bootstrap CI is about -0.18 to 0.51. Permutation p is 0.03-0.17 depending on null. A within-family-shuffle null gives p = 0.07-0.16. The per-model mean deviation correlation is -0.17. Transplanting the other-dataset deviation, measured against the global mean, gives a squared-error ratio of 1.54-1.57 against the 2.0 expected with no persistence. That is not the claimed 1.90.
- **1-NN same-family:** 46% (29 labels), 35% (17 labels), 45% (twins kept), against about 14% chance. The claimed 30% is not reproduced; mine is higher.
- **Not run:** the RMSD within/between tests and the SciFact text test.
verdict.issues:
1. The headline "family ~ a fifth of variance, above chance" reproduces (20-21%, p about 0.01-0.02), but the p-value is an order of magnitude weaker than the stated 0.0013. It is sensitive to label set and twin handling.
2. "Family mean predicts no better than the global mean" reproduces in direction, but my ratios are 1.09-1.18, not 0.96. Two of three specifications have a CI that includes 1. The data say "no demonstrable advantage", and in one specification a small disadvantage. The "mixed by family" picture is only partly reproduced (qwen3.5 helps, colqwen2/smolvlm/qwen3vl hurt, others near equal).
3. "Individual deviations do not persist" is too strong. The correlation is small and positive (0.12-0.19), the CI spans zero (-0.18 to 0.51), and the transplant ratio (1.54-1.57) is below the 2.0 no-signal value. The 1.90 figure was not reproduced. Persistence is weak and unresolved with this n, not shown to be absent. The per-model mean deviation correlation is negative (-0.17), which is also noisy.
4. 1-NN is much higher than claimed (35-46%), so "modest family structure" understates the nearest-neighbour evidence.
5. Confounds hold: family is hand-assigned post hoc, there are only 7 families (several of size 2), siblings are correlated, retention above 1 is not clipped, and the query-bootstrap ignores corpus sampling. Dataset and modality are confounded only for the SciFact comparison, which I did not test. The image analysis uses DocVQA and InfoVQA only. Several baselines are float16 inference; I did not analyse that effect.
6. Counts do not match exactly (26 models in my runs vs 30 claimed; family assignments and the 17 labels are unspecified), so reproduction is approximate.
verdict.corrected_claim: On image data (about 26-30 models, 7 post-hoc families), family accounts for roughly a fifth of profile variance (about 17-21%), above permutation chance (p about 0.01-0.02), and same-family models are the nearest profile more often than chance (about 35-46% vs about 14%). A family mean gives no detectable improvement over the image-wide mean for held-out models (squared-error ratio about 1.0-1.2, CIs mostly including 1). A model's DocVQA deviation from its family mean shows at most a weak, statistically uncertain carry-over to InfoVQA (r about 0.1-0.2, bootstrap CI spanning zero). The data cannot establish that individual deviations fail to persist.

findings.title: Binary-codec loss falls with embedding dimension, within and across families
findings.claim: Models with higher embedding dimension lose less under binary quantisation. This accounts for much of what looks like a newer-generation Qwen3 family effect.
findings.evidence: Mean binary loss in points of retention by dimension (image profiles, 66): 128-d 2.34 (42 profiles), 320-d 0.87 (12), 640-d 0.43 (4), 2048-d 0.17 (2), 2560-d 0.66 (2), 4096-d 0.50 (4). Spearman (loss, log dim) -0.65 (DocVQA) and -0.74 (InfoVQA), n=33 each; pooled dataset-demeaned Pearson -0.50, model-level permutation p=0.0012; within family x dataset (demeaned) rho -0.34, p=0.008 (n=60). Within the Qwen3-VL backbone on DocVQA: 2.49 (128-d), 1.75 (320), 0.78 (640), 1.10 (2560), 0.96 (4096). Regression on 33 de-duplicated image models, 66 profiles, cluster bootstrap: Qwen3-generation indicator alone -1.59 points (CI -2.19 to -1.01); with log vectors/page, dimension>128 and float16 added, generation -0.20 (CI -1.12 to +0.65) and dimension>128 -1.36 (CI -2.10 to -0.60); float16 -0.48 (CI -0.98 to -0.02).
findings.method: Group means, Spearman, model-level permutation of dimension, OLS with model-cluster bootstrap CIs.
findings.confounds: Dimension is collinear with generation and float16 (86% of Qwen3-generation models have dimension above 128); only about 8 models exceed 128-d and the effect is flat beyond 640-d (EVIE-4.5B 0.17 points vs EVIE-8B 0.50). Dimension and fraction of 128-d older models are tied to training recipe. Image datasets only; text 48/64-d results are entangled with int4 collapse (F1).
findings.practical_implication: Predict binary viability from dimension: 128-d models cost about 2 to 3 points on binary, 320-d and above about 1 point or less. Dimension is a more useful predictor than family.
findings.question: families

verdict.recomputed:
Recomputed from measured.json (own code; binary row, loss = 100*(1-retention), registry dimension). I get 37 image models x 2 datasets = 74 profiles (the analyst's 66 profiles / 33 models is a de-duplicated subset; I did not rebuild that exact subset).
Group means by dimension (all 74 profiles): 128-d 2.24 (50), 320-d 0.87 (12), 640-d 0.44 (4), 2048-d 0.17 (2), 2560-d 0.67 (2), 4096-d 0.50 (4). The values above 128-d match the claim exactly. The 128-d mean is 2.24 against the claimed 2.34 (42 profiles), a difference in model selection.
Spearman(loss, log dim): DocVQA -0.60 (n=37), InfoVQA -0.73 (n=37), model-mean over both datasets -0.72 (n=37). After dropping the hf/merged duplicate checkpoints, -0.76 (n=32). The claim gave -0.65 and -0.74 at n=33; the sign and size are reproduced. A model-level permutation of dimension gave p<1e-4 (10,000 permutations).
Dimension is a step, not a trend. Among models with dim>128 only (n=12): Spearman -0.24, p=0.45. Mean loss is 0.66 for dim>128 against 2.29 for non-Qwen3 128-d models. Within the Qwen3-generation models alone (n=14), rho -0.50 with permutation p=0.07.
OLS on model-mean loss (n=37; gen3 indicator, dim>128, float16 flag), model bootstrap with 3000 resamples: intercept 2.36; gen3 -0.31 (95% CI -1.05 to +0.45); dim>128 -1.23 (-1.91 to -0.54); float16 -0.32 (-0.78 to +0.14). So the generation coefficient shrinks to roughly zero and dimension keeps its size, as claimed. The float16 CI includes 0 here, whereas the claim's float16 CI (-0.98 to -0.02) only just excluded it.
Leave-one-family-out (nemotron, EVIE, webAI, tomoro, Vultron): the dim>128 coefficient stays between -1.14 and -1.27 and the rho between -0.68 and -0.72. No single family drives it.
Dropping the SauerkrautLM-ColQwen3 pair is the sensitive case. The two 128-d Qwen3 models (Sauerkraut 2b and 4b) are the only thing separating generation from dimension. Without them the coefficients become gen3 -0.77 and dim>128 -0.77. They also average 1.73 against 2.29 for non-Qwen3 128-d models (n=2 against 23), and the two differ a lot from each other (1.22 and 2.23).
Per-profile noise: the binary retention bootstrap CI is on average 3.2 points wide (median 2.9), against effect sizes of 1 to 2 points. This is exploratory and post-hoc; I ran about 15 tests.
verdict.issues:
1. Dimension above 128 is a binary step. Nothing separates 320-d from 4096-d (rho -0.24, p=0.45 within dim>128; means are 0.87, 0.44, 0.17, 0.67 and 0.50 with 2 to 12 profiles each). The wording "falls with dimension" overstates a continuous trend, so "128-d vs larger" is the accurate description.
2. The separation of dimension from generation depends on only 2 models (Sauerkraut Qwen3 at 128-d). That is too thin to say that dimension "accounts for much of" the generation effect. The data are equally consistent with a shared cause, such as a larger backbone hidden size, a newer training recipe, or a projection head trained with a different loss, that raises both dimension and binary robustness. Dimension is not shown to be causal.
3. Only 12 models exceed 128-d, drawn from 6 families (tomoro, Qwen3.5 variants, ColVec, EVIE, nemotron), and several are siblings. The models in the 128-d bin are mostly older ColPali and ColQwen2 checkpoints, so recipe is confounded with dimension.
4. The permutation test shuffles dimension across models and ignores family structure. The within-Qwen3-generation test (n=14) is only borderline, p=0.07.
5. Float16-inference baselines are mixed in (about 40% of the >128-d models). Their effect is small and its sign is not stable, but they are not fully controlled.
6. Image datasets only, DocVQA and InfoVQA at 500 pages each. The query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling, and per-profile noise (about 3 points) is comparable to the effects.
7. Small differences in model selection and deduplication change the 128-d mean (2.24 against 2.34) but not the conclusion. A literal check of the claim's other details (the demeaned pooled Pearson, the within-family rho of -0.34, and the exact Qwen3-VL DocVQA values) was not run.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory and post-hoc, image datasets only: image models with embedding dimension above 128 lose less under sign-bit binary quantisation than 128-d models (about 0.7 against 2.3 points of ndcg@5 retention, a roughly 1.2-point gap with a 95% model-bootstrap CI of about 0.5 to 1.9, across 12 vs 25 models). Within the larger-dimension group there is no detectable trend with dimension (rho -0.24, n=12, p=0.45). The newer-generation Qwen family effect shrinks to indistinguishable from 0 (-0.3, CI -1.05 to +0.45) once a dim>128 indicator is included, but this separation rests on just two 128-d Qwen3 models, and dimension is collinear with generation, backbone size and training recipe, so dimension should not be called the cause. A weak-to-moderate association, not an established mechanism.

findings.title: Model size and float16 inference have no detectable consistent effect on compressibility
findings.claim: Across sibling size pairs and a family-fixed-effects regression, neither parameter count nor float16 inference shifts mean compression loss by more than a fraction of a point; the apparent DocVQA gap between float16 -hf and float32 checkpoints is confounded with preprocessing.
findings.evidence: Large minus small mean loss over shared labels (points): nemotron 4b>8b -0.05, EVIE 4.5B>8B +0.19, Vultron 0.8B>4.5B +0.16, Vultron 4.5B>8B -0.08, Sauerkraut 2b>4b -0.34, tomoro 4b>8b +0.01, nomic 3b>7b -0.26, NeoMME 260M>800M +0.17 (image-only mean -0.03, larger worse in 4/8); binary-only image mean -0.39, larger worse 3/8; mxbai-edge 17m>32m -12.1 (collapse-driven text pair). Vultron DocVQA mean loss 1.03, 1.25, 1.09 (not monotone). Spearman(loss, log size) over 16 image models with known size: +0.17 (DocVQA, p=0.54), -0.68 (InfoVQA, p=0.004), opposite signs. Float16 coefficient in a family fixed-effects regression (68 image profiles, 13 float16 models): +0.03 points (CI -0.29 to +0.45); merge-only +0.10 (-0.20 to +0.49); codec-only -0.07 (-0.35 to +0.26). Paired float32 vs -hf profile RMSD on DocVQA 0.0136, 0.0133, 0.0214 against an identical-weight replicate floor of 0.0044 and 0.0054; on InfoVQA 0.0040, 0.0037, 0.0049 against 0.0025 and 0.0011. The -hf baselines also differ (0.558 vs 0.579; 0.575 vs 0.590).
findings.method: Paired sibling differences with bootstrap over pairs and sign test; Spearman; family-fixed-effects OLS with model-cluster bootstrap; RMSD against replicate floor.
findings.confounds: Absence of evidence with wide intervals. 8 image size pairs; only 3 float32/float16 twin pairs, all colpali, with -hf also changing processor and code path. Size is confounded with dimension, vendor and recipe in sibling pairs. Float16 models are compared to a float16-inference baseline, so float16 error in the vectors is invisible. DocVQA and InfoVQA differ, with the float16 gap only visible on DocVQA.
findings.practical_implication: Do not treat parameter count or float16 inference as a reason to expect better or worse compression; do not transfer a smaller sibling's numbers to a larger one without a check, but expect them within about 0.5 points on merge and codec pipelines.

verdict.recomputed:
Recomputed from measured.json (loss = (1 - ndcg@5 retention) x 100, averaged over shared labels, float32/float16 labels excluded, DocVQA and InfoVQA averaged); registry strings give the float16 flag (13 float16 image models, as stated).

1. Sibling pairs on the 22 labels with no project() stage. Larger minus smaller, in points:
- nemotron -0.06, EVIE +0.20, Vultron 0.8B>4.5B +0.17, Vultron 4.5B>8B -0.11, Sauerkraut -0.31, tomoro +0.15, nomic -0.26, NeoMME +0.17.
- These match the claim except tomoro (+0.15 here, +0.01 claimed).
- Mean over the 8 image pairs is -0.01 (bootstrap over pairs, CI -0.15 to +0.12); larger is worse in 4/8.
- Codec-only labels: mean -0.13 (CI -0.33 to +0.08), 4/8. Merge-only labels: +0.05 (CI -0.08 to +0.21), 4/8.
- Binary-only: mean -0.39, larger worse 3/8, sign-test p 0.73. This matches the claim.
- mxbai 17m>32m on binary alone is -45.6 points and about -11.7 over the 30 shared non-trivial labels, so it is collapse-driven as claimed.

2. The conclusion depends on the label set. Larger is worse when project() labels are included:
- All shared non-trivial labels, including project(16/32/64): image mean +0.65 (CI +0.08 to +1.27), larger worse in 7/8, sign p 0.07.
- Labels excluding project(16/32/64): mean +0.56 (CI -0.01 to +1.23), 6/8.
- Projection-containing labels only: mean +1.04 (CI +0.17 to +2.00), 7/8.
- Per pair on projection labels: Vultron 0.8B>4.5B +3.6, tomoro +1.6, EVIE +1.5, NeoMME +1.4, nomic +0.9, Sauerkraut -1.0, nemotron +0.15. Heterogeneous but mostly positive.
- Vultron 0.8>4.5B is the largest single effect (+2.4 over all shared labels).

3. Spearman(loss, log params). I used my own size table of 23 image models, not the claim's 16, and the no-project label mean.
- DocVQA +0.08 (p 0.71); leave-one-out range -0.01 to +0.20.
- InfoVQA -0.35 (p 0.10); leave-one-out range -0.51 to -0.28.
- The claimed InfoVQA -0.68 (p 0.004) does NOT reproduce. I could not identify the 16-model subset.
- With all 30 common labels: DocVQA +0.37 (p 0.08), InfoVQA +0.03.
- Within-family demeaned: DocVQA +0.05 (p 0.82), InfoVQA -0.30 (p 0.18).
- The sign flips between datasets and label sets, so there is no consistent monotone size trend.

4. Float16 coefficient in a family fixed-effects OLS with model-cluster bootstrap. Profiles are 74 over 37 image models, with a dataset dummy and the Python-registry family. It reproduces:
- 22 no-project labels +0.04 (CI -0.28 to +0.42); merge-only +0.11 (-0.29 to +0.45); codec-only -0.07 (-0.32 to +0.26); 30 labels including project(128) +0.11 (-0.21 to +0.48).
- Six older -merged profiles lack the current label set, so I dropped them.

5. Float32 vs -hf twins (RMSD in retention units).
- 22 no-project labels, InfoVQA: 0.0039 (colpali-v1.2) and 0.0045 (colpali-v1.3). This matches the claimed 0.0040 and 0.0037 approximately.
- All 52 shared labels, DocVQA: 0.0152 (v1.2) and 0.0210 (v1.3). The claimed 0.0136 and 0.0133 are only approximately reproduced.
- Replicate floor, all labels: 0.0062 and 0.0045 (DocVQA), 0.0045 and 0.0025 (InfoVQA).
- Including project labels, InfoVQA twin RMSD is 0.0365 for colpali-v1.2, and individual labels differ by up to 9.4 points, for example merge0.33>project(16)>binary. The -hf profile retains more. For v1.3 the InfoVQA RMSD is 0.0099, with a worst label of 3.6 points.
- DocVQA v1.3 mean retention difference is +0.017 (float32 minus -hf). Baselines are 0.5748 vs 0.5902 (v1.3) and 0.558 vs 0.5789 (v1.2).
- I could not reproduce the third (colqwen2) twin because the -merged profile has a different label set.

Tests and exploration: about 5 label-set variants x 8 pairs, 4 FE regressions, 4 Spearman variants, plus the twin RMSDs. None are preregistered, and none are corrected for multiplicity.
verdict.issues:
1. Label-set dependence, the main problem. The "fraction of a point" result for size holds only on mild pipelines: codec and merge labels, with no dimension projection. Adding project(16/32/64) labels, the most aggressive and highest-loss pipelines, makes the larger sibling lose about 0.6 to 1.0 points more on average, with larger worse in 6 to 7 of 8 pairs. The claim does not say which label set it used (I inferred no-project from the matching per-pair values), and the "no effect" wording overreaches for projection pipelines.
2. The InfoVQA Spearman of -0.68 (p 0.004) is not reproducible. With a 23-model size table I get -0.35 (p 0.10), and the DocVQA value is +0.08 rather than +0.17. The headline "opposite signs" is weaker than stated; it is closer to two null-ish correlations. Size values for several models are approximate and carry high uncertainty (colqwen-omni, colpali, colqwen2 and others).
3. Size and float16 are nearly collinear within pairs. The larger sibling is float16 in 6 of 8 pairs, while the smaller is float32 in 5 of them. Size-pair differences therefore mix size, float16, dimension, vendor and recipe. The null on both factors is mutually consistent, but the design cannot separate them.
4. The twin RMSD agreement depends on excluding projection labels. On InfoVQA with projection included, the float32 vs -hf gap is up to 9 points, far above the replicate floor of 0.0025 to 0.0062. Both the DocVQA gap and the InfoVQA projection gap are plausibly preprocessing or code-path differences (the -hf checkpoints also change processor and code), but this is untested, since no twin varies float16 alone. Hence "confounded with preprocessing" is an unproven attribution. The bounded claim is only that no twin isolates the float16 effect.
5. The float16 coefficient is estimated against float16-inference baselines. Error in float16 vectors is invisible, and 13 float16 models in 5 to 6 families give a wide CI (about +/-0.35). It excludes effects larger than about 0.5 points on average, not zero. Query-bootstrap retention CIs ignore corpus sampling. Retention above 1 is noise. There are only 8 image pairs, and the 3 colpali twins are one family.
6. Minor: the tomoro pair gives +0.15 here, not +0.01. The mxbai text pair shares no dataset with the image pairs.
verdict.corrected_claim: On codec and token-merge pipelines (no dimension projection), parameter count shows no detectable consistent shift in mean compression loss. Over 8 image sibling pairs the larger-minus-smaller mean is -0.01 points (bootstrap CI -0.15 to +0.12; larger worse in 4/8). The float16-inference coefficient in a family fixed-effects regression over 37 image models is about +0.04 points (CI -0.28 to +0.42; merge-only +0.11, codec-only -0.07). Effects larger than roughly 0.5 points are excluded only for these mild pipelines. For dimension-projection pipelines, particularly project(16/32/64), the larger sibling loses more on average (about +1.0 point, CI +0.2 to +2.0, 7/8 pairs; driven by Vultron 0.8B>4.5B +3.6), so the claim does not extend to them. Cross-model Spearman of loss against log size is not stable: DocVQA is about +0.1 and InfoVQA about -0.35 (p about 0.10) in my recomputation, not the reported -0.68 (p 0.004). The float32 vs -hf twin gap on mild pipelines is about 3 to 4 times the replicate floor on DocVQA (RMSD 0.015 to 0.021 vs 0.005 to 0.006), but the three twins cannot separate float16 from the processor and code-path change. This is exploratory, post-hoc, and based on a few correlated sibling pairs.

findings.title: The two colbertv2.0 copies differ in baseline and vector count but share the most similar compression profile of all text pairs
findings.claim: colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 (nDCG@10 0.646, 157 vectors/doc) and lightonai/colbertv2.0 (0.692, 236 vectors/doc) have nearly identical compression profiles, whereas other sibling text pairs differ widely, so text family or lineage is not predictive.
findings.evidence: Profile RMSD 0.0167, rank 1 of 91 text pairs (median pair 0.122, minimum 0.0167); merge-only labels rank 9/91. No pipeline out of 54 shared has non-overlapping retention intervals; mean retention 0.852 vs 0.863; largest pointwise difference 0.060 on hierarchical_merge(0.25) > project(32) > binary. Other sibling text pairs: LFM2 vs LFM2.5 0.135 (rank 49/91), LateOn vs mLateOn 0.151 (rank 55), mxbai-edge 17m vs 32m 0.221 (rank 75); within-lineage vs between text distance 0.117 vs 0.165, permutation p=0.17.
