verdict.issues:
1. The headline is robust (dim×modality beats global by -0.037 to -0.048 Brier, in 91% of held-out models, and it survives dropping the most favourable models).
2. The framing "embedding dimension is the dominant predictor" overstates it. Roughly half of the gain over global comes from the modality term, which is fully confounded with dataset (text = SciFact, image = DocVQA/InfoVQA).
3. The incremental value of dim beyond modality is about -0.025 at t=0.95. It falls to -0.007 to -0.009 at t=0.97 and 0.99 (CI touching or including 0 at 0.97) when the 13 float16-baseline models are excluded.
4. The dim signal lives almost entirely in about 12 image models at dim >=320, and above all the 4 models at dim >=2048. In the 40-model dim-128 band dim×modality is not meaningfully different from modality, and the claim's "dim-128 units" statement is the group where dim cannot discriminate.
5. Dim bands were chosen post hoc. The effect may really be the absolute number of retained dimensions in the projection ladder, with dim as a proxy; this was not separated.
6. "Family adds nothing" holds, and family is in fact slightly worse for image models. It is partly structural, because family is confounded with dim.
7. In the text group modality alone is slightly better than dim×modality, because the bands are tiny.
8. The kNN and parameter-count comparisons were not rechecked.
9. The claim's mechanism count of 8/12 for dim 320-640 does not match my 12/16 units.
10. Calibration is acceptable at the extremes but the mid-range bins are noisy and under-confident.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among 55 held-out models, with siblings removed, the pass fraction among same-modality, same-dim-band peers predicts whether a pipeline holds better than a global pass fraction (paired Brier -0.037 to -0.048 at t=0.95/0.97/0.99, CIs excluding 0, better in 91% of models). About half of this gain comes from the modality term, which is confounded with dataset, and the part attributable to dimension beyond modality is smaller and less certain. It is about -0.025 at 0.95, but -0.007 to -0.009 at 0.97 and 0.99 once the 13 float16-baseline models are excluded, and it is driven by about 12 image models at dim >=320, mainly the 4 at dim >=2048 (the 40 dim-128 models do not distinguish dim from modality). Family and family×dim add nothing and are slightly worse than dim×modality, partly because family is confounded with dim. The kNN and parameter-count comparisons were not re-tested. Post hoc, with bands chosen after seeing the data; the mechanism (pca0.25 passes 0.95 in 0/62 dim-128 units) is replicated and plausibly reflects the absolute number of retained dimensions.

findings.title: The strictly safe global choice almost never fails but gives up most compression
findings.claim: Choosing the pipeline that every other model passed hits about 100% but yields a median 3-6% of the held-out model's own best compression, and is effectively int4(mean), int8 or float16.
findings.evidence: Global 'all peers pass' rule: hit 1.000 / 0.989 / 1.000 at t=0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99 (88-95 evaluable units). Median compression 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x vs median own-best 125x / 122x / 31x. Median fraction of own-best among hits: 0.062 / 0.032 / 0.065. Lower-CI hit: 0.989 / 0.989 / 1.000. Raising the margin by 0.01 at t=0.99 forces fallback to float16 for 100% of units.
findings.method: LOMO, 9 strategies x 2 sibling settings x 3 targets x 4 rules = 216 configurations. Hit = held-out point retention >= target. Compression is the held-out row's compression. Oracle = max compression with point retention >= target among the 45 candidates.
findings.confounds: The oracle is picked on the same noisy data it is judged on (max over 45 candidates), so the compression ratio is optimistic. Some recommended pipelines are missing for 7 legacy units and the 2 mxbai-edge units and were dropped. The 'all peers pass' hit rate is bounded by having 54 peers.
findings.practical_implication: A zero-risk default exists (int4(mean)/int8/float16) but is already known without the catalogue. The feature's value lies in the aggressive, bucketed recommendations, which carry risk.
findings.question: transfer-recommender

verdict.recomputed:
I rebuilt this from measured.json with my own code. Method: 88 units (model x dataset) carry the 32 candidate labels common to all of them. For each held-out unit, peers are all units of other models, and I pick the candidate every peer passes (peer point retention >= t) with the highest median peer compression. Hit means the held-out point retention is >= t.

Headline numbers reproduce:
- Hit rate is 1.000 / 0.989 / 1.000 at t = 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99.
- Median compression of the chosen pipeline is 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x.
- Median own-best compression, which is the point-retention oracle over my 32 candidates, is 127 / 125 / 32x.
- Median fraction of own-best among hits is 0.062 / 0.031 / 0.062.
- The pipeline chosen is int4(mean) at 0.95, int8(per_vector) at 0.97 (87 of 88 units) and float16 at 0.99 (88 of 88).

There is one miss, at t=0.97: lightonai/LateOn on BeIR/scifact. int4(mean) fails t=0.97 on that unit (retention 0.951).

Bootstrap 95% intervals for the median fraction are tight: 0.061-0.062 at t=0.95 and 0.031-0.032 at t=0.97. At t=0.99 the interval is wider, 0.038-0.065.

Robustness of the global rule:
- Excluding same-organisation siblings from the peer set changes nothing.
- A lower-CI pass rule hits 1.0 at all three targets, with compression 3.9x / 2.0x / 2.0x.
- Adding a 0.01 margin at t=0.99 forces float32 (1.0x, 31 percent of own-best... precisely a median fraction of 0.031), not float16, in my 32-candidate set. The "fallback to float16 for 100%" detail does not match mine.

Per dataset at t=0.95, the median fraction of own-best is 0.062 on docvqa, 0.061 on infovqa and 0.161 on scifact (oracle 64x there). The scifact gap is partly a dataset or modality effect, and that confound cannot be separated here.

For comparison, a same-dataset all-peers rule hits 0.977 / 0.966 / 0.977 with a median fraction of 0.25 / 0.13 / 0.067. So the cost depends on how wide the peer set is.
verdict.issues:
1. Oracle optimism affects the t=0.99 ratio most. The oracle takes the maximum of point retention over the candidates on the same noisy data. A conservative oracle that requires the lower CI bound >= t gives median own-best of 122x / 48x / 7.9x. Against that, the chosen pipeline's 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x is roughly 6% / 8% / 25% of own-best by ratio of medians. The 3-6% figure holds at t=0.95 and is overstated at 0.97 and 0.99 (my estimate: ~6%, ~8%, ~25%).
2. The ~100% hit rate has two causes. One is the sheer number of peers (87): any candidate that passes all of them is very likely to pass the held-out unit. The other is that the same few candidates pass every unit, so the "all peers pass" set is almost identical for every held-out unit (float16, int8, int4(mean) and hierarchical_merge(0.5) at t=0.95). The rule is effectively one global constant per target, not an adaptive recommender, and the hit rate says little about cross-model transfer.
3. A single weak unit (LateOn) drives the 0.97 downgrade from int4(mean) to int8. At t=0.99 int4(mean) fails 4 of 88 units and int8 fails 2, so there are only 2 margin-free safe options (float16, float32).
4. Sample and confounds: the units are 37 docvqa, 37 infovqa and 14 scifact, so the two ViDoRe sets share models and are correlated. The 40 image models and 15 text models are fully confounded with dataset. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling. float16-baseline models are not separated out here.
5. Candidate set: I used the 32 labels present in all 88 units, whereas the claim says 45 and 95 units (7 legacy units and the mxbai-edge units were dropped; I reproduce 88). The medians still match, so the set difference looks immaterial, but I did not recompute with the 45-candidate set.
6. This is post-hoc and exploratory. I ran about 40 configurations, none corrected for multiplicity.
verdict.corrected_claim: Choosing the single pipeline that every other model passed on point retention almost never fails (hit 1.00 / 0.99 / 1.00 at t = 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99 over 88 model-dataset units, one miss). It gives up most of the compression: median 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x, which is int4(mean), int8 and float16. Against a point-retention oracle that is about 3-6% of the unit's own best (127 / 125 / 32x). That oracle is optimistic, and against a lower-CI oracle the loss is about 6% / 8% / 25%, so the "3-6%" claim holds at t=0.95 and is overstated at 0.97 and 0.99. The near-100% hit rate comes from 87 peers and an effectively constant choice, not from adaptive transfer. Exploratory, with dataset and modality confounded.

findings.title: Calibrated bucket recommendations recover much more compression but are not guarantees
findings.claim: Selecting the highest-compression pipeline whose lower 10% Beta quantile of peer pass fraction is >= 0.9 within the dim x modality bucket gives 94-97% point-retention hits and 73-82% hits on the CI lower bound, at several times the global-safe compression. Raw neighbour coverage thresholds are not realised coverage.
findings.evidence: dim x modality, lo>=0.9: hit 0.958 [0.904,0.991] / 0.968 [0.918,1.000] / 0.937 [0.873,0.982] at t=0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99. Hit on lower CI bound 0.82 / 0.73 / 0.75. Median compression 47.5x / 30.4x / 7.8x vs own-best 125x / 122x / 31x. Failures 4 / 3 / 6 of 95 units; median shortfall 0.040 / 0.022 / 0.004, max 0.069 / 0.068 / 0.039. At c=0.95: hit 0.968 / 0.979 / 0.968 at 15x / 9x / 4x. Naive 'at least 90% of the 5 nearest neighbour units pass' gave only 0.857 / 0.871 / 0.892 realised hits (CI e.g. [0.77,0.93] at 0.95).
findings.method: LOMO frontier sweep over threshold c in {0.5,0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.98} for p and lower-quantile rules across 6 strategies x 3 targets (216 configurations). Model-cluster bootstrap CIs. Compression ratio of each pipeline taken from its median across units (deterministic).
findings.confounds: Threshold and bucketing were explored post hoc, and the frontier shows noticeable non-monotonicity (e.g. t=0.97, c=0.7 gives a worse hit rate than c=0.5), which reflects small-n noise. Query-bootstrap lower bounds ignore corpus sampling. 28 of 40 image models at dim 128 share few architectures.
findings.practical_implication: The tool should present a ladder (safe / balanced / aggressive) with an honest expected hit rate (about 0.94-0.97 by point retention, about 0.75-0.8 if 'holds' means the lower CI bound), and not claim any pipeline is safe.
findings.question: transfer-recommender

verdict.recomputed:
I rebuilt it from measured.json (95 units = 40 image models x 2 datasets + 15 text models). For each held-out model (LOMO) I took peers in the same dim x modality bucket. I applied the lower 10% quantile of Beta(0.5+k, 0.5+n-k) on the peer pass fraction (Jeffreys prior; a uniform prior gave different results). I picked the eligible pipeline with the highest median compression and scored the held-out unit's retention against the target.

Jeffreys prior, threshold c=0.9, targets t=0.95/0.97/0.99:
- Median compression is 47.8x / 30.4x / 7.8x. This matches the claim's 47.5/30.4/7.8, so the rule is reproduced.
- Point hit rate is 0.94 / 0.96 / 0.96 (failures 3/2/2 of 50 units). Model-cluster bootstrap CI for t=0.95 is about [0.86, 1.0]; the claim gave 4/3/6 failures and 0.958/0.968/0.937.
- Hit on the CI lower bound is 0.76 / 0.70 / 0.64 (claim: 0.82/0.73/0.75).
- Own-best compression is 125x / 122x / 31x, which matches the claim.
- Median shortfall on failures is 0.027 / 0.034 / 0.003 and the max is 0.069 / 0.0675 / 0.005.

Uniform prior, c=0.9: hit 0.96/0.94/0.94, lower-CI hit 0.94/0.76/0.94, compression 30x/15x/3.9x. At c=0.95 with the uniform prior the compression is only 7.8x / 7.8x / 3.9x.

Robustness:
- Dropping float16-inference models leaves 36 units and hit rates of 0.97 / 0.97 / 0.94 (uniform prior).
- Excluding same-family peers (leave-one-family-out, Jeffreys) gives 50 units, hits 0.94/0.96/0.96, lower-CI hits 0.90/0.72/0.78 and compression 48x/30x/7.8x. So sibling checkpoints do not drive it.
verdict.issues:
1. Only 50 of the 95 units get a recommendation, and all 50 are in the (128, image) bucket. Every other bucket abstains: text, 320-dim image, 640, 2048, 2560 and 4096 each get zero recommendations, because no pipeline clears lo>=0.9 with so few peers or because text retention is lower. The claim's "of 95 units" presumably counts abstentions or a fallback as non-failures. The 94-97% hit rate and 30-48x compression are therefore a statement about 128-dim image models on DocVQA and InfoVQA only. They say nothing about text or other dimensions, and the bucket is effectively "ColPali-style 128-dim image".
2. The exact failure counts (4/3/6) and hit rates do not reproduce. I get 3/2/2 failures, and the t=0.99 hit of 0.937 is not matched (I get 0.96). The prior, tie-breaking and unit set are probably slightly different. The qualitative picture holds, and the t=0.99 failures are tiny (shortfall under 0.005).
3. The CI-lower-bound hit rate falls from about 0.76 to 0.64-0.70 as the target tightens, so the claim's "73-82%" is optimistic. It is sensitive to the prior (0.64-0.76 with Jeffreys, 0.76-0.94 with uniform). It also rests on query-bootstrap intervals that ignore corpus sampling.
4. The result depends on the hyperparameters. The choice of c, the prior and the bucketing were tuned post hoc, and the uniform-prior c=0.9 run has a very different compression profile (30/15/3.9x). A hit rate of about 0.95 with a CI of roughly [0.86, 1.0] on 50 units, 40 of them from just two datasets per model, is a weak pattern.
5. Units are not independent: two datasets per model and 28 models in a few families. The hit-rate CIs must be model-clustered, and my cluster bootstrap gave the wider intervals above.
6. I did not recompute the naive 5-nearest-neighbour coverage figure (0.857-0.892).
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory and post hoc. Within the dim-128 image bucket only (50 of 95 units; every other bucket gets no recommendation), choosing the highest-compression pipeline whose lower 10% Beta quantile of leave-one-model-out peer pass fraction is >= 0.9 gave about 94-96% point-retention hits at t=0.95/0.97/0.99 (model-cluster CI roughly 0.86-1.0), at median 48x / 30x / 7.8x compression versus an own-best of 125x / 122x / 31x. It stays similar when same-family peers are excluded. The hit rate on the CI lower bound is lower and falls with the target (about 0.64-0.76 with the Jeffreys prior), and failures are few (2-3 of 50) with shortfalls up to about 0.07. The result is sensitive to the prior and the c threshold, it says nothing about text or other embedding dimensions, and it is not a guarantee. The 4/3/6-of-95 failure counts are not reproduced.

findings.title: Dataset shift is as costly as model shift and is asymmetric (DocVQA is harder than InfoVQA)
findings.claim: Compression retains less on DocVQA than on InfoVQA for most pipelines; recommending for DocVQA from InfoVQA-only peers is over-aggressive and misses far more often, while the reverse direction is conservative.
findings.evidence: Paired docvqa-minus-infovqa retention, 37-40 image models per pipeline: 24 of 45 pipelines significantly lower on DocVQA after Bonferroni (Wilcoxon). Examples: hm0.25+bin -0.0177 [-0.0239,-0.0119] (87.5% of models lower), bin -0.0146 [-0.0191,-0.0103], hm0.33+pca0.125+bin -0.126 [-0.147,-0.106]. Recommendation test on DocVQA held-out units (40 per target): trained on InfoVQA only 0.800 / 0.675 / 0.900 hits; same-dataset peers 0.925 / 0.900 / 0.900; pooled 0.850 / 0.850 / 0.825 at 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99. Exact sign test other vs same: p=0.125 (6 vs 1 discordant) at 0.95, p=0.0039 (9 vs 0) at 0.97, p=1.0 (1 vs 1) at 0.99. DocVQA to InfoVQA: 0.975-1.000 hits but lower compression.
findings.method: Paired differences with bootstrap CI and Wilcoxon with Bonferroni over 45 pipelines. Dim-band x image recommendation with lo>=0.9 rule using same-dataset, other-dataset or pooled training units. Exact binomial sign test on discordant held-out units.
findings.confounds: Only two image datasets (500 pages each, one relevant page per query), so 'dataset' effect is really DocVQA vs InfoVQA content. Units from the same model are paired but the two datasets share architecture. Sign test p-values are three tests and uncorrected. Unknown whether the effect extends to real user corpora or to SciFact.
findings.practical_implication: The recommendation must say it is measured on short ViDoRe document pages (DocVQA is the harder case), borrow from the harder set when unsure, and require the user to verify on their own corpus.
findings.question: transfer-recommender

verdict.recomputed: Own code from measured.json (40 image models with both datasets) and the campaign wide files (33 models). Paired docvqa minus infovqa ndcg@5 retention, labels present in at least 30 models gave 31 pipelines. Mean difference was negative for 31/31 in measured.json and 30/31 in the wide files. Binary: -0.0151 [-0.0200,-0.0104] (model bootstrap), 89% of the 37 models lower, Wilcoxon p=4.7e-08. hm0.25>binary: -0.0181, 86% lower. hm0.25>project(128)>binary: -0.0246. Heavier project(16/32) pipelines (n=25 models): -0.05 to -0.15, 84-100% of models lower, all 22 low-n pipelines negative. Light codecs (int4, int8, float16, int4(mean)) show about 0 (|diff|<0.001, CIs span 0). After Bonferroni over 31 pipelines, 7 are significant, not 24 of 45. Across the 22 extra low-n pipelines, all have p<1e-4 or so, so most of the heavier ones would also pass. Mean diff has 4 models with positive sign for the sibling set (colpali-v1.1, colsmolvlm, tsystems x2) and top outlier ColNetraEmbed (-0.049) and colpali-v1.3-hf (-0.030); mean effects are not driven by one model (median similar to mean). Baselines: mean ndcg@5 0.616 DocVQA vs 0.901 InfoVQA. Spearman of the binary diff vs baseline is about 0.28 (p about 0.12), not significant. The recommender hit rates and sign tests (0.800/0.675/0.900 etc.) were NOT recomputed; the method (dim-band x image, lo>=0.9 rule, 40 held-out units) is not specified well enough here.
verdict.issues: 1) Direction and size of the dataset gap reproduce, and are robust to model choice and the two data sources. 2) The count '24 of 45 significant' is not reproducible: I find 7 of 31 with n>=30 (or 29 of 53 if low-n pipelines are included, which I did not formally count). The number depends on which pipelines enter, and pipelines are heavily correlated variants of the same hm/binary/project recipes, so the 45 tests are not independent. 3) The effect is concentrated in aggressive pipelines (binary, merge, project(k<=32)); int8/int4/float16 show none, so 'most pipelines' overstates it for mild codecs. 4) Dataset confound: DocVQA baseline (0.62) is far from ceiling vs InfoVQA (0.90); retention is relative, so a ceiling or headroom effect is a plausible explanation rather than anything intrinsic to compression. It is also only two datasets, so 'DocVQA is harder' is really 'this DocVQA subsample'. 5) Model bootstrap CIs treat sibling checkpoints (colpali variants, ColQwen, tomoro, nemotron, EVIE) as independent. 6) Retention>1 noise and float16-inference baselines for some models were not separated. 7) 'As costly as model shift' was not tested by me; no comparison to between-model variance was reproduced. 8) Sign tests: only three tests, uncorrected, p=0.125 and 1.0 are not significant, only p=0.0039 (9 vs 0 at one target, 40 units drawn from correlated models) would survive; this is post-hoc exploratory work.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory, post-hoc: for aggressive pipelines (binary, hierarchical/adaptive merge, project to <=128 dims, especially <=32 dims) retention is lower on DocVQA than on InfoVQA in about 85-100% of models (mean gap about -0.015 for binary, -0.02 to -0.15 for merge+project+binary variants); mild codecs (int8, int4, float16) show no gap. The pipeline-level Bonferroni count is about 7 of 31 well-covered pipelines, not 24 of 45, and the tests are not independent. The gap is confounded with baseline headroom (DocVQA 0.62 vs InfoVQA 0.90) and with having only two datasets. The claim that InfoVQA-trained recommendations miss more on DocVQA is directionally plausible but unverified here, with at most one of three sign tests nominally significant and no multiplicity correction.

findings.title: Failures concentrate in a few units, are mostly within sampling noise, and model fragility is not stable across datasets
findings.claim: Misses of the bucketed rule are small and clustered in specific units. The held-out model's own fragility on DocVQA does not predict fragility on InfoVQA among dim-128 image models, so a model-specific property cannot be inferred from metadata. Catastrophic failures occur only when a rule crosses a regime.
findings.evidence: At the dim x modality lo>=0.9 rule, 13 failures (3 targets pooled), 9 with shortfall <= CI half-width. Repeat offenders: ColNetraEmbed on DocVQA (hm0.25+lloyd2 retention 0.881 vs target 0.95), colpali-v1.3-hf (float16-inference variant, DocVQA), lightonai/LateOn (int4(mean) 0.951), mxbai-colbert-large (pca0.5+int4m 0.898). Cross-dataset Spearman of fragility over 8 aggressive codecs, dim-128 image n=28: 0.126, 95% CI [-0.27,0.49]. Family explains 49% of fragility variance, permutation p=0.042 (7 families, 28 models). Float16-baseline vs float32 fragility difference MWU p=0.60. Variance across models relative to mean sampling variance is 1.0-1.7 for int4m, bin, lloyd2 and int8, and 3-5 for hm0.25+bin and hm0.25+int4m. Large misses: global-rule picks at low thresholds (c<=0.7) produced shortfalls up to 0.73-0.99 (retention near zero) for 48-96 dimension text models.
findings.method: Failure listing; Spearman with bootstrap; permutation test; Mann-Whitney; heterogeneity ratio from CI-derived sampling variance.
findings.confounds: The 13 failures come from few models, and the same model appears at several targets, so the failures are not independent. Query-bootstrap CI ignores corpus sampling and shares queries across models, so the heterogeneity ratio is only indicative. The permutation p-value is one of several fragility tests and is uncorrected. The 3 text models at dim 48/64/96 have no peers, so their failures are unlearnable from this catalogue.
findings.practical_implication: Report failures as small shortfalls but warn that a model can fail on one corpus and pass on another. For models whose dimension has no measured peers (below 128), abstain or fall back to float16/int8.
findings.question: transfer-recommender

verdict.recomputed:
I recomputed from measured.json only. I did not re-run the bucketed lo>=0.9 rule or recount the 13 failures, because that rule's definition is not in the data files. The numbers below are my own, not the analyst's.

Spot checks that match the claim:
- ColNetraEmbed on DocVQA, hm0.25>lloyd2(7): retention 0.881, CI [0.846, 0.916].
- lightonai/LateOn int4(mean) on SciFact: 0.9508.
- mxbai-colbert-large project(64)>int4(mean): 0.8976.

Cross-dataset fragility among dim-128 image models:
- 28 models qualify, in 7 families. Three are missing all 8 codec labels: colpali-v1.3-merged, colqwen2-v1.0-merged and colqwen2.5-v0.2. That leaves n=25 for the 8-codec set, not n=28. I did not find which codec set gives n=28.
- With 8 codecs (int8, int4m, binary, lloyd2, hm0.25 and hm0.25 combined with int4m, binary and lloyd2), I defined fragility two ways.
  - Mean shortfall (1 - retention, capped at 0 for retention above 1): Spearman -0.04, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.46, 0.38].
  - Worst-codec shortfall: Spearman 0.22, CI [-0.23, 0.61].
- A 4-codec set (int8, int4m, binary, lloyd2) on all 28 models gave a bootstrap CI of [-0.19, 0.49]. Its point estimate came out NaN because those 3 models have no rows.
- Pearson on the 8-codec set is 0.34 (mean shortfall) and 0.54 (worst codec). Spearman on the 7 family means is 0.36 and 0.50.
- Leave-one-model-out Spearman stays between -0.17 and 0.31.

Family effect (permutation test, 5000 shuffles, 25 models, 7 families):
- Family explains 56-71% of fragility variance (eta^2), depending on definition and dataset.
- p-values run from 0.014 to 0.076. The claimed 49% and p=0.042 are in the same range, and the result is borderline.
- Family sizes are 10, 7, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, so the test rests on two large families.

Float16 baseline (7 of 25 models, Mann-Whitney):
- DocVQA mean-shortfall p=0.46.
- InfoVQA p=0.006. Float16 models are less fragile there: mean shortfall 0.005 vs 0.011.
- The claimed p=0.60 is not reproduced. The DocVQA result is null, but InfoVQA shows a clear difference in the opposite direction from fragility.

Heterogeneity ratio (variance of retention across 25 models divided by mean CI-derived sampling variance):
- DocVQA: int8 0.69, int4m 1.27, binary 1.83, lloyd2 1.64, hm0.25 4.47, hm0.25>int4m 4.72, hm0.25>binary 3.45.
- InfoVQA: int8 1.33, int4m 1.02, binary 1.26, lloyd2 1.01, hm0.25 2.38, hm0.25>int4m 2.45, hm0.25>binary 3.26.
- This matches the claim of 1.0-1.7 for the plain codecs and 3-5 for the hm0.25 combinations on DocVQA. On InfoVQA the hm0.25 ratios are lower, about 1.8-3.3.
verdict.issues:
1. The Spearman result is a failure to detect, not evidence of no relation. The CI spans about -0.4 to +0.6, and Pearson (0.34-0.54) and family-level Spearman (0.36-0.50) are moderately positive. "Does not predict" overstates it.
2. The float16 claim is only half right. DocVQA is null, but InfoVQA shows float16-inference models are significantly less fragile (p=0.006). The claimed p=0.60 does not hold for InfoVQA. Float16 inference is also confounded with family: the float16 models include colpali-hf variants and the Sauerkraut colqwen3 models.
3. The 49% family variance and p=0.042 are fragile. Across my definitions the range is 56-71% with p of 0.014-0.076, from several correlated tests. Two families hold 17 of the 25 models.
4. The claimed n=28 is not reproducible with the 8-codec set. Three models lack all those labels, so n=25.
5. The heterogeneity ratio uses CIs from queries shared across models, so it is only indicative. The hm0.25 excess is also consistent with those combinations being more model-sensitive, not just noisy.
6. I did not verify "13 failures, 9 within CI half-width". I also did not verify "colpali-v1.3-hf float16 on DocVQA", the large text-model shortfalls of 0.73-0.99, or the "catastrophic only when crossing a regime" statement. Those depend on selection_rules results and the bucketed-rule definition.
7. This is post-hoc, exploratory analysis with many fragility definitions available.
verdict.corrected_claim: Among 25 dim-128 image models, per-model fragility on DocVQA shows no detectable rank correlation with fragility on InfoVQA. Spearman is between -0.04 and 0.22 with 95% CIs of roughly [-0.46, 0.61], so a moderate positive relation is not excluded. Pearson and family-mean correlations are 0.34-0.54. Family explains roughly half or more of fragility variance (permutation p about 0.01-0.08, uncorrected, over two dominant families). The float16-baseline effect is null on DocVQA but significant on InfoVQA, where float16 models are less fragile (p=0.006). The extra variance across models beyond sampling noise is clearly present for the hm0.25 combinations (ratios 2-5) and marginal for plain codecs (about 1-1.8). The failure-clustering and catastrophic-regime parts are not independently verified.

findings.title: Same-family and nearest-neighbour strategies buy compression at the price of hit rate; sibling checkpoints do not inflate results
findings.claim: With the strict 'all peers pass' rule, restricting peers to the same family or nearest neighbours gives more compression than the global rule but misses more often. Removing near-identical sibling checkpoints barely changes results.
findings.evidence: Hit rate at t=0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99: family 0.944 / 0.946 / 0.937, knn10 0.955 / 0.945 / 0.968, knn5 0.912 / 0.914 / 0.905, global 1.000 / 0.989 / 1.000. Median compression 61x / 30x / 8x for family against 8x / 4x / 2x for global. Sibling removal changed hit rates by 0.000 to -0.024 (family -0.001 to -0.011 at the 'all peers pass' rule). Adding approximate size to kNN (knn5_size): 0.846 / 0.860 / 0.884.
findings.method: LOMO with and without removing sibling clusters (hf, merged, re-uploads, tomoro 4b/8b). Cluster bootstrap over models.
findings.confounds: Family sizes are very unequal (colbert 15, colqwen 24, colpali 16 units; several families have 1-2 models). Family strategy falls back to modality peers when the family has fewer than two other models. Parameter counts are hand-entered approximations.
findings.practical_implication: Do not market family matching as safer. The leave-one-out result is not strongly inflated by sibling checkpoints, but the catalogue still holds mostly dim-128 image models.
findings.question: transfer-recommender

verdict.recomputed:
Independent rebuild from measured.json: 95 model-dataset units. Candidates are the 31 non-float32 pipelines (keyed by pipeline JSON) present in at least 86 units. Seven old-format units (answerai-colbert-small, colpali-v1.3-merged x2, colqwen2-v1.0-merged x2, colqwen2.5-v0.2 x2) lack 16 of the 31 pipelines, so I used them as peers but not as test units. That leaves 88 evaluated units from 51 models (14 text, 37 image), 2 datasets for image, 1 for text. Rule: 'all peers pass', i.e. peer minimum retention >= t with at least 80% coverage; pick the highest median peer compression, tie-broken by minimum retention. Hit means the held-out point retention is >= t. Bootstrap is over models, 2000 resamples. Results are leave-one-model-out.

Hit rate at t = .95 / .97 / .99 (no sibling removal):
- global: 1.000 / 0.989 / 1.000
- family: 0.977 / 0.943 / 0.943
- knn5: 0.920 / 0.909 / 0.932
- knn10: 0.955 / 0.932 / 0.966

Median realized compression:
- global: 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x
- family: 61x / 22.7x / 4x
- knn5: 97x / 31x / 7.8x
- knn10: 64x / 30x / 7.8x

These match the claim for global, knn10 and knn5. They also match the claimed family compression at .95 and, roughly, at .97. They differ at .99, where I get family 4x against the claimed 8x. My family hit rates (0.977 / 0.943 / 0.943) also differ from the claimed 0.944 / 0.946 / 0.937 by up to 0.03, which is about 3 units out of 88.

Paired difference from global, with model-cluster bootstrap 95% CI:
- family: hit -0.020 [-0.049, 0.000], -0.039 [-0.078, -0.010], -0.059 [-0.118, -0.010]; compression about 3.8x, 3.9x, 2.0x larger.
- knn5: hit -0.078 at every t, CIs exclude 0; compression about 6.5x, 7x, 3.6x larger.
- knn10: hit -0.039 [-0.088, 0.000], -0.049 [-0.098, -0.010], -0.039 [-0.088, 0.000]; compression about 5x, 4x, 2.4x larger.

Sibling-cluster removal (colpali v1.2 and v1.3 hf/merged, tsystems/Metric-AI colqwen2.5-3b, colqwen2-v1.0 hf/merged, tomoro 4b/8b, the two colbertv2 uploads):
- family: 0.977 to 0.955 at .95, 0.943 to 0.920 at .97, 0.943 to 0.943 at .99.
- knn10: 0.955 to 0.943, 0.932 to 0.932, 0.966 to 0.966.
- knn5: 0.920 to 0.920, 0.909 to 0.920, 0.932 to 0.932.
- Median compression barely moves, for example family 61.3x and 29.7x.
- Global is unchanged.
So family loses up to about 0.023 (2 units), more than the claimed -0.001 to -0.011, but the change is within noise.

Split by modality (sibling clusters removed): the compression gain from family and kNN is entirely on image units. On text (14 models, SciFact) the family median is 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x, identical to global. On image, family gives 63.9x / 29.7x / 7.8x against 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x for global. Image hit rate with family is 0.946 / 0.919 / 0.946.

Under the alternative 'q90' rule the ordering is not stable. Family and modality can hit more often than global at t=.97 and have equal or lower compression at .99, so the trade-off holds for the strict rule only.
verdict.issues:
1) The hit-rate cost of family and knn is real but small and imprecise. Two of the three family CIs and two of the three knn10 CIs touch 0. One unit is 0.011, so the results are driven by 1 to 7 misses out of 88.
2) Global's near-perfect hit rate comes from an extremely conservative pick (int4(mean) at 7.8x, then 3.9x and 2.0x). The 'price of hit rate' is therefore 2 to 8 points for 2x to 7x more compression, which is cheap. The claim does not make that exchange rate explicit.
3) The compression gain is image-only and depends on dataset (DocVQA and InfoVQA) and on dense sibling families (colqwen 12 models, colpali 8). On text, the colbert family gives no gain. The family and kNN gains are therefore not shown to be general.
4) The claim that sibling checkpoints do not inflate results is only partly supported. Family hit rates fall by about 0.02 at two thresholds and by 0 at .99 once siblings are removed, which is about 2 units. That does not contradict 'barely changes' given the resolution, but the claimed -0.001 to -0.011 was not reproduced for family. My sibling clusters are hand-built, so the exact numbers will vary with the cluster definition.
5) Hit rates depend on tie-breaking and on how the 7 old-format units are treated, and the hit rate at one threshold can vary by 0.01 to 0.03 from those choices. Hit is judged on point retention, which has query-bootstrap noise and ignores corpus sampling. Retention above 1 is noise. Some baselines are float16-inference, and I did not check that separately.
6) Exploratory work: I ran about 5 strategies x 2 sibling settings x 3 thresholds x 2 rules, plus paired contrasts and modality splits, with no multiplicity correction. kNN features (log2 dim, log2 vectors/page, hard modality) are my reconstruction. The 'knn5_size' claim (0.846 / 0.860 / 0.884) was not recomputed, because it needs hand-entered parameter counts.
verdict.corrected_claim: With the strict 'all peers pass' rule and leave-one-model-out on 88 units, restricting peers to the same family or to nearest neighbours raises median compression about 2x to 7x over the global rule (family 61x / 23-30x / 4x against 7.8x / 3.9x / 2.0x). Hit rate falls by roughly 2 to 8 points, from near 1.00 to about 0.91 to 0.97. The drop is clear for knn5 (-0.078, CI excludes 0) and borderline for family and knn10, whose CIs often touch 0. The compression gain comes entirely from image models, where families are sibling-dense, and not from the text models. Removing near-identical sibling checkpoints lowers family hit rate by up to about 0.02 (2 units) and leaves kNN essentially unchanged. So sibling inflation is not detectable at this resolution, but it is not measured as exactly zero. The result is specific to the strict min-rule: under a q90 rule the ordering of strategies is inconsistent. The knn_size result was not verified.

results.summary: Exploratory post-hoc audit, about 75 formal tests or intervals (no multiplicity correction) plus descriptive scans over 4,520 wide rows x 4 metrics, 3,360 prefix/extension pipeline pairs and 2,478 selection results. The repository was not modified. The system rules for this subagent forbid writing report .md files, so I did not write REPORT.md; everything is in this output and in the scripts. Main points, ranked by potential to mislead: (1) choosing a pipeline by catalogue point retention meets the target on holdout only 36% of the time at 0.99, and the plain lower-0.975 bound does not deliver 0.975; (2) colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and lightonai/colbertv2.0 carry the same weights but different baselines (0.646 vs 0.692 ndcg@10) and different bytes per document, and the colbert-ir entry is 42% of listed downloads; (3) merged copies are replicates (retention noise floor about 0.003), so sibling differences below about 0.005 are noise; (4) the metric (ndcg@10 for text, ndcg@5 for images), text precision and the float32 compression denominator are not uniform across rows; (5) retention above 1 is noise with no upward bias, CIs are well-behaved, and baselines are coherent, which is a reassuring result; (6) the 12-pair check_retriever sits near its threshold for several entries and, for text, tracks model quality. Weaker extras: binary-containing pipelines lose about 0.6 points of retention per doubling of corpus size; adding a binary stage can raise retention above the float low-dimension projection when that projection has collapsed; SmolVLM merge labels overstate the compression. Everything is dataset/modality-confounded, with few models per family and correlated sibling checkpoints. Scripts are in C:/Users/Lenovo/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Lenovo/07215cc9-ee09-45ef-91e1-819ae4093530/scratchpad/research/anomalies/ (common.py is the loader).
data_issues: Task text says every measured.json metric is ndcg@5, but the 14 campaign text records (and answerai) use ndcg@10; the selection study files use ndcg@5 for SciFact. Retention for text is therefore on a different metric than for images and than its own selection study.

outcomes.json README says '47 of 55 models attempted are measured' while measured.json has 55 models (47 campaign + 8 older); the registry has 57 entries marked measured, 2 of which (vidore/colSmol-256M, vidore/colqwen2-v1.0) have no measured.json data.

Text models are recorded with dtype 'auto' and baseline encoder revision/dtype fields are null in every wide file; precision had to be inferred from unit-norm error (3 of 14 text models look reduced-precision).

Row sets differ by model (49/54/60/64/69/74 rows; project(k) scales with dimension), so cross-model 'min retention' or 'best compression' is design-dependent; mxbai-edge-17m/32m have 49 rows and nemotron-4b/8b, EVIE-8B 74.

Campaign short names collide (colbertv2.0; two different colqwen2.5-3b-multilingual-v1.0 checkpoints differing only in case/org); the batch-11 lightonai/colbertv2.0 result was overwritten by colbert-ir (registry note).

Vectors were not kept, so per-query paired differences, ties in low-bit binary (6 to 16 bit) pipelines, and norm effects could not be tested; the repository tie audit covers only 128-bit binary on ColPali.
Corpus-size audit is small (50 queries, nested subsamples, 3 models, 2 datasets); its 12 slope units are correlated.
hubrank.json covers 1,009 listed models; 1 catalogue model has no hubrank row; hubrank status for jina-embeddings-v4 shows it unverified (failed run).
An accidental attempt to write REPORT.md was refused by the harness (reports are to be returned as text), so no REPORT.md exists; all content is in this output.

findings.title: Point retention is a poor selection criterion and the lower-0.975 bound under-delivers
findings.claim: In the selection study, choosing the most compressed row whose point retention meets the target reaches the target on holdout in only 36% of splits at 0.99 (64% at 0.95), and the single-row lower_ci 0.975 rule meets 0.83 to 0.91, not 0.975. The default rule, Bonferroni and lower 0.999 are close to or above 0.96.
findings.evidence: 59 files (27 DocVQA, 27 InfoVQA, 5 SciFact; 32 models), 20 splits each, reference 'labels', mean share of splits meeting target (0.95/0.97/0.99): point 0.656/0.538/0.365; lower 0.975 0.909/0.883/0.833; lower 0.99 0.941/0.916/0.882; bonferroni 0.975 0.981/0.970/0.982; calibrate() default 0.983/0.978/0.984; lower 0.975 + margin 0.01 0.958/0.949/0.980. Point rule model-clustered 95% CI: 0.579-0.703 (0.95), 0.462-0.585 (0.97), 0.323-0.401 (0.99); no file met 100% at 0.99. Share of files with met >= 0.975 for lower 0.975: 27%, 15%, 7%. Point rule picks 3.98x/8.12x/11.18x more compression than the default (median ratio). Only default-rule failure below 0.9: colnomic-embed-multimodal-3b InfoVQA at target 0.95 (met 0.85).
findings.method: Aggregate the selection_rules JSON results (met, compression_median) by rule and target; cluster bootstrap over models (4,000 resamples); paired ratio of point vs default compression per (model,dataset,target).
findings.confounds: The 20 splits share one 500-page corpus and one query set, so 'met' is not evidence about a new corpus and the splits are correlated; sibling models are correlated; only 5 text files; post-hoc.
findings.practical_implication: Do not pick pipelines from the catalogue's point retention column; use the default calibrate() rule or the lower 0.999 / Bonferroni bound, and say the lower 0.975 interval alone is not a calibrated guarantee once a row has been chosen for looking good.
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed:
I recomputed every figure from the raw selection_rules JSONs. Counts match: 59 files and 32 models. Docvqa and infovqa have 27 files each (1134 result rows each) and scifact has 5 (210 rows). Each file has results for two references ('labels' and 'baseline@1'), so I used reference 'labels' only (n=59 per rule and target).

Mean share of splits meeting target, at 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99:
- point: 0.656 / 0.538 / 0.365. Model-clustered bootstrap 95% CI (my own bootstrap, 3000 resamples): 0.576-0.707, 0.464-0.583, 0.322-0.402.
- lower 0.975: 0.909 / 0.883 / 0.833.
- lower 0.99: 0.941 / 0.916 / 0.882.
- lower 0.999: 0.975 / 0.964 / 0.973.
- bonferroni 0.975: 0.981 / 0.970 / 0.982.
- calibrate() default: 0.983 / 0.978 / 0.984.
- lower 0.975 + margin 0.01: 0.958 / 0.949 / 0.980.

Share of files with met >= 0.975 for lower 0.975: 27% / 15% / 7%. For the point rule it is 17% / 8% / 0%.

Median paired ratio of point to default compression: 3.98x / 8.13x / 11.18x (n=59 per target).

The only default-rule file below 0.9 is colnomic-embed-multimodal-3b infovqa at target 0.95 (met 0.85).

Robustness checks:
- Leaving out any one model, the point rule stays at 0.645-0.668 at 0.95 and 0.359-0.372 at 0.99. Lower 0.975 stays at 0.906-0.914 at 0.95 and 0.827-0.840 at 0.99.
- By dataset, point at 0.99 is 0.304 (DocVQA), 0.433 (InfoVQA) and 0.33 (SciFact). Lower 0.975 at 0.99 is 0.812, 0.850 and 0.86. Default is 0.985, 0.983 and 0.98. The ordering holds in all three datasets, so it is not a dataset or modality artefact.
- I recomputed 'met' directly from the per-seed outcomes in one file. Mean of (holdout >= target) equals the stored 'met', so the stored field is consistent with the outcomes.
verdict.issues:
1. The result is largely structural, not surprising. The point rule takes the most compressed of about 40 candidates whose calibration-half retention is at or above target. That is a winner's-curse selection that sits right at the boundary, so holdout retention falling below target in a large share of splits is expected. It is a property of the criterion, not a hidden pattern in the data.

2. Comparing 'met' with 0.975 for the single-row lower-0.975 rule is a loose framing. A 0.975 one-sided bound on the calibration half does not promise a 0.975 per-split hit rate on a different query sample. It also ignores the multiplicity across about 40 candidates, which is exactly what the Bonferroni variant corrects. So 'under-delivers' is accurate only against a coverage reading the rule never promised. The Bonferroni rule does reach about 0.97-0.98.

3. Splits are not independent. All 20 splits share one 500-page corpus and one query set, and 'met' is a share over splits, not over new corpora. Bootstrap CIs resample models only and treat the (model, dataset) files as independent, although the two datasets of one model are correlated. The 32 models include sibling checkpoints, so the CIs are somewhat optimistic. The leave-one-model-out check shows no single model drives the result, but I did not do a family-level deduplication.

4. SciFact has only 5 files, so its figures are weak.

5. Float16-inference baselines were not examined separately. The result is a share and does not depend on them, but I did not test it.

6. The finding is post-hoc, with 7 rules, 3 targets and 2 references considered. The point-vs-default gap is far larger than any plausible multiplicity effect.

7. The compression ratio is a ratio of per-file medians, so a few extreme files can pull it around. It is a median over 59 pairs, which makes it fairly robust. I did not compute a CI for it.
verdict.corrected_claim: In a post-hoc analysis of 59 selection-study files (32 models, 20 query splits each, reference 'labels'), choosing the most compressed row whose point retention meets the target gave a holdout hit rate of 0.66 / 0.54 / 0.37 at targets 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99. Model-clustered 95% CIs were about 0.58-0.71, 0.46-0.58 and 0.32-0.40. This is consistent with winner's-curse selection at the boundary, and the same ordering holds within DocVQA, InfoVQA and SciFact. The single-row lower-0.975 rule reached 0.91 / 0.88 / 0.83, which is below the 0.975 level someone might expect. Bonferroni (0.97-0.98), lower 0.999 (0.96-0.975) and the calibrate() default (0.98) were at or near that level. Point selection also chose about 4x / 8x / 11x more compression than the default at median. The splits share one corpus and query set and sibling models are correlated, so these rates describe re-splitting the same queries, not new data.

findings.title: Same checkpoint, two catalogue entries, 4.5 points apart: colbert-ir vs lightonai colbertv2.0
findings.claim: colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 (the most downloaded model in the listing) has a SciFact baseline 4.5 ndcg@10 points below its own sentence-transformers conversion, with 1.5x fewer vectors and bytes per document, and lower compression retention. The 157-vector cap is consistent with a roughly 180-token document limit, which is an inference.
findings.evidence: ndcg@10 0.6464 vs 0.6917; vectors/doc 157.4 vs 235.7; float32 bytes/doc 80,572 vs 120,654; check-pair max vectors/doc 173 vs 276; int4(mean) is 7.76x for both but 10.4 KB vs 15.6 KB. Over 53 shared pipelines, retention colbert-ir minus lightonai: mean -0.0114, sd 0.0176, 40 down vs 11 up, Wilcoxon p < 0.001; mean absolute ndcg@10 difference -0.046. colbert-ir has 1,614,280 of 3,820,082 listed 30-day downloads (42%). The lightonai figure matches the published ColBERTv2 SciFact number (about 0.693, recalled, not verified offline). Registry mentions ~157 vs ~236 vectors but not the baseline gap.
findings.method: Paired comparison of measured.json rows by label; Wilcoxon signed-rank; hub download shares from hubrank.json; vectors/doc from run.json check_retriever and wide baselines.
findings.confounds: Cause (document truncation) inferred from vectors/doc, not logged; different loaders or revisions possible; one dataset (SciFact, 300 queries); both runs are fp32-like by norm fingerprint.
findings.practical_implication: Show the two entries as different operating points of one set of weights (state the document length), report absolute bytes per document next to the ratio, and do not compare the two retention columns as if they were independent models.
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed: Recomputed from the raw wide JSON files. Baseline ndcg@10 is 0.6464 (colbert-ir) vs 0.6917 (lightonai), a gap of 0.0453. Vectors/doc are 157.37 vs 235.65 and float32 bytes/doc are 80,572 vs 120,654. Check-pair vectors/doc max is 173 vs 276. int4(mean) compression is 7.7575 for both, at 10,386 vs 15,553 bytes/doc. All of this matches the claim. Both runs use the same 5,183 docs and 300 queries, the same T4 environment, and the same 12 check pairs. The revision and dtype fields are null for both. Paired retention on ndcg@10 covers 54 shared labels, not 53; there may be a baseline-like row or an exclusion in the original count. The difference (colbert-ir minus lightonai) has mean -0.0112, sd 0.0175, 40 down, 12 up, 2 ties, and Wilcoxon p = 3.7e-5. Mean absolute ndcg@10 difference is -0.0463. By group, codec-only rows (7) differ by +0.0004, so there is no retention gap without token pruning. Token-pruning groups differ by -0.007 to -0.019 (token+codec 12 rows: -0.019; token+dim+codec 18 rows: -0.011; dim 2 rows: -0.011). Mean query-bootstrap CI width on retention is about 0.063. The hub total is 3,820,082 downloads, colbert-ir has 1,614,280 (42.3%), and it is the top entry among 1,009 listed. lightonai has 7,371.
verdict.issues:
1. The 'same checkpoint' premise is not verified by the data. Revision is null for both, and the weights, tokenizer and config could differ. The 157 vs 236 vector gap and the 4.5-point gap show only that the two entries behave differently in this pipeline.
2. The truncation cause is an inference, as the claim says. The data show a lower ceiling (max 173 vs 276) but no doc_maxlen is logged.
3. The retention gap is small (about 1.1 points) against a per-row CI width of about 0.06. The Wilcoxon p-value treats 54 nested, highly correlated pipelines as independent, so p < 0.001 overstates the evidence. Row-level direction is consistent, but the effect is small and the pairing shares the same 300 queries.
4. The retention gap is concentrated in token-pruning pipelines (-0.007 to -0.019) and absent in codec-only rows (+0.0004). Retention is relative to each model's own baseline, and token-pruning pipelines compress different token counts. It is therefore not a general compression-quality difference. The number of vectors, not the codec, plausibly drives it.
5. It rests on one dataset (SciFact) and one pair, with no multiple-comparison context. The 'most downloaded' and 42% figures are 30-day snapshot counts.
6. The published ColBERTv2 SciFact figure (about 0.693) is recalled, not verified.
verdict.corrected_claim: On SciFact (5,183 docs, 300 queries), colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 has an ndcg@10 baseline of 0.646 against 0.692 for lightonai/colbertv2.0, a 4.5-point gap. It produces about 157 vs 236 vectors per document, so float32 bytes/doc are about 1.5x lower. Check-pair maximum vectors/doc is 173 vs 276. The cap is consistent with shorter document truncation, but this is inferred and not logged. Whether the two share identical weights is unverified, because revisions are null. Retention is equal for codec-only pipelines (+0.0004 over 7 rows), and about 1.1 points lower for colbert-ir over 54 shared pipelines, mainly in token-pruning ones. That is 40 down, 12 up, 2 ties. The effect is small relative to per-row CI width (about 0.06), and the Wilcoxon p-value (3.7e-5) ignores dependence between nested pipelines. colbert-ir has 42% of the listed 30-day downloads (1.61M of 3.82M). Exploratory, single dataset, single pair.

findings.title: Merged and ported copies are replicates; a noise floor for sibling comparisons
findings.claim: Merged-adapter copies reproduce the original's retention profile to a mean absolute difference of about 0.003 (cos 0.99999 per the registry), so they are replicates, not independent models; differences below about 0.005 between siblings are noise, while HF ports differ by 0.01 to 0.02 in both retention and baseline (port, fp16 and processor confounded).
findings.evidence: Mean abs retention difference over 54 shared pipelines (DocVQA/InfoVQA): tsystems colqwen2.5-3b vs -merged 0.0033/0.0014 (InfoVQA baselines equal to 16 digits); colpali-v1.2 vs -merged 0.0043/0.0030; colpali-v1.2 vs -hf 0.0095/0.0220 (baseline gaps 0.021/0.013); colpali-v1.3 vs -hf 0.0177/0.0064 (0.015/0.001); Metric-AI vs tsystems 3b (distinct checkpoints with the same name) 0.0316/0.0080; median over all pairs 0.0347/0.0294 (5th percentile 0.0138/0.0077). Different models can also coincide: Tomoro-8b and Vultron-Core DocVQA baselines are both 0.656 (coincidence at the 5th digit). The registry marks vidore/colSmol-256M and vidore/colqwen2-v1.0 as measured but they have no entry in measured.json; the campaign's batch-11 lightonai/colbertv2.0 results were overwritten by colbert-ir (same short name).
findings.method: All pairwise mean absolute differences of retention over shared labels, per dataset (669+669+91 pairs), then named sibling pairs.
findings.confounds: No per-query vectors, so replicate status of merged copies rests on the registry's cosine statement and on retention agreement; ports confound fp16, processor and weights; nearest-neighbour pairs among unrelated models use only 32 shared labels for newer runs.
findings.practical_implication: Count merged copies once in any family statistic, treat sibling retention gaps under about 0.005 as noise, and key results by full model id (short names collide).
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed: Rebuilt from measured.json (54 shared labels). Mean abs retention diff, DocVQA/InfoVQA: tsystems colqwen2.5-3b vs -merged 0.0033/0.0014 (InfoVQA baselines equal 0.9326); colpali-v1.2 vs -merged 0.0043/0.0030; v1.2 vs -hf 0.0095/0.0220 (baseline gaps -0.021/-0.013); v1.3 vs -hf 0.0177/0.0064 (-0.015/-0.001); Metric-AI vs tsystems 0.0316/0.0080. All match the claim. Extras: colpali-v1.2 vs v1.3 0.036/0.056; v1.1 vs v1.2 0.034/0.032; Tomoro 4b vs 8b 0.021/0.010 (64 labels). All-pairs (>=20 shared labels, 669 pairs each): median 0.0243 DocVQA, 0.0166 InfoVQA, 5th pct 0.0083/0.0044 (the claim's median 0.0347/0.0294 and 5th pct 0.0138/0.0077 do not reproduce with my filter; the claim's pair selection differs). Tomoro-8b and Vultron-Core DocVQA baselines both 0.656 confirmed. Merged-pair differences are not uniform: for colpali-v1.2 merged, rows with retention>0.98 differ by 0.0021 on average, rows with retention<0.9 by 0.0049, max 0.0216 (hierarchical_merge(0.33) > project(16) > binary). Median query-bootstrap CI half-width of those rows is 0.0154, 3x larger than the mean merged gap.
verdict.issues: 1) Only two true merged-vs-original pairs have shared labels (tsystems, colpali-v1.2); colpali-v1.3-merged has zero shared labels with colpali-v1.3, and cos 0.99999 in the registry is for vidore/colqwen2-v1.0-merged on 6 pages, not these pairs. So 'replicates' rests on n=2 pairs plus an extrapolated cosine. 2) The 0.005 noise floor is not a usable threshold: the mean is dragged down by many near-1 rows (float16, int8, mild codecs; about 60 percent of rows are >0.98 and agree to ~0.001-0.003 for any model), and unrelated models also fall under 0.005 (InfoVQA: 54 of 669 pairs; e.g. EVIE-4.5B vs webAI-ColVec1.1-8b 0.0023, EvoQwen vs colqwen3.5 0.0024 on 32-37 shared labels, all easy rows). A mean below 0.005 therefore does not identify siblings. Max single-pipeline merged gap is 0.011 to 0.022, so the floor for aggressive pipelines is about 0.01-0.02, comparable to the CI half-width. 3) Port differences of 0.01-0.02 are consistent with the claim but confound fp16, processor and weights, as noted; sign is inconsistent (v1.2-hf DocVQA mean signed diff 0.0001, absolute 0.0095), indicating pipeline-specific reshuffling rather than a bias. 4) The all-pairs median and 5th percentile quoted do not reproduce exactly; depend on label-count filter. 5) Post-hoc, about 10 named pairs plus all-pairs; no formal test.
verdict.corrected_claim: For the two merged/original pairs that share pipelines (tsystems colqwen2.5-3b, colpali-v1.2), mean abs retention difference over 54 pipelines is 0.001 to 0.004, driven by many near-1 rows; per-pipeline gaps reach 0.011 to 0.022 on aggressive pipelines, similar to query-bootstrap CI half-widths (~0.015). These are consistent with replicates but not shown to be (registry cosine 0.99999 is a 6-page check on a different checkpoint). A mean difference under 0.005 does not by itself indicate siblings, since unrelated models reach 0.002 to 0.003 on small sets of shared easy labels. HF ports differ by about 0.006 to 0.022 in mean absolute retention and 0.001 to 0.021 in baseline, with fp16, processor and weights confounded. Weak, exploratory.

findings.title: Metric, precision and compression denominator are not uniform across catalogue rows
findings.claim: Text rows use ndcg@10 retention while image rows use ndcg@5 (and the SciFact selection study uses ndcg@5); text 'auto' dtype hides that at least 3 of 14 text models ran in reduced precision; compression is always vs float32, which no float32 encoding exists for 13 of 55 models; nominal merge labels are not achieved for SmolVLM models.
findings.evidence: measured.json baseline equals the wide ndcg@10 for all 14 campaign text records and ndcg@5 for all 66 image records; over 746 text rows ndcg@10 retention exceeds ndcg@5 by 0.0076 mean (range -0.018 to +0.038), and 27 of 126 rows passing 0.99 under either metric change verdict (21 of 340 at 0.95). Unit-norm-error fingerprint: 23/23 float32 runs <= 1.8e-7, 10/12 float16 runs 3e-4 to 6e-4; text: mxbai-colbert-large-v1 5.8e-4 (fp16-like), jina-colbert-v2 4.3e-3 and LFM2.5-ColBERT-350M 4.2e-3 (bf16-like), LFM2-ColBERT-350M 1.2e-7 (fp32), so a sibling pair differs in precision. Compression recomputed as float32 bytes / bytes matches to 2e-16 for all 4,520 rows, so arithmetic is right, but ratios are about 2x the saving vs fp16 storage for the 13 float16-inference models. hierarchical_merge(0.1) keeps 21% (colSmol-500M) and 27% (colsmolvlm) of vectors, giving 4.7x and 3.7x rather than 10x. Row sets differ by model (49/54/60/64/69/74 rows; 259 distinct labels, none common to all).
findings.method: Compare measured.json baseline and retention with the four wide metrics; recompute compression and bytes from vectors x dim x bits; norm-error fingerprint calibrated on the 35 image runs with recorded dtype; actual/nominal vectors ratio for merge rows.
findings.confounds: The fingerprint has false negatives (2 of 12 float16 runs show 1.2e-7), so precision for fp32-like text models is not proven; metric choice is documented per record but not in the user-facing table; modality and metric are confounded with dataset.
findings.practical_implication: State the metric and inference dtype beside every retention and compression number, add compression vs the stored baseline dtype, and avoid cross-modality retention comparisons.
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed: Recomputed from raw files with my own scripts. (1) Metric: measured.json baselines match wide ndcg@10 for 14/14 text records and ndcg@5 for 66/66 image records, within 6e-5 because measured.json is rounded to 4 dp. Text retention matches ndcg@10 in all 746 rows. Selection-study JSONs (59 files) all say metric ndcg@5, including the 5 SciFact ones. (2) Over 746 text rows, ndcg@10 retention minus ndcg@5 retention has mean +0.00758, min -0.0181, max +0.0381. Verdict flips: 27 of 126 rows passing 0.99 under either metric, and 21 of 340 at 0.95. Both match the claim. (3) Precision: all 14 text records have dtype None, and the wide baseline encoder dtype is null. Unit-norm error: 11 of 14 are about 1.2e-7, mxbai-colbert-large 5.8e-4 (fp16-like), jina-colbert-v2 4.3e-3 and LFM2.5 4.2e-3 (bf16-like), LFM2 1.2e-7. That gives 3 of 14 reduced-precision. Image runs: 23 float32 runs have norm error <=1.8e-7; of 14 float16 runs, 10 are 3e-4 to 6e-4, 2 show 1.2e-7 (EvoQwen, colnomic-7b), 2 have no value. (4) Compression: float32 bytes / bytes matches recorded compression_vs_float32 to a max relative error of 2.2e-16 over all 4,520 wide rows. Registry evidence text mentions float16 for 13 of the 55 measured models (run.json spec dtype=float16 gives 14 image runs). (5) hierarchical_merge(0.1): colSmol-500M keeps 19.6% and 22.9% of vectors (mean 21.3%) with compression 5.10x and 4.36x (mean 4.7x). colsmolvlm keeps 25.7% and 28.5% (mean 27.1%) with 3.90x and 3.51x (mean 3.7x). Every other model sits at 0.100 to 0.114 (colpali 0.107, colqwen2/2.5 0.114). (6) Row sets in measured.json: 54 rows for 62 model-dataset entries, 60 for 7, 64 for 12, 69 for 6, 74 for 6, 49 for 2. That is 259 distinct labels with 0 common to all, as claimed. Wide files alone give 172 labels and 32 common, so the basis matters.
verdict.issues: 1. The "at least 3 of 14 text models reduced precision" rests on a norm-error fingerprint that the claim itself says has false negatives (2 of 12 float16 runs read fp32-like). The 3 is a lower bound, and the other 11 are unproven fp32. The sibling pair LFM2 (fp32-like) vs LFM2.5 (bf16-like) is the strongest case; there is no recorded dtype to confirm it. 2. The "13 vs 14 float16 models" count depends on the source. The registry evidence gives 13 and run.json spec dtype gives 14; the claim's 13 is not wrong but is not the only count. Text models that ran in bf16 or fp16 are not in the 13. 3. The 126 and 340 denominators are rows passing under either metric, so the 27/126 and 21/340 flip shares are conditional on that selection. They are not shares of all text rows. The rows are heavily correlated (same queries and same model), and the retention CIs are query-bootstrap only. 4. The flips are a real metric-definition effect, but it is a mean shift of under 0.01, so it matters only for rows near the threshold. The metric difference is confounded with dataset (SciFact vs ViDoRe) and modality. 5. Merge shortfall: it is not specific to SmolVLM, since all models land at 0.100 to 0.114 of nominal, but only the two SmolVLM models are far off (about 2x). Only 2 models (4 dataset runs) back this. The mechanism was not verified. 6. The claim that the arithmetic is right but the denominator is float32 is correct, and the ~2x overstatement versus fp16 storage holds only for models whose true baseline is fp16, as the claim says.
verdict.corrected_claim: The catalogue mixes metrics and denominators. Text rows use ndcg@10 retention and image rows use ndcg@5, while all selection-rule studies, including 5 SciFact ones, use ndcg@5. Switching metric on SciFact rows shifts retention by +0.0076 on average (range -0.018 to +0.038) and changes the pass/fail verdict for 27 of the 126 rows that pass 0.99 under either metric (21 of the 340 rows that pass 0.95 under either). At least 3 of 14 text models (mxbai-colbert-large, jina-colbert-v2, LFM2.5-ColBERT) show a reduced-precision fingerprint, and the registry notes float16 inference for 13 of the 55 models (run.json shows 14 float16 specs). The text dtype is not recorded, so the fingerprint is the only evidence, and it has known false negatives. Compression is float32 bytes divided by stored bytes, computed exactly. For models whose true baseline is fp16, the quoted ratios are about 2x the saving versus fp16 storage. hierarchical_merge(0.1) keeps 10.0 to 11.4% of vectors for most models, but 21% for colSmol-500M and 27% for colsmolvlm, giving 4.7x and 3.7x. Row sets differ by model: 259 distinct labels in measured.json, none common to all 55 models. This is exploratory and post-hoc.
