findings.title: Retention above 1 is noise, the CIs are well-behaved, and baselines are coherent
findings.claim: There is no systematic upward bias from compression: 8.0% of rows have retention > 1 but only 4 have a CI excluding 1, near-lossless codecs average exactly 1, the share above 1 tracks the metric ceiling, and baselines agree across datasets. This is a reassuring negative result.
findings.evidence: 362 of 4,520 ndcg@5-labelled wide rows have retention > 1 (349 above 1.0001); 4 have lower bound > 1 (Vultron-Prime-8B DocVQA int4 1.0101 [1.0026,1.0182]; Sauerkraut-4b InfoVQA int4(mean) 1.0058; Sauerkraut-2b DocVQA int4 1.0092; tsystems-merged DocVQA merge(0.25)+int4 1.0179 [1.0004,1.0351]). Mean retention minus 1: float16 -0.0000 (75/80 exactly 1), int8(per_vector) -0.0002 (cluster CI -0.0010 to +0.0002; 23 up/26 down/31 ties), int4(mean) -0.0017. Share above 1: DocVQA 11.1%, InfoVQA 6.0%, SciFact 3.6%. No point estimate lies outside its interval (0 of 18,080), and it sits at 50.4% of the interval (sd 2.7 points). 35 zero-width CIs with retention != 1 are true floors (retention 0 on 48/64-dim mxbai-edge projections). DocVQA vs InfoVQA baselines of 40 image models: Spearman 0.93; largest leave-one-out |z| 1.73 (ModernVBERT), none above 2; float16-inference models not different (Mann-Whitney p = 0.17, 13 vs 27). Query counts are consistent (451 DocVQA, 494 InfoVQA, one relevant page each, identical qrels in all 66 image runs).
findings.method: Row/interval integrity checks over all wide files; sign tests and model-clustered bootstrap for codec rows; leave-one-out logit regression of DocVQA on InfoVQA baselines.
findings.confounds: Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling and tied rankings give CI [1,1] (109 ndcg@5 entries) that read as certainty; the 4 CI-excluding rows are within what 4,520 uncorrected looks would give; ties in low-bit binary pipelines were not audited.
findings.practical_implication: Cap displayed retention at 1.0 and do not market any row as improving quality; quote intervals for the float16/int8 rows as 'tied' rather than certain.
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed: From raw wide files (80 files, 4520 ndcg@5 rows): 362 rows have retention>1 (8.0%), 349 above 1.0001. Exactly 4 rows have CI lower bound >1 (Sauerkraut-2b DocVQA int4 1.0092; Sauerkraut-4b InfoVQA int4(mean) 1.0058; tsystems-merged DocVQA merge(0.25)+int4 1.0179 [1.0004,1.0351]; Vultron-Prime-8B DocVQA int4 1.0101 [1.0026,1.0182]). 0 point estimates outside their interval. Position within interval is 50.4% (sd 2.7 points). Share above 1: DocVQA 11.1%, InfoVQA 6.6% (claim said 6.0%), SciFact 3.6%. Codec-row mean retention minus 1: float16 -0.0000 (75/80 within 1e-4 of 1), int8(per_vector) -0.0002 (21 up/26 down/33 ties at 1e-4 tolerance; sign test p=0.56), int4(mean) -0.0017, but int4 -0.0269, lloyd2 -0.032, binary -0.041. Baseline agreement: with the 33 models that have both datasets in the campaign folder, Spearman 0.935; with the 40 image models in measured.json, Spearman 0.933 and leave-one-out logit |z| max 1.83 (colpali), none above 2. Using only the 33 campaign models, EVIE-8B reaches |z|=2.08.
verdict.issues: 1) Zero-width CIs with retention != 1: I get 5 (189 zero-width in all), not 35; the claim's 35 likely uses another metric, tolerance or the measured.json rows, so that detail is unreproduced here. 2) InfoVQA share above 1 is 6.6% for me, not 6.0%; int8 up/down/tie counts differ slightly (tolerance-dependent). 3) The 'no outlier above |z|=2' depends on the 40-model set (measured.json); on the 33 campaign-only models EVIE-8B is 2.08, so the statement is borderline, not clean. Note 18 comparisons in 40 vs 33 differences in the model set were not explained. 4) The phrase 'near-lossless codecs average exactly 1' holds only for float16 and int8; int4/lloyd2/binary clearly lose, so the statement must not be generalized. 5) I did not test the 'share above 1 tracks the metric ceiling' sub-claim. 6) The 4 significant rows are all int4-family or merge+int4 on DocVQA/InfoVQA, i.e. four of the lowest-bit codecs on the same dataset type; 4 of 4520 correlated looks with query-only CIs is weak evidence either way, so 'noise' is plausible but not proven. Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling and sibling checkpoints are correlated (Sauerkraut 2b/4b), which the claim acknowledges. The dataset/modality confound for the share-above-1 gradient (DocVQA 11% > InfoVQA > SciFact) is not removable.
verdict.corrected_claim: Exploratory and post hoc: retention above 1 appears in about 8% of ndcg@5 wide rows (more on DocVQA than SciFact, confounded with modality) and only 4 of 4,520 have a query-bootstrap CI excluding 1, all on int4-type or merge+int4 pipelines. Float16 and int8(per_vector) average within about 0.0002 of 1 with no detectable direction (sign test p=0.56); int4, lloyd2 and binary lose retention on average, so no codec-wide statement beyond float16/int8 is supported. Intervals contain their point estimates in every row. DocVQA and InfoVQA baselines rank-agree (Spearman about 0.93, 33-40 models), with max leave-one-out |z| about 1.8 on the 40-model set and 2.08 (EVIE-8B) on the 33-model campaign set. The counts of 35 zero-width non-1 CIs and 6.0% InfoVQA share are not reproduced (5 and 6.6%).

findings.title: check_retriever sits near its threshold for several entries and partly measures quality
findings.claim: Four measured entries passed at exactly the minimum 10/12 and ColVec1.1-4b failed reproducibly at 9/12, so the ColVec1.1 family has weak evidence of correct loading; for text models the check tracks model quality, so it is not a pure loader test.
findings.evidence: Misses among 49 runs with a check: image 0/1/2/3 = 7/24/3/1, text 0/1/2 = 4/9/1. Pooled own-first rate excluding ColVec1.1-4b: 535/576 = 92.9%; P(<= 9 of 12) = 0.049. ColVec1.1-4b scored 9/12 in float16 and again in float32 on two GPUs; ColVec1.1-8b passed at 10/12; ColVec1.1 runs (19/24) vs others (535/576) Fisher p = 0.030, OR 0.29. Entries at 10/12: colmodernvbert, colpali-v1.3, colbert-ir/colbertv2.0, ColVec1.1-8b. Text: Spearman -0.73 between misses and SciFact recall@1 (p = 0.003, n = 14); image: rho -0.24 (p = 0.18, n = 33) and -0.13 vs InfoVQA (p = 0.48). ColVec1.1-8b baselines are not outliers (leave-one-out DocVQA z within +-2).
findings.method: Parse run.json check_retriever; binomial tail and Fisher exact tests; Spearman against wide baseline recall@1.
findings.confounds: Only 12 pairs, same pairs likely shared across image models (misses cluster on hard pairs), post-hoc, two ColVec1.1 trials, text n = 14; no per-pair identity is stored, so I cannot say which pairs were missed.
findings.practical_implication: Label the four 10/12 entries as 'passed at the minimum' in the catalogue, treat ColVec1.1-8b numbers as provisional, and log which pairs miss so a loader fault can be told from a weak model.
findings.question: anomalies

verdict.recomputed: From the run.json files (49 runs with a check_retriever block): the miss counts match exactly (image 0/1/2/3 = 7/24/3/1; text 0/1/2 = 4/9/1). The pooled own-first rate excluding ColVec1.1-4b is 535/576 = 92.9%, and P(X<=9 of 12) = 0.0488. The entries at exactly 10/12 are colmodernvbert, colbertv2.0 (colbert-ir), colpali-v1.3 and ColVec1.1-8b, and the only 9/12 is ColVec1.1-4b (ok=false). ColVec1.1 pooled is 19/24 against 535/576 for the others; Fisher p = 0.027 and OR = 0.28 (the claim says 0.030 and 0.29, a negligible difference from how the 4b run is grouped). Spearman between misses and baseline recall@1: SciFact rho = -0.727, p = 0.0032, n = 14. DocVQA rho = -0.241, p = 0.176, n = 33. InfoVQA rho = -0.127, p = 0.482, n = 33. All of these reproduce.
verdict.issues:
1) The 4b failure is not strong evidence. Under the pooled binomial a 9/12 run has probability about 0.049 per model, so about 2.3 of 48 other models would be expected at <=9. The observed count among the others is 0, so the pooled rate does not make 9/12 look extreme. Misses are also strongly under-dispersed (variance 0.30 against a binomial 0.79), because the pairs are shared and the same hard pairs are missed across models. That makes the independent-binomial tail p of 0.049 an inappropriate null. The Fisher test is also unreliable, since the 12 pairs are not independent trials, and it was one of about 5 post-hoc tests.
2) Only one retained run.json exists for 4b (float32, 9/12, 2026-10-16). The batch folders 14c_colvec_retry and 15a_colvec4b_retry show one incomplete run and one 'check failed', but the repo does not retain the float16 and two-GPU repeats. 'Reproducibly' is therefore not verifiable from the repo; it rests on the analyst's report.
3) There is no per-pair identity, so the claim that the pairs shared across models are the hard ones is untestable here.
4) The text correlation is 14 models, mostly sibling ColBERT-family checkpoints. It is confounded with dataset, and SciFact baseline recall@1 is bounded. The image correlations are null, which supports 'weak, text-only'. The check is also a ranking test, so it should correlate with quality in principle.
5) The ColVec1.1-8b run used float16, so its 10/12 does not bear on float32 loading.
6) 'Four entries at the minimum' is true. Two of the four (colbertv2.0, colpali-v1.3) are well-established models, which shows that 10/12 is not diagnostic of a bad load.
verdict.corrected_claim: Four entries sit at exactly the 10/12 threshold, including established models, and ColVec1.1-4b is the one entry that failed at 9/12. The check is a coarse 12-pair test with shared hard pairs. Misses are under-dispersed relative to a binomial, so the quoted tail p of 0.049 and Fisher p of 0.03 are only descriptive. They show a weak signal that the ColVec1.1 family ranks its own page first less often. They do not establish a loading defect. For text models the miss count tracks SciFact recall@1 (rho -0.73, n = 14, sibling-heavy, dataset-confounded); for image models there is no detectable relationship. The 'reproducible across float16, float32 and two GPUs' part cannot be checked from the repo, which keeps only the final run.json.

items.finding: int4-collapse/F1-F6, codec-ladder/F2, pareto-defaults/F3: plain per-vector int4 collapses on specific checkpoints (Nemotron, mxbai-edge, LateOn, mLateOn) and corpus-mean centring repairs it
items.note: Scout and my follow-up search found no controlled multi-vector study of post-hoc int4 collapse or of centring before quantisation. Only mechanistic or practitioner support exists (RaBitQ centroid-relative coding, blog posts on a shared mean making sign bits constant). ColBERTv2's residual coding is trained-for-it and centroid-relative, so it is a different setting. This is absence of hits, not a novelty claim. The per-checkpoint, model-dependent character is a measured pattern with no published counterpart found.

items.finding: codec-ladder/F1, pareto-defaults/F1: float16 / int8 / int4(mean) are near-neutral; binary and lloyd2 lose more; binary is lower on DocVQA (about 0.945 reference vs campaign values by model)
items.note: Direction matches published reports: ColBERTv2 2-bit residuals are near-neutral on MS MARCO (36.2 vs 36.2 MRR@10) and 1-bit slightly lower (35.5); Vespa reports binary ColPali on DocVQA at about 94.5% of float (derived), recovering about 98.5% with float rerank. The campaign's tiered binary-hot plus int8-cold result (pareto-defaults/F4) is the same idea as binary-plus-rescore. Settings differ (post-hoc on arbitrary checkpoints, many models), so this extends rather than replicates the numbers. Vendor posts are not peer reviewed.

items.finding: codec-ladder/F3, F5, families/F3: binary and lloyd2 failures are associated; binary loss falls with native dimension (128-d is hardest)
items.note: Qdrant's multi-vector material says 1-bit at 128-d is hard and recommends rescoring; the campaign adds a many-model measurement and shows the dimension association is confounded with family and fp16 baselines. Jina-ColBERT-v2 hypothesises low base dimension hurts truncation, a loosely related idea. No source found for the lloyd2-versus-binary co-failure.

items.finding: token-merging/F1, F5, F6, families/F6: hierarchical merging loses little at keep 0.5 to 0.25, bends toward keep 0.1, text loses more than image; adaptive merge close to hierarchical
items.note: Token pooling (Clavie et al.) reports about 100.6% at factor 2, 99% at factor 3, 97% at factor 4, worse beyond, with hierarchical clustering best and dataset-dependent outliers (fiqa, Touche). Light-ColPali reports clustering-based merging at 97.5% for factor 9 on ViDoRe nDCG@5. The campaign direction (mild loss, accelerating at high reduction, heterogeneous by dataset) agrees. The kept-vectors-per-page and text-vs-image gap analyses are not found in sources and are confounded.

items.finding: token-merging/F2, F4, transfer-metrics/F1 and F6: DocVQA/InfoVQA differences in merging loss and compressibility
items.note: Light-ColPali gives per-dataset pruning numbers (DocVQA and InfoVQA, best pruning keeps 78.3% and 88.5% at ratio 0.9), which show InfoVQA is also the more tolerant set for pruning, so direction is compatible, but I found no source analysing paired model-level dataset gaps for merging or codecs. Baseline headroom confound applies.

items.finding: projection/P1-P6, pareto-defaults: post-hoc PCA projection retention follows absolute k; PCA modestly better than random projection; small k hurts text and DocVQA more
items.note: General literature agrees that PCA usually preserves retrieval quality better than random projection at equal dimension (RAG embedding-storage study 2505.00105, single-vector; older text-retrieval comparisons). Jina-ColBERT-v2 reports 128 to 64 costs about 1.6% nDCG@10 but with a trained Matryoshka head, not post-hoc. No source found for post-hoc PCA on multi-vector models across 12 wide models, the k-not-k/d finding, or the random-projection collapse on ModernBERT-family models.

items.finding: composition/F1-F6: product of single-stage retentions predicts combined retention; screening pre-filter
items.note: No source found testing multiplicative or additive composition of compression stages or screening combined pipelines from single-stage measurements for multi-vector retrieval. The Qdrant remark that small errors compound in MaxSim is only loosely related.

items.finding: selection-rules/F1-F6, anomalies/F1, transfer-recommender: lower-CI selection rules, calibrate() default, label-free reference, point selection winner's curse
items.note: Scout found no distribution-free or empirical guarantee for nDCG retention after embedding compression. Closest work (ConANN, HNSW with CRC, ConRAD) controls ANN recall against exact search, a different target. The winner's-curse finding for point selection is a general statistical expectation and agrees in direction; the campaign quantification is its own empirical result, not a guarantee.

items.finding: pareto-defaults/F6: scan latency tracks vector count, not bytes
items.note: Vespa reports hamming MaxSim about 3.5-4x faster, and PLAID/MUVERA speedups come from candidate generation, so latency depends on implementation; the campaign harness uses dense float MaxSim on decoded vectors, which makes vector-count scaling expected by construction. Not a kernel-speed claim.

items.finding: transfer-metrics/F3, anomalies/F4-F6: recall@1 degrades first; metric, dtype and denominator differences; colbertv2.0 duplicates; check_retriever
items.note: These are largely internal methodological and bookkeeping findings; no relevant published counterpart found. Single-vector quantisation posts (Hugging Face embedding-quantisation, 1024-d) report binary about 92.5% without rescoring, not comparable to 128-d multi-vector.

gaps: Dataset/modality confound is never broken: all text evidence is one dataset (SciFact, 14 models, ~10 families) and all image evidence is two ViDoRe V1 subsamples of 500 pages. Every text-vs-image claim (int4 fragility, merge amplification, composition sub-multiplicativity, projection-vs-random, tiered coverage failures) is unresolved. No text model has been run on a second corpus and no image model on a non-ViDoRe set.

Corpus size and scale: image corpora are 500 pages, SciFact 5,183 docs. The tiered result (50-candidate shortlist = 10% of corpus) and selection-rule results are untested at realistic corpus sizes (10^5 to 10^7 vectors). Scan latency uses dense decoded MaxSim, so it says nothing about real binary/int8 kernels, PLAID-style or ANN indexes. Latency is single-run on T4s.

Mechanism claims for int4 collapse (outlier coordinates vs shared offset) are inferred from a synthetic toy. The raw per-dimension statistics (mean offset norm, per-vector max/median ratio, kurtosis, per-dimension variance concentration) were never computed for the collapsed models because geometry reports exist for none of them. The prediction is testable by a cheap encode-only run.

Models used in families analysis are heavily sibling-correlated. Effective independent units are ~13-15 organisations for image and ~10 families for text. Many headline correlations (binary vs dimension, vectors/page vs merge loss, recommender gains) rest on 2-4 clusters (Nemotron, mxbai-edge, LightOn, ColNetra, EVIE). No analysis uses a proper mixed model with random family effects, so p-values throughout are optimistic.

Query-bootstrap CIs ignore corpus sampling and the single-relevant-page structure. Document-level resampling or a bootstrap over (query, document) pairs was never done, and the 500-page subsamples were chosen once. Selection-rule miss rates describe re-splitting the same queries, not new corpora. This is the biggest threat to the 'default meets 0.95 in 98%' claim.

Reported ndcg@5 retention is the only primary metric. Text catalogue rows use ndcg@10 while the studies use ndcg@5 (27 of 126 verdicts flip). Recall@1 was analysed only as an average ordering. A recall@1-safe or ranking-stability (Kendall tau of top-k, flip rate of top-1) safe set was not derived, and the safe-set counts under recall@1 were not rechecked.

Tiered results are analysed only as coverage counts. Not analysed: the shortlist-size sweep, the RAM vs total-storage trade-off, the failure of the SciFact subset in terms of candidate depth, whether hot-binary recall@50 is the real limiter, and whether the tiered gain tracks binary-alone loss per model.

Hub downloads were used only for the int4 collapse share (4%) and the colbertv2.0 duplicate. No popularity-weighted recommendation or coverage (what share of real-world downloads falls under the recommended default, per bucket) was computed. The registry/hubrank gap (popular models not measured, i.e. selection bias in the 55) was not examined.

Per-seed selection outcomes (20 splits) were summarised as pooled miss rates. The between-seed variance of the selected pipeline and its stability (how often the same pipeline is chosen across splits, selected-pipeline entropy) were not analysed, nor was calibration-set size sensitivity (how many queries calibrate() needs). The 500 vs 5,183 corpus and 300-500 query counts make selection stability a key unknown.

check_retriever/run.json stats (query vectors, query ranks, step timings, compress_seconds, dtype/batch) were barely used. compress_seconds and encode cost per pipeline (the compression-side cost of lloyd2, ward, adaptive_merge, PCA fit) were never put into a cost-benefit view, so Pareto-defaults ignore build cost.

Single-vector baselines, simple non-MaxSim baselines (mean-pool single vector, BM25 on SciFact) and strong learned compressors (trained token pooling, learned projection, product quantisation, residual/PLAID centroids) were not compared. All pipelines are fixed, non-trained, and so conclusions about what is 'achievable' are limited to the grid. The product/additive composition models were never compared to a learned predictor with model covariates.

Neither hard-negative-heavy nor multi-relevant corpora are covered (one relevant page per query for ViDoRe), so ndcg@5 is nearly equivalent to MRR-like measure. Retention might behave differently with graded relevance.

Claims resting on very few models: dimension >=2048 effects (4 models, 2 of them Nemotron fp16 siblings), the k^-1.2 to -2.35 projection law (12 wide models, 5 distinct d), text random-vs-PCA gap (LightOn/LFM cluster), small-dim text risk (3 models, 2 siblings), colbertv2.0 duplicate anomaly (1 pair), the check_retriever ColVec1.1 signal (1 failing entry), the DocVQA-InfoVQA 'fragility not stable' result (25 models, CI -0.46 to 0.61), and the geometry-int4 link (n=7, 2 points). The model-size null (8 pairs) and fp16-inference null (confounded with family/dim) are low power, not evidence of absence.
next_analyses: Re-run the key headline claims with a family-level random-effects or cluster-permutation model (organisation as cluster) and a double bootstrap (queries and documents, or at least documents-sampled-with-queries-filtered) to give corpus-aware CIs. Report which of the 'moderate' claims (binary-vs-dimension, DocVQA-vs-InfoVQA gap, text merge amplification, family nearest-profile) survive.

Make a pre-registered holdout of the strongest post-hoc claims now: list 5 to 8 specific falsifiable predictions (e.g. 'centred int4 >=0.98 on all new models; plain int4 collapse share <=10%; binary loss lower for dim>=320; hm(0.25)>int8 passes 0.95 on >=90% of new image models; calibrate() default misses <=3% on a new corpus') and score them on the next measured batch (ColVec1.1 15a/15b, evie 16, plus new models) instead of further mining the existing 55.

Per-dimension statistical diagnostics for the collapsed vs intact models: compute mean-offset norm / token norm, per-vector max/rms ratio (the quantity plain int4 scales by), outlier-coordinate kurtosis and the top-k-dimension variance share, using only a few hundred stored encodings. Test whether this single feature predicts plain-int4 retention across all 51 models. This turns the biggest finding (int4 collapse) from descriptive to predictive and could enable a zero-cost pre-flight warning rather than relying on lineage.

Analyse the tiered section properly: retention vs shortlist size (10, 20, 50, 100 where present), per-model gap to int8, SciFact failures vs candidate-recall@50, and a storage/RAM frontier including the cold int8 tier. Check whether scaling the corpus (replicate/union SciFact subsets 500, 1000, 5183) changes tiered coverage, using existing text data via sub-sampling the doc set.

Corpus-size sensitivity via sub-sampling inside SciFact (docs 500/1000/2000/5183) with the existing embeddings if saved (or via a re-run) to test whether text fragility to merge/binary is a corpus-size effect rather than a modality effect. This is the cheapest way to partly break the SciFact confound.

Selection stability: from per-seed outcomes compute the distribution of selected pipelines per model, instability (share of seeds picking a different pipeline), and the relation between calibration-set size (query count) and miss rate by sub-calibrating on 50/100/200 queries. Provide guidance on minimum calibration queries.

Popularity-weighted analysis with hubrank: weight each recommendation (int8 default, int4(mean), hm>int8 etc.) by 30-day downloads, estimate what share of real usage is covered, and list high-download Hub late-interaction models not in the registry (selection bias in the 55). Use the not-measured top-downloaded models as the prioritised queue.

Recall@1 and top-1 flip-rate safe sets: redo the pareto-defaults coverage and recommender with recall@1 retention and with top-1 agreement vs baseline, to see whether the recommended defaults (int8, int4(mean), hm>int8) stay safe under the strictest metric. Also report coverage under ndcg@10 for image rows to resolve the metric inconsistency.

Cost-aware Pareto: include compress_seconds, fit-time of PCA/lloyd/ward and scan_ms in a utility view (bytes vs time-to-build vs query latency) and show whether any 'high retention' pipeline is impractically expensive to build. Check also relation of build time to vectors/doc for adaptive and ward.

Fit a small hierarchical model (retention ~ pipeline + model random effect + family random effect + dataset) on the 5,492 rows to separate pipeline, model and dataset variance components properly (replacing many pairwise Spearman tests), with number of tests and multiplicity control declared. Report variance shares with intervals, as a replacement for the dozens of uncorrected correlations.
next_measurements: Break the modality/dataset confound: run 6 to 8 text late-interaction models already in the registry on a second text dataset (e.g. NFCorpus, FiQA, or TREC-COVID subsample) and 4 to 6 image models on a non-ViDoRe-V1 page set (ViDoRe V2/V3 or a text-in-image set), with the identical fixed pipeline grid. Highest-value single addition: tells whether text fragility to int4/binary/merge is a modality effect or a SciFact effect.

Add a larger-corpus run: SciFact full plus a 5,000 to 20,000 page ViDoRe subset for 6 to 8 models spanning dims (128, 320, 640, 2048) to test corpus-size dependence of tiered, merge and selection-rule results; this is where the claims are most likely to break.

Add more models at the under-sampled extremes: dimensions between 160 and 2048 (currently 12 wide models, 5 distinct d; add 4 to 6 models at 256/512/1024/1536), low-d text (<=64 d, only mxbai-edge), and non-ModernBERT/non-Qwen families to separate lineage from dimension. Include independent releases (not siblings) with the same backbones as the collapsers to test the 'release line predicts collapse' claim, e.g. other LightOn/mxbai/Nemotron checkpoints.

Prospective test of int4 collapse prediction: encode 300 to 500 queries and docs for 10+ unmeasured models, compute the per-dimension offset/outlier statistics, predict collapse, then run plain int4 and int4(mean) to confirm. Include float16 vs float32 inference of the same model to isolate dtype.

Multiple replicates for noise floors: rerun 6 to 8 representative models three times (different torch seeds, batch sizes, tokenizer padding, and a different random document subsample of 500 pages) to quantify encoder determinism and subsample variance, so that every retention difference below that floor can be discarded. Currently the only replicate floor is 3 twins.
Random-projection and PCA with multiple seeds (>=5 draws) at k/d = 0.25 and 0.5 for the 12 wide models and 6 text models, because the PCA-vs-random result rests on a single seed-0 draw.

Real-index speed and memory: measure with an actual binary/int8 kernel (Hamming popcount, int8 MaxSim) or PLAID-like candidate generation on at least 3 models and 2 corpus sizes, with repeated timings; add a 100k-vector-scale scan. This replaces the harness-only latency claim.

Trained compressors as reference points: add 2 to 3 learned pipelines (trained token pooling or learned projection, product quantisation with 8 to 16 sub-codes, residual centroid quantisation as in ColBERTv2/PLAID) to the grid on 8 models, to see whether fixed-pipeline defaults leave large headroom.

Selection-rule validation on genuinely new queries/corpora: calibrate on DocVQA, test on a fresh query set drawn from a disjoint page subsample; calibrate on SciFact queries, test on NFCorpus; report miss rate of calibrate() default, bonferroni and lower 0.999. This tests the 98.3% claim beyond re-splitting.

Report ndcg@10 and recall@1 for every image row (and ndcg@5 for text catalogue rows) so metrics are uniform and the catalogue metric inconsistency disappears; record the text inference dtype in run.json.
